text:
🇸🇦Both Of Saudi Arabia's Chokepoints Are Now Live At Once...

Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery at 550,000 bpd, sits on the Gulf side, exposed to Hormuz. 

Jazan, 400,000 bpd, sits on the Red Sea side, exposed to Bab el-Mandeb. 

Both have taken repeated strikes since the war started. 

Lately the Houthis seized Mocha and pushed on to the Hanish Islands, closing in on Bab el-Mandeb itself and the UN's own envoy called it "a direct presence on the approaches to one of the world's most vital straits".

Saudi Arabia already built a workaround for Hormuz, the East-West pipeline that moves Gulf crude overland to Yanbu on the Red Sea. 

That pipeline only solves half the problem. 

Oil landing at Yanbu still has to go out through Bab el-Mandeb to reach Asia, which is most of Saudi's actual customers. 

If that strait closes too, the only route left is north through Suez and then all the way around Africa, a trip that goes from roughly 24 days to 54, and VLCCs can't even fit through Suez, so it also means smaller tankers and less volume moving per trip.

This is what "no spare capacity" actually looks like when you follow it past the refinery gate. 

It's not just that Ras Tanura and Jazan represent 28.5% of Saudi refining capacity sitting in the strike zone, it's that the export route Saudi built specifically to survive a Hormuz closure was designed around Bab el Mandeb staying open.

text:
MY 2 CENTS | 401(K), WALL STREET AND BITCOIN: WHY A BULL MARKET IS NOT ALWAYS GOOD NEWS FOR RETIREMENT — AND WHY BTC CHANGES PART OF THE EQUATION

1️⃣ To understand the apparent contradiction, we first need to understand what a 401(k) really is. It is not a traditional pension promising a predetermined income for life; it is a tax-advantaged defined-contribution account in which the employee, and often the employer through a matching contribution, accumulates capital that is invested in funds, equities, bonds or other instruments offered by the plan. In 2026 an employee can defer up to $24,500, with additional catch-up provisions for older workers. This structure has enormous advantages because automatic contributions, tax efficiency, employer matching and decades of compounding can create substantial wealth. But it also changes where the risk sits. In a traditional defined-benefit pension, the institution promises an income and assumes much of the investment and longevity risk. In a 401(k), the final outcome depends on how much the worker contributes, how markets perform, how much is lost to fees, when retirement begins and how withdrawals are managed. The 401(k) is therefore an extraordinarily powerful accumulation vehicle, but it is not a guaranteed pension cheque. That distinction is fundamental.

2️⃣ This is why saying that “a rising stock market is good for retirees” is only partly correct. It is certainly good for somebody who already owns a large portfolio and is benefiting from higher asset prices, but retirement economics changes according to where someone sits in the financial life cycle. A 30-year-old employee is still accumulating assets and buying future corporate earnings every month. When valuations become very expensive, each new contribution purchases less ownership than it would at lower prices, potentially reducing future expected returns. A 67-year-old retiree is in the opposite position: decades of accumulated financial assets are gradually being converted into spending. The same market level can therefore be excellent for the existing owner and less attractive for the new accumulator. Wall Street measures wealth primarily through market capitalization and asset prices; a retiree ultimately measures wealth through the quantity of housing, healthcare, energy, food, travel and time that those assets can finance. Those measures are related, but they are not identical. A record index is not automatically a record standard of living.

3️⃣ The distinction becomes even more important when accumulation turns into decumulation. During working life, a market crash can actually benefit a disciplined saver with secure employment because regular contributions purchase more shares at lower prices. Once retirement begins, the same decline can become destructive because the portfolio must finance withdrawals at precisely the moment asset prices are depressed. This is sequence-of-returns risk, one of the most important and least intuitive concepts in retirement finance. Two retirees can experience exactly the same long-term average return and still end up with dramatically different outcomes simply because their gains and losses occurred in a different order. Fidelity illustrates this with hypothetical portfolios beginning with the same capital and withdrawing the same amount: the portfolio experiencing poor returns early in retirement can eventually be exhausted, while the portfolio receiving strong returns first can remain worth millions decades later. The mathematics did not change; the sequence did. That is why the first years of retirement often matter much more than the average return printed in a thirty-year backtest.

4️⃣ This is also where the interests of the stock market and those of an individual pensioner can temporarily diverge. A central bank can ease financial conditions, lower interest rates and support higher equity valuations, which looks extremely positive on the screen of a 401(k) statement. Yet the same monetary environment can reduce yields on deposits and bonds, making it harder for retirees to generate conservative income without taking additional risk. If inflation remains elevated at the same time, the account balance may rise nominally while real purchasing power improves much less. The opposite problem appears when interest rates rise. Newly issued bonds begin offering more attractive income, which can ultimately help savers and retirees, but existing bonds and equities may experience painful valuation adjustments while markets reprice the new discount rate. There is therefore no monetary-policy setting that is universally positive for workers, savers, retirees and asset owners at the same time. The correct retirement question is not simply whether Wall Street is rising. It is whether the portfolio can convert accumulated wealth into sustainable real purchasing power under the monetary conditions prevailing when the money is actually required.

5️⃣ The scale of the 401(k) system makes this relationship between pensions and financial markets structurally important. At the end of the first quarter of 2026, Americans held approximately $9.9 trillion in 401(k) plans, while total employer-based defined-contribution assets stood at about $13.8 trillion. These are enormous pools of capital that receive fresh contributions with every payroll cycle. Millions of workers therefore provide markets with a recurring stream of long-term investment, much of it automatically directed toward mutual funds, target-date strategies and equities. This has been extremely beneficial for capital formation and for workers who have remained invested over long periods, but it can also create a subtle misconception: because pension contributions continuously support financial markets, the prosperity of financial markets can begin to look like proof of the prosperity of the pension system itself. It is not. The market can reach record highs while individual workers remain underfunded, while inflation erodes expected retirement consumption or while somebody retiring at the wrong point in the cycle faces severe sequence risk. Asset prices measure one component of retirement health, not the entire system.

6️⃣ The regulatory direction is now making this debate even more interesting. In May 2025, the U.S. Department of Labor withdrew its previous guidance telling fiduciaries to exercise “extreme care” before considering cryptocurrency options in 401(k) plans, restoring its historically neutral approach under ERISA. Then, in March 2026, the Department proposed a broader framework explaining how fiduciaries could evaluate alternative assets within defined-contribution plans, potentially expanding the investment universe available to more than 90 million Americans. The important point is what Washington did not say. The Department did not declare Bitcoin safe, superior or appropriate for every retirement account. Its position is essentially that fiduciaries should evaluate investment options through a prudent, context-specific process rather than having regulators pre-emptively pick winners and losers among asset classes. That distinction matters because Bitcoin is gradually moving from the perimeter of the retirement debate toward the institutional toolkit, but access is not the same thing as endorsement. Whether BTC deserves a place in a particular portfolio remains a question of allocation, volatility, horizon and risk tolerance.

7️⃣ Bitcoin becomes particularly interesting because its economic architecture is fundamentally different from the financial architecture underlying equities, bonds and pension liabilities. A share represents ownership in a productive enterprise whose value ultimately depends on earnings, margins, growth, competition, management and the discount rate investors apply to future cash flows. A government or corporate bond is somebody else's liability and depends on the issuer's capacity and willingness to repay. Bitcoin is neither. It promises no dividend, pays no coupon and has no management team that can increase earnings. Its monetary proposition rests instead on scarcity, network security, ownership and adoption. The issuance schedule is predetermined by protocol, with new supply declining through successive halvings and total supply converging toward 21 million BTC. If demand for a company rises dramatically, that company can issue additional shares. If governments require additional financing, they can issue more debt. If the banking system expands credit, new financial claims can be created. Bitcoin does not respond to increased demand by changing its monetary schedule. This is the first important way in which BTC changes the traditional retirement equation: the saver is holding an asset whose supply cannot be expanded simply because the financial system needs more units.

8️⃣ This is where the monetary argument developed in The Bitcoin Standard becomes relevant, provided we treat it as a framework rather than an unquestionable economic law. The Austrian-school interpretation asks whether a savings asset with a credibly difficult-to-expand supply can preserve purchasing power over long horizons more effectively than monetary instruments whose supply is managed according to economic and political objectives. The traditional retirement model effectively says: earn currency during your working life, then transform a portion of that currency into equities, bonds, real estate and other claims capable of compounding faster than cash loses purchasing power. Bitcoin introduces another possibility. Instead of requiring the savings asset to produce corporate profits or interest, its long-term thesis rests on digital scarcity itself becoming valuable as adoption expands. That proposition can succeed or fail, and Bitcoin's market price remains highly sensitive to liquidity, interest rates, leverage, regulation and investor psychology. But its monetary supply is not altered by those variables. The distinction is subtle but important: Bitcoin does not escape markets, yet the monetary rules governing the asset are external to the discretionary decisions that govern much of the traditional financial system.

9️⃣ There is also a second characteristic that makes Bitcoin particularly unusual in a retirement discussion: ownership can exist outside the financial intermediary itself. A 401(k) necessarily operates within an institutional structure involving employers, plan administrators, custodians, funds and fiduciaries. Traditional securities also require intermediated ownership infrastructure. Native Bitcoin can instead be withdrawn and self-custodied, allowing the holder to control the asset directly through private keys. That characteristic is largely lost when BTC exposure is held through a 401(k), ETF or retirement wrapper, but it remains part of the underlying asset's architecture. For somebody thinking about financial sovereignty over decades rather than merely quarterly portfolio performance, that distinction matters. The risk also changes. Instead of relying exclusively on institutional solvency and market infrastructure, self-custody introduces responsibility for key management, operational security and succession planning. Bitcoin therefore does not eliminate counterparty risk without cost; it permits the individual to exchange some forms of institutional dependency for direct responsibility. In my view, this is one of the most important financial innovations behind BTC and one of the reasons it cannot be analysed simply as another technology stock.

🔟 But this is precisely where the argument needs discipline, because Bitcoin does not abolish the mathematics of retirement. A retiree who requires $50,000 next year and holds the entire portfolio in BTC remains exposed to sequence-of-returns risk, and because Bitcoin is still significantly more volatile than a diversified stock-and-bond portfolio, that risk can actually become more severe. If BTC falls 50% at the moment regular withdrawals are necessary, fixed supply does not pay the grocery bill, and monetary scarcity does not prevent the retiree from being forced to sell into weakness. This is why my argument is not “replace the 401(k) with Bitcoin,” nor is it “stocks are bad and BTC is good.” These instruments solve different economic problems. The 401(k) is an efficient tax and accumulation wrapper. Equities provide ownership of productive businesses and exposure to economic growth. Bonds and cash can provide income, liquidity and lower volatility as retirement approaches. Bitcoin introduces an additional category: a globally portable, digitally scarce monetary asset whose supply does not expand in response to demand and whose existence does not depend on the solvency of a corporation, pension sponsor or sovereign issuer.

MY 2 CENTS is therefore that Bitcoin does not replace the retirement system; it breaks one of the assumptions underneath it. For decades, workers have effectively been told that preserving purchasing power requires continuously transforming monetary savings into financial claims capable of outrunning inflation and currency dilution. Bitcoin introduces the possibility that part of long-term savings can instead be held in an asset whose scarcity is embedded in the protocol itself. That does not guarantee appreciation, and it certainly does not eliminate volatility, but it changes the source of the monetary risk.

My base case is a future in which 401(k)s remain the backbone of American retirement accumulation because their tax advantages, employer contributions and automatic investment mechanisms are simply too useful to disappear. Equities remain fundamental because productive companies create real economic value. Bonds and cash remain essential because retirees need income and liquidity. Bitcoin, however, increasingly becomes a separate reserve or growth sleeve within and outside those structures, particularly for savers who view monetary scarcity and financial sovereignty as long-term portfolio characteristics rather than short-term speculative narratives.

In a bullish scenario, deeper institutional access, clearer regulation, more mature custody infrastructure and continued global adoption gradually move BTC from a satellite allocation toward a recognized long-duration monetary reserve. In a bearish scenario, volatility remains too high, regulatory or custody problems persist, adoption disappoints and Bitcoin remains a relatively small component of diversified retirement portfolios. Both outcomes are possible, which is why allocation matters more than ideology.
The broader conclusion is the part I consider most important. A rising S&P 500 is excellent news for somebody who already owns enough of it at the right point in life, but a record index is not, by itself, proof of retirement security. Retirement ultimately concerns purchasing power, cash flows and time, not points on a financial index.

Bitcoin does not magically solve retirement.
What it does is introduce a savings architecture whose monetary supply is not managed in response to Wall Street valuations, government financing requirements or pension liabilities.
That is why BTC changes the equation.
It does not eliminate risk.
It changes where part of the risk comes from.
And for a long-term saver, that distinction may prove more important than another all-time high on the S&P 500.

text:
Everyone Talks About U.S. Debt But Europe May Be in Worse Trouble

America’s debt problem is impossible to miss. Federal debt has crossed $40.08T, another $1.9T deficit is expected this fiscal year and the 30-year Treasury yield is around 5.25%, its highest since 2007.

Yet the next Western debt crisis may begin across the Atlantic.

Washington has advantages that buy it time. The United States issues the world’s principal reserve currency, collects taxes through one federal government and sells debt through one enormous Treasury market. It can attract foreign capital and push part of the cost abroad. That does not make $40T harmless, but it can delay the reckoning.

The eurozone has no comparable safety valve. It has one currency and one central bank, but 20 governments issuing their own debt, running separate budgets and answering to different voters. The ECB must set one monetary policy for economies with very different debts and growth rates.

France shows why this is dangerous. Its 10-year bond yield has risen to about 4.15%, its highest since 2008 and now slightly above Italy’s. The European Commission expects a 5.1% French deficit this year and public debt near 120% of GDP by 2027.

The problem can no longer be blamed on Greece or another small southern economy. France is the eurozone’s second-largest economy and one of the states meant to support rescue mechanisms for everyone else. If its debt starts trading like the old European “periphery,” the line between rescuers and rescued begins to disappear.

Germany offers little comfort. Its 10-year yield is near 3.3%, a 15-year high, while its industry remains weak. Europe’s two central powers are paying more to borrow just as Brussels prepares another spending surge.

The EU plans to mobilize up to €800B for rearmament. Member states must also finance ageing populations, expensive energy, social programs and support for Ukraine. Budget cuts provoke resistance. More borrowing raises yields. ECB intervention places more national debt risk onto the shared monetary system.

The United States can abuse the dollar’s global role for longer. Europe may hit the wall first because it carries heavy debts without a genuine federal state standing behind them. One central bank cannot reconcile every national budget forever.

So yes, America’s debt matters. But the louder surprise may come from a European Union that spent years presenting itself as the responsible alternative. Washington has a dangerous debt problem. Europe has the same problem inside a system poorly designed to survive it.

No sympathy is required. Both created this predicament through wars, sanctions, subsidies and promises they can no longer finance cheaply. Now we get to see which model breaks first.

Warren Buffett reveals that the insurance business behind Berkshire came from three accidents he did nothing to arrange:

"Many, many, many pieces of luck, but I had three extraordinary pieces of luck in terms of the insurance business."

He was 20 when he went to Washington uninvited on a Saturday, and Lorimer Davidson of GEICO spent four hours explaining an industry Buffett says he could not have learned that well at any business school in the United States.

"We not only couldn't have done that a day later, we couldn't have done it an hour later."

That was National Indemnity in 1967, sold by Jack Ringwalt, who wanted to sell for about five minutes a year whenever a claim made him angry, so Buffett had asked his friend Charlie Heider to bring him in the next time the mood struck.

"I've never worked in the insurance business, but maybe I can do you some good."

That was Ajit Jain walking into the office on a Saturday in the mid 1980s, and he went on to build Berkshire's reinsurance business.

"But the whole thing in businesses is being open to ideas as they come along."

Buffett is careful about why those four hours in Washington were worth anything to him. Insurance was already a business he could follow, and he says that if Davidson had explained a different industry to him that afternoon it would have done him no good at all.

He stayed reachable on Saturdays to people with no claim on his time, and he understood insurance well enough to tell what he was being handed while the offer was still open.

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting, Omaha, May 2015.

DOUBLE STAR DAYS — Starbucks runs days where every star is doubled. Most members don't know when they happen or that they need to register.

Starbucks periodically runs Double Star Days — promotions where every star earned is doubled for the entire day. A $5 purchase that normally earns 10 stars (with a preloaded card at 2 stars/dollar) earns 20 stars. She said most members miss these days entirely.

"Double Star Days are promoted through the Starbucks app — in the Offers section and sometimes via push notification. But only if you have notifications enabled. Most members have either turned off Starbucks notifications or don't check the Offers tab. The Double Star Day happens. They visit Starbucks. They earn regular stars. The double opportunity passes."

HOW TO CATCH THEM: Open the Starbucks app → check the Offers section every few days. When a Double Star Day is announced, register for it by tapping the offer — some promotions require activation before the stars apply.

She said combining Double Star Days with a preloaded card creates the fastest path to free drinks.

"Preloaded card: 2 stars/dollar. Double Star Day: 2x multiplier. Result: 4 stars per dollar. A $5 drink earns 20 stars. On a Double Star Day, a $5 drink earns 40 stars. The 150-star free drink threshold is reachable in $37.50 of normal spending — or in $18.75 on a Double Star Day. That's 3–4 visits for a free drink."

She said she specifically shifts her Starbucks spending to Double Star Days.

"If I know a Double Star Day is coming on Thursday, I'll skip my Wednesday visit and double up on Thursday. Same total spending. Double the stars. It's not about spending more — it's about spending on the right day."

THE REWARDS SYSTEM — You're earning 1 star per dollar. You should be earning 2–3. Here's how.

The Starbucks Rewards program gives you 1 star per dollar when you pay with a credit card, debit card, or cash. She said that's the slowest way to earn stars — and the one most members use by default.

"When you load money onto your Starbucks card — through the app — and pay with the preloaded balance, you earn 2 stars per dollar instead of 1. That's double the earning rate. Same drink. Same price. Same store. Double the stars. Most members pay with their credit card and earn 1 star per dollar because they never loaded money onto their Starbucks card."

HOW TO SET IT UP: Open the Starbucks app → go to Card → tap Add Money → load $25, $50, or $100 onto your Starbucks card. Now pay with the Starbucks card balance every time you order. 2 stars per dollar — automatically.

She said the preloaded card also stacks with other bonuses.

"When you reload your Starbucks card, Starbucks occasionally runs reload bonuses — 'Load $20 or more and earn 50 bonus stars.' These bonuses appear in the Offers section of the app. If you check Offers before reloading, you can earn 50–150 bonus stars on the same money you were going to load anyway."

She said the star earning rate changes the math on free drinks significantly.

"At 1 star per dollar, you need $75 in spending to earn a free drink (150 stars at the reward threshold). At 2 stars per dollar with the preloaded card, you need $37.50 in spending. That cuts the free-drink threshold in half. At $5 per visit, 5 times per week, you earn a free drink every 1.5 weeks instead of every 3 weeks. Same spending. Double the rewards."

 Once the right to counsel has been clearly asserted with respect to further interactions, government agents may not initiate or continue contacts designed to elicit information or create pressure outside the presence of counsel. The recent attempted communication violated this settled principle.

4. Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment Due Process
 Conversion of voluntary petitioning into an atmosphere of threat or coercive leverage, followed by disregard of a formal demand for counsel, fails both procedural and substantive due-process requirements.

5. Separation of Local Administrative Matters from Federal Subjects
 Ordinary local administrative or code matters must not be leveraged, prolonged, or used as a vehicle for pressure related to speech concerning a high-profile federal investigative subject.

6. Public-Interest and Newsworthiness Protection
 Organization and transmission of already-public materials on a matter of intense national concern carries heightened First Amendment protection.

7. No Waiver
 Prior voluntary cooperation, public documentation, or any non-compliant contact does not waive any constitutional right. All rights under the First, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Fourteenth Amendments, and under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, remain fully reserved and are hereby reasserted.

8. Chilling Effect and Selective Treatment
 Persistent non-compliant contacts directed at a citizen who brought public-record information forward, while ordinary administrative parties are not subjected to similar treatment, create both a systemic chill and potential equal-protection concerns if viewpoint-driven.

IV. Renewed Formal Demands

Accordingly, Mr. Russell-Barnett renews and strengthens the following demands:

• Any further in-person interaction, interview, questioning, detention, or physical contact by Oakland County personnel or cooperating federal agents shall occur only in the physical presence of counsel of his choosing.

Counsel remains prepared to facilitate a formal, on-the-record interview or production of materials through appropriate legal channels should Oakland County authorities or the FBI determine that such a step is warranted. Informal or coercive contacts continue to be rejected.

All constitutional and statutory rights are expressly reserved. Classical Christendom’s Arc Across The First 1600 Years of Can-Do-Otherwise Free Will Mechanisms Per Historical & Demographic Data vis-à-vis Determinism & Synergy & 92% of all Christians who have ever lived on planet Earth and the  Historically & Theologically Isolated 8%
→ → 
Historical & Demographic Core:

When evaluating the history of Christian theology, strict theological determinism (monergism) represents a highly localized minority position rather than the historical baseline. A data-driven analysis of global Christian demographics across time reveals a definitive 92% to 8% split in favor of human agency and resistible grace.

•The Demographic Data: Approximately 20% of all Christians who have ever lived on planet Earth have been Protestant. Within that Protestant pool, a safe conservative estimate shows that 60% affirm Prevenient Grace prior to a human decision, ensuring that an individual can freely accept or reject God.

•The Mathematics: 60% of 20% equals 12%. This means that 12% of the historical Christian pool consists of Protestants who affirm Prevenient Grace, leaving roughly 8% of all-time Protestants who reject it in favor of strict Calvinist determinism.

•The Big-Picture Arc: If we look at the total pool of Christians across history, roughly 80% belong to historical Catholic and Eastern/Oriental Orthodox traditions that universally affirm synergistic free will. When combined with the 12% of synergistic Protestants, roughly 92% of Christian history affirms a "can-do-otherwise" view of human agency, leaving strict theological determinism as a highly localized 8% historical minority.

Theological Foundations & Axioms:

To maintain analytical precision, several core definitions must be established regarding the terminology of divine and human action:

•The Definition of "Classical": As a term of classification here, "Classical" explicitly references the overarching 92% historical consensus affirming a "can-do-otherwise" libertarian free will in man, tied directly to the preservation of human moral responsibility.

•Classical ≠ Thomism: While Thomism is a prominent school within this tradition, it is a subset of Classical philosophy, not the whole thing. Conflating Classical Christian anthropology strictly with Thomism is a historical error.

•The Multi-School Landscape: The term "Classical" encompasses various distinct theological schools (including Thomism, Scotism, Molinism, and Arminianism). While these schools fiercely debate the microscopic, interior mechanics of grace, all of them remain fundamentally Classical because they universally reject strict determinism and uphold the core metaphysical attributes of God alongside real human freedom.

•The Key to the Arc: Mechanisms for libertarian free will are intrinsically tied to the *Imago *Dei (Image of God). Classical anthropology dictates that because God has perfect intellect and a completely free will, the human soul must possess a finite, structural mirror of that freedom—specifically the real power to choose otherwise—to truly bear His image.

The Three-Era Historical Timeline:

The structural mechanics protecting libertarian free will were uniquely forged, robustly defended, and fully developed across three distinct windows in Christian history:

[ 1 ]  The Patristic/Byzantine Foundation (100s–700s AD)

To extend the map backward to the Early Church, this foundational window represents the frontline defense of Christian anthropology. The early Church faced a massive ideological war against Gnostic, Marcionite, and Manichaean cosmic fatalism, which taught that human souls were locked into fixed spiritual destinies by nature or fate. To defend the Imago Dei, the early Church Fathers consistently weaponized the concept of Autexousion (αὐτεξούσιον)—literally meaning "self-governing authority" or "power over oneself"—which serves as the precise historical verbiage for "can-do-otherwise" libertarian free will. This vital theological baseline was kept robust by a linear chain of six primary giants:

•Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD): First systematically deployed the concept of autexousion against pagan fate to preserve moral responsibility, arguing that if human actions are determined, praise, blame, rewards, and punishments are completely meaningless.

•Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD): Anchored autexousion directly to creation to defeat Gnostic determinism, explicitly writing that man is "possessed of free will from his beginning" because he is made to mirror a free Creator.

•Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD): Provided the first systematic, metaphysical mapping of human choice, demonstrating that while external impressions strike the mind, the rational soul possesses an active, internal power to approve, reject, or redirect its assent.

•John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD): Championed a fierce synergism of human cooperation with divine grace, mapping them as a dynamic partnership where God's grace initiates and provides the capacity, but human autexousion must actively step forward to cooperate.

•Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD): Engineered a highly sophisticated psychological map during the Monothelite crisis, brilliantly separating our natural will (our natural desire for the good) from our deliberative will (our actual, choice-making faculty).

•John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD): Synthesized centuries of this Greek patristic framework into a unified system, defining autexousion as the rational power to act or not act.

The Transmission Bridge (1150s AD) → 

The historic link that physically joined the Patristic world to the Medieval world occurred when Burgundio of Pisa (1153 AD) translated John of Damascus’s masterwork into Latin (De Fide Orthodoxa). Shortly after, Peter Lombard (c. 1155 AD) imported the Damascene's exact definitions into his Sentences—the mandatory, universal textbook for European universities. This directly handed the Greek "can-do-otherwise" map straight to the medieval university system.

[ 2 ]  The Medieval & Late Scholastic Development (1200s–1600s AD) 

Spanning a four-century arc, Western scholasticism took the patristic foundations and elevated them into microscopically precise metaphysical maps designed to reconcile human freedom with divine foreknowledge, omnipotence, and primary causality.

•Bonaventure (c. 1221–1274): Maintained a voluntaristic focus on the soul, ensuring that the will possesses a distinct, inherent dignity and freedom that cannot be entirely subjugated by external or purely intellectual necessities.

•Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274): Formulated an intricate intellectualist map of choice, tracing how the intellect deliberates on the "good" and presents options, while the will retains the free, structural power to move itself to act or not act upon those options.

•Henry of Ghent (c. 1217/1240–1293): Strongly defended the independence of the will against radical intellectual determinism, arguing that the will acts as a self-moving, primary agent that commands its own choices.

•Peter John Olivi (c. 1248–1298): A radical champion of free will who argued that if the will is determined by any prior cause, the Imago Dei is utterly destroyed. He mapped the will's freedom as an intrinsic, self-generating energy.

•John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308): The supreme pivot point who revolutionized philosophy by mapping synchronic contingency. He demonstrated that at the exact logical instant (T₁) a free agent chooses option A, they retain the real, structural, simultaneous power to choose option B.

•Francisco Suárez (1548–1617): Brought medieval metaphysics to its peak by developing Congruism. He mapped exactly how God’s grace is perfectly tailored to a creature's disposition, ensuring it is 100% effective while guaranteeing the human will retains the intrinsic power to resist it at the exact moment it accepts it.

[ 3 ]  The Protestant Scholastic Refinement (1600s–1700s AD)

During a century-long refinement, Jacobus Arminius and his immediate Remonstrant successors faced the rise of strict Calvinist compatibilism. Realizing that determinism reduced the Imago Dei to a fiction, they imported the high-level metaphysical mechanisms of Scotus and the late Scholastics/Jesuits to build a rigorous Protestant counter-map.

•Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609): Re-engineered Protestant soteriology by utilizing the concept of Middle Knowledge. He mapped out a system where God’s election is conditional upon foreseen faith, and where Prevenient Grace actively liberates the bound human will, placing it in a state of genuine equilibrium.

•Simon Episcopius (1586–1643): The primary academic chair successor to Arminius who formalized the school’s curriculum and drafted the Remonstrant Confession of 1621, embedding "can-do-otherwise" mechanics firmly into Protestant systematic theology.

•Hugo Grotius (1583–1645): Formulated the Governmental Theory of Atonement, which flipped the legal mechanics of the cross. By mapping the atonement as a universal offer satisfying God's moral government rather than a deterministic transaction for a select few, he structurally left the door open for human libertarian choice.

•Jan Uytenbogaert (1557–1644): The tactical architect who codified the movement into the Five Articles of Remonstrance (1610), forcing the global debate onto the explicit hinges of Conditional Election and Resistible Grace.

•Thomas Goad (1576–1638): An English theologian who brought high-level metaphysical precision to Great Britain, mapping a system where God intentionally poises certain events in an "equal possibility of being or not being," actively withdrawing absolute necessity from human moral choices.

•Philipp van Limborch (1633–1712): Compiled the final master blueprint of the era by writing the first comprehensive Arminian systematic textbook (Theologia Christiana). He mapped how Prevenient Grace illuminates the intellect while leaving the will in a state of libertas indifferentiae (liberty of indifference), ensuring that the final causal mechanism of tipping the scale rests entirely in the non-determined power of human choice. 

Christendom’s Arc → 

When we look at the total pool of Christians across history, roughly 80% belong to historical Catholic and Eastern/Oriental Orthodox traditions that universally affirm synergistic free will. When combined with the 12% of synergistic Protestants, roughly 92% of Christian history affirms a "can-do-otherwise" view of human agency, leaving strict theological determinism as a highly localized 8% historical minority.

text:
How do you choose the title of your book or article?

Writing a quality book or article will not bring sales or clicks if your title is poor. Your title should make people stop and click on your book or article.

A good title offers a solution to a problem and must be specific.

For example:

❌ How to Bake Cake

✅ How to Bake Cake at Home Under 30 Minutes

❌ Fish Farming Guide

✅ How I Lost ₦500,000 in Fish Farming and the Mistakes to Avoid

❌ How to Save Money

✅ How to Save ₦100,000 in 6 Months on a Low Income

❌ Writing an Ebook

✅ How to Write and Publish an Ebook with Only Your Phone

People are more likely to click on the second titles because they are specific and promise a clear outcome.

A poorly written book or article can get more clicks and sales than a well-written one if it has a better title.

A great title can make people stop and click.
A boring title can hide a great book.

Sunderland vs Arsenal. My preferred line up and a few basic notes. #AFC

One of the toughest grounds to go to. The fans are always up for it

Sunderland will be set up in a compact mid block in an attempt to completely close down central space. They like to force teams wide which could play into our strengths. I’d say you can expect the RHS triangle to be in full force today.

Sunderland like to play direct at times and are not stubborn in their way of escaping pressure. The out ball to Brobbey is a strong route. Set pieces are also relied upon.

GK: Raya

Big day with set pieces. He had 3 high claims vs Chelsea. Feel the numbers will be similar

RB: White

Timber is almost back and that will be crucial to maintaining fitness. For the time being, White has to start. Will have a tough day vs Angulo. Tricky player

RCB: Konsa

Like vs Napoli Konsa will likely be the targeted CB for a long ball. Brobbey will be a lot to handle. He seemed to struggle physically when Hojlund played his back to him. He's a superb defender when faced up. 

LCB: Gabriel

More of the same from the Napoli game hopefully. Will need to help Konsa

LB: Calafiori

Hincapie was excellent vs Napoli but I feel Calafiori should start. Will cause Sunderland loads of problems. He works so well with Tzolis

DM: Rice

Just has to play. Will be in that RCB role again. Rest him vs Ipswich

RCM: Odegaard

4 MOTM performances in 5 games. No brainer. I assume he won't  finish 90 as he loock knackered after Napoli. Clutch in the right sided triangle. Lateral movements across the LHS and RHS, will be in the LHS when Odegaard drops, will likely be below in the RHS when Odegaard pushes, due to our right sided bias (will do a short post with images later). Likely the 1 in our 3-1-6. Him or Myles today? Who do you want?

Saka didn't have his shooting boots on vs Napoli and neither did Noni tbf. i feel Noni could cause Reinildo real problems in 1v1 situations. I also wouldn't be surprised if we see Saka start.

text:
Warren Buffett paid more than $55 million for control of a furniture company without an audit. The contract was one page.

Six years later, its 95-year-old founder walked out and opened a rival business across the street.

Her name was Rose Blumkin. She arrived in America from Russia with no formal education and learned English from her daughter. In 1937, she used $500 to open Nebraska Furniture Mart.

Her rule was simple: sell cheap and tell the truth.

When suppliers tried to cut her off for underpricing established retailers, she simply found new sources. By 1983, a single Omaha location was generating more than $100 million in annual sales, more than its local competitors combined.

Buffett had watched that record for years. On August 30 of that year, his 53rd birthday, he made the cash offer. Mrs. B was 89.

Berkshire did not count the inventory, verify the receivables, or check the property titles. Mrs. Blumkin gave Buffett her word.

He wrote the check.

The 13-minute footage attached to this post captures the acquisition as it happened. Buffett says buying a company without an audit was almost unheard of.

Mrs. B remained chairman. Her son Louie and grandsons Ron and Irv continued managing Nebraska Furniture Mart with her.

Then, in May 1989, at 95, a management dispute with her relatives pushed her out.

Three months later, she opened Mrs. B's Warehouse directly across the street from Nebraska Furniture Mart.

At the end of 1992, now 99, Mrs. B returned to Nebraska Furniture Mart.

This time, Buffett made sure she signed a non-compete agreement.

He later admitted that failing to get one the first time had been a mistake.

Mrs. B had never broken her word. Nothing in the original agreement prevented her from leaving or competing.

Trust closed the first deal.

The missing clause brought Buffett back nine years later.

Watch this rare 13-minute video. It's the only handshake deal Berkshire ever made at that size.

The river does not look dangerous. It moves quietly over the stones,
carrying the sounds of the forest with it. But for one animal standing
at the edge of the water, this moment is a test written by nature
itself.

A small figure moves through the current. Its body is covered with thick
fur, its eyes carefully watching every movement around it. It is not
simply exploring the river. It is following an ancient instinct that has
guided generations before it.

This is a bear searching for one of the most important resources in its
world: food.

The scene in this footage reveals a side of bears that is often hidden
behind their powerful image. People usually imagine bears as symbols of
strength, large predators capable of dominating their environment. But
the daily reality of a wild bear is much more complicated. Survival
depends on patience, memory, and the ability to understand the
landscape.

A river is a place of opportunity and uncertainty. Beneath the surface,
food may appear for only a short time. The bear must use its senses,
timing, and experience to succeed.

The movement looks simple, but every step has a purpose. The bear
watches the water, listens to the surroundings, and reacts to changes
that humans might never notice.

Bears are among the most adaptable mammals on Earth. They can live in
forests, mountains, tundra, and coastal regions. Their success comes
from their ability to change their behavior depending on what the
environment offers.

Some populations rely heavily on plants and berries. Others search for
insects, small animals, or fish. In regions where salmon return to
rivers, bears become part of one of nature’s most dramatic seasonal
events.

A river full of migrating fish becomes a place where the lives of
different species connect. The fish carry nutrients from the ocean back
into forests. The bears help spread those nutrients across the land. A
single feeding moment becomes part of a much larger ecological story.

The animal in this video represents thousands of years of adaptation.
Its powerful claws, strong sense of smell, and thick fur are not random
features. Each one developed because it helped ancestors survive
changing conditions.

But strength alone is not enough.

Young bears must learn from experience. They observe, practice, and
slowly understand the rules of their environment. A mistake can mean
lost energy, and in the wild, energy is everything.

The peaceful image of a bear near water hides a difficult reality.
Seasons change. Food becomes scarce. Weather creates challenges.
Competition with other animals and human expansion can affect where
bears can live.

Yet these animals continue because they are incredibly intelligent
survivors.

Scientists studying bears have discovered complex behaviors, strong
memories, and impressive problem-solving abilities. Bears can remember
locations, recognize patterns, and adapt their strategies when
conditions change.

The moment captured in this footage is more than an encounter with a
wild animal. It is a glimpse into a world where every movement has
meaning.

The bear is not performing for the camera. It is simply following the
rhythm of nature, repeating behaviors shaped by countless generations.

For a few seconds, the distance between humans and the wild becomes
smaller. We are reminded that forests and rivers are not empty places.
They are living systems filled with stories happening every day.

The bear walks forward, carrying the history of its species with every
step. It is a survivor of changing landscapes, changing climates, and a
world that never stops transforming.

The more we learn about bears, the clearer it becomes that they are not
just powerful animals. They are important parts of the ecosystems they
inhabit. Their movements connect different parts of nature, from rivers
and forests to the countless organisms that depend on them.

A quiet moment beside a stream can contain millions of years of
evolution. The bear searching through the water is following a path
created long before humans recorded history.

Every ripple, every footprint, and every careful movement tells a story
of adaptation. Nature often hides its greatest lessons in ordinary
moments, and this encounter is one of them.

The animal eventually disappears back into the landscape, but the story
continues. The river keeps flowing, the forest keeps growing, and the
ancient relationship between animals and their environment moves

text:
2/5🌊 ROMANTICISM: THE SUBLIME

Skying

Constable’s most radical journeys sometimes required little more than looking upward.

Around Hampstead, he watched clouds change and tried to paint them before they became something else.

The practice acquired a wonderfully direct name: skying.

A cloud cannot remain still for a portrait. Its edges alter. Light changes its density. Wind moves it in relation to other clouds, and the arrangement that first attracted the painter may already have vanished.

The study becomes a record of attention working against disappearance.

Some sketches carry notes about date, time, wind and weather. Luke Howard’s developing classification of clouds belonged to the scientific culture through which the sky was becoming newly describable.

One surviving study records an afternoon in September 1822 with the precision of a field observation.

Physical explanation could intensify feeling. Closer observation let Constable distinguish one atmosphere from another.

A field under heavy cloud and the same field under clearing light are geographically identical. Their emotional pressure is different.

Constable’s local knowledge gave him an unusual basis for these discoveries. Born into a prosperous milling family in Suffolk, he repeatedly returned to the Stour Valley and the working landscape he knew.

Mills, cottages, wagons and water belonged to memory as well as observation.

Familiarity made comparison possible.

He knew enough about the place to notice what the passing conditions had altered.

The apparent simplicity of his finished landscapes can conceal the scale of their preparation. His large oil sketches allowed him to test composition, colour and light across canvases close to the dimensions of the intended exhibition work.

A sketch could become approximately six feet wide.

Later viewers often found these working versions especially exciting. Their visible uncertainty seemed to preserve the movement of a mind still deciding what the painting should become.

The history of The Hay Wain adds another reversal. Its English debut did not produce the triumph suggested by its later fame. At the Paris Salon of 1824, however, Constable’s work attracted major attention and earned a gold medal.

A landscape rooted in one small English geography helped change what French painters thought paint could do.

The local travelled farther than its maker needed to.

Constable’s coastal studies carry a more intimate history. Visits to Brighton were connected with hopes that sea air might benefit his wife Maria, who suffered from tuberculosis.

He disliked much of fashionable resort life. The sea and sky still gave him subjects.

On the beach, changing weather could be studied with paper and a portable paint box. Rainstorm over the Sea turns a passing downpour into marks whose speed remains visible.

The brush almost seems to share the weather’s urgency.

It would be too simple to assign grief to every dark cloud. Yet biography helps us understand why transience need not be an abstract problem.

Weather passes while a painter watches.

A person’s life changes while the painting is being made.

After Maria’s death, Constable’s Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows brought a turbulent sky, enduring architecture and a rainbow into the same scene.

The light does not abolish the darkness that gives it force.

This is a quieter Romantic intensity than the polar wreck or the collapsing mountain. The world becomes moving because it cannot be kept exactly as it is.

Attention offers a temporary form of care.

A painter looks long enough to distinguish the passing thing from every other thing that resembles it.

Then the cloud changes.

The painting remains, carrying evidence that somebody noticed.

The extraordinary discovery is that this can be enough to make a landscape serious.

A place need not be remote.

Its weather need not be unprecedented.

The encounter becomes singular because it happens once, to someone who is there.

#fiction #cozymystery #dogs #mystery
 Can historical facts enhance mysteries? For cozy mystery readers, the answer is a happy yes - especially when the facts become part of the puzzle rather than a dusty lecture tucked between chapters.

History gives a mystery roots. It explains why a seemingly ordinary small town has old grudges, locked doors, peculiar traditions, and secrets that have survived longer than anyone expected. Add a clever sleuth, a suspicious neighbor, and perhaps a dog with an excellent nose, and the past can become one of the most enjoyable suspects in the room.

## How Historical Facts Enhance Mysteries

A good mystery needs more than a crime and a list of possible culprits. It needs a reason for readers to care about the people, the place, and the truth waiting beneath the surface. Historical details can provide all three.

Consider a Florida town with a century-old boardinghouse. Perhaps it once welcomed railroad workers, traveling salesmen, and families escaping northern winters. Decades later, the building is being restored, and a hidden room turns up behind a pantry wall. That detail does more than create an intriguing setting. It raises questions. Who used the room? What did they hide? Why does someone in town want the renovation stopped?

The best historical elements give the present-day mystery a believable foundation. A disputed land deed can explain a modern inheritance battle. An old newspaper clipping can expose a false family story. A historic festival can bring together residents who would rather avoid one another. The past does not solve the crime by itself, but it gives the crime a meaningful trail to follow.

For readers, this kind of background makes a fictional town feel lived in. The bakery has a history. The town square has seen parades, storms, weddings, and perhaps one scandal nobody mentions before dessert. When trouble arrives, it matters because the setting already feels like a place worth protecting.

## The Sweet Spot: Fact, Fiction, and a Fine Mystery

There is a small trick to using history well in a cozy mystery. The facts should feel flavorful, not heavy. Readers pick up a whodunit to enjoy the chase, spend time with familiar characters, and see justice served. They do not necessarily want a textbook with a body on page fifty.

That means choosing historical details with story potential. A date alone is rarely exciting. A date connected to a missing will, a vanished ship, or a family who changed its name can be irresistible. The difference lies in what the fact does.

A historical tidbit earns its place when it creates a clue, a motive, a complication, or a surprise. It may also reveal character. The local museum volunteer who knows every detail about the town founder may be generous and charming. Or she may be protecting a version of history that benefits her family.

The details should also be accurate enough to feel trustworthy. Readers do not expect a cozy mystery to read like a scholarly journal, but they appreciate care. A writer who gets the broad history of a region right can take imaginative turns without breaking the spell. In Florida, for example, a story might draw on old citrus groves, pioneer communities, fishing villages, historic hotels, or hurricane seasons. Each offers atmosphere, but each also comes with real human stakes.

### Let the Clue Do Some Work

History becomes especially satisfying when it is woven into the investigation. A sleuth should be able to use it, question it, and occasionally be misled by it.

Imagine that Doc Sue MacVety and Daisy are helping a friend clear out a historic cottage before it is sold. Daisy catches an unfamiliar scent near a loose floorboard, while Doc Sue notices that the house plans do not match the rooms upstairs. A local record reveals that the cottage belonged to a midwife who once kept careful notes on every family in town. Suddenly, an old fact is not just scenery. It is evidence.

Canine forensics can make this even more fun. Dogs notice the physical world in ways people miss: a new scent in an old room, disturbed soil beside a garden shed, or a treasured object that has been handled recently. Daisy may not read a brittle document, but she can certainly help point Doc Sue toward the person who did.

https://t.co/AXhz3xAyHC

That partnership keeps historical research from slowing the story. One clue can come from the archives, another from a conversation at the diner, and another from a determined canine nose. The investigation keeps moving, and readers get to enjoy the town’s past along the way.

## History Makes Motives More Personal

The strongest mysteries are rarely about a thing alone. They are about what that thing means to someone. A vintage locket might represent a lost inheritance. An old photograph might prove that a respected citizen was not where she claimed to be. A piece of waterfront property may carry generations of pride, resentment, and unfinished business.

Historical facts can make motives richer because they reveal what characters stand to lose. Someone may fear that an old document will ruin a family’s carefully polished reputation. Another person may want to preserve a beloved landmark, even if the truth about its founding is less charming than the town’s brochure suggests. A third may be convinced that an ancestor was cheated and feel entitled to set matters right.

None of this requires a dark or grim tone. Cozy mysteries thrive on community, wit, and the comfort of seeing tangled problems put right. But even a lighthearted story benefits when the characters’ choices come from somewhere real. A suspect who is merely greedy is easy to understand. A suspect who believes they are defending their great-grandmother’s legacy is more complicated - and more interesting.

There is room for tenderness, too. History can connect generations. A grandparent’s story may help a younger character see their hometown differently. A neglected cemetery may remind residents that forgotten people still deserve respect. These moments deepen a mystery without taking away its playful spark.

## When Less History Is Better

Not every mystery needs a century-old secret. Sometimes a present-day conflict is enough, and adding a historical subplot can make the story feel crowded. The key is to ask whether the past changes the stakes of the current mystery.

If removing the historical detail would leave the plot exactly the same, it may only be decoration. A lovely detail can still add charm, of course, but it should not distract from the suspect list or bury the central question. Readers want clues they can follow, not a history lesson they must survive.

Writers also need to be thoughtful when borrowing from real events. Communities can have painful histories involving violence, displacement, discrimination, or disaster. Those subjects deserve care, research, and a tone that does not treat real suffering as a cute plot device. Sometimes the wiser choice is to create a fictional event inspired by an era or setting, rather than borrow a specific tragedy for entertainment.

For cozy mysteries, warmth matters. The past can contain sorrow, but the story should handle it with compassion and leave room for hope, connection, and a satisfying sense that truth has value.

## A Town With a Memory Is a Town Worth Revisiting

One of the pleasures of a mystery series is returning to a place that feels familiar but still has secrets left to share. Historical details help make that possible. Every book can reveal another corner of town: the old train depot, the garden club’s original meeting house, the family cemetery behind a church, or the storm shelter beneath a renovated shop.

Readers begin to recognize the town’s rhythms and legends. They may know which neighbor tells the best stories, which building gives Daisy an uneasy sniff, and which cheerful local tradition has a surprisingly complicated origin. That sense of continuity turns a setting into a companion.

A well-chosen historical fact is like an old key found in a kitchen drawer. At first, it is only an interesting object. Then someone discovers the lock it fits. The door opens, the clues shift, and the mystery becomes larger, warmer, and much more fun to solve.

text:
TRON Is Rethinking The Cost Of On-Chain Interaction

What if using a blockchain didn’t always begin with the question, “Do I have enough gas?”

That question is still one of the quietest sources of friction in Web3. A user may have the asset they want to use, yet still need another token simply to make the transaction happen.

TRON approaches this differently through a resource model built around Energy and Bandwidth, creating more flexible ways to support on-chain activity.

➠ Energy Turns Network Capacity Into Something Users Can Manage

Smart contract execution requires computational resources.

On TRON, Energy represents those resources.

Users can obtain Energy through TRX staking, effectively turning staked capital into access to network resources.

But that doesn't mean staking is the right answer for everyone.

An occasional user may not want to lock additional TRX just because they need to execute a few smart contract transactions.

That is where flexibility becomes important.

➠ JustLend Adds An On-Demand Option

JustLend DAO’s Energy Rental gives users another route to obtaining Energy without requiring them to stake additional TRX specifically for that purpose.

This can be particularly useful when interacting with:

▫️DeFi protocols
▫️Token swaps
▫️Lending and borrowing platforms
▫️Smart contracts
▫️Other supported TRON applications

The interesting part is the change in mindset.

Instead of thinking, “How much capital do I need to lock?”

Users can also think, “How much resource do I actually need right now?”

That distinction can make network-resource management considerably more practical.

➠ GasFree Removes Another Piece Of Friction

Energy Rental and GasFree solve different problems.

Energy Rental helps users access Energy.

GasFree, where supported, can allow applications to sponsor eligible transaction fees so users don't necessarily need to acquire TRX just to pay for those transactions.

That can dramatically simplify the first interaction with a blockchain application.

The user doesn't have to understand the entire resource model before getting started.

They can simply focus on completing the action.

➠ One Network, Different Paths For Different Users

Blockchain users don't behave the same way.

A frequent DeFi trader may prefer maintaining resources through staking or renting Energy when necessary.

A developer may care about predictable access to resources during repeated contract interactions.

A newcomer may benefit most from a GasFree experience that removes the need to manage fees altogether.

Instead of forcing every participant into one approach, TRON’s resource ecosystem provides different mechanisms for different situations.

That is a powerful usability principle.

➠ The Best Fee Experience Might Be The One You Don't Notice

Users don't wake up wanting to manage blockchain resources.

They want to swap.

Lend.

Stake.

Pay.

Trade.

Interact.

The more infrastructure can handle the complexity underneath those actions, the closer Web3 gets to feeling like a normal digital service rather than a technical environment that users must learn before they can use it.

This is where resource design becomes more than a technical detail.

It becomes part of adoption.

➠ Making The Blockchain Easier To Use

Through Energy, staking, Energy Rental, and supported GasFree experiences, TRON offers multiple ways to approach the cost of on-chain activity.

No single mechanism has to serve every user.

And that may be the bigger advantage.

Because blockchain adoption won't come only from networks processing more transactions.

It will also come from making those transactions easier to understand, easier to access, and less disruptive to the user experience.

Less time thinking about gas.
More time using the application.

text:
Some of my best memories from childhood are with my brother. An N64 cost real money at the time, and my dad—despite his many failures—went out of his way to get one for me and my brother on a meager Brazilian wage.

Him at the controller, and me, being younger, sitting comfortably beside him, helping work out the puzzles together.

Each new puzzle solved was a promise that a whole new world would open up to us. What strange new scenery, new weapons, new people would we find?

I don’t remember what we used to look things up on back then, if anything. We mostly just brute-forced our way through it. I distinctly remember GameFAQs being around, but at the time there were also many more fan sites—even Brazilian ones—available. It was a better web, in contrast to today, when everything seems concentrated on YouTube.

I think my brother solved the Water Temple on his own. I may have gotten frustrated and, being younger, fallen asleep quickly.

Only to wake up, open the save file, and explore the new world he had unlocked.

Watching the teaser that came out last week brought that feeling back—the nostalgia for what I consider the best time of my life, two and a half decades later.

If I’m ever blessed with children of my own, I’ll offer them—not force upon them—the same kind of apparatus that allowed my brother and me to bond back then. And as they grow older, if they ever look back on their time with me with anything like the same nostalgia I have for those days with my brother, I’ll die satisfied knowing that, at the very least, I tried.

I thank Nintendo for giving us that opportunity back then. And I thank Nintendo once again now for not having forgotten what made it great.

text:
Mistake 8: Your Notifications Are Waking the Screen 200 Times a Day

The Problem:
Every app can send you notifications. Every notification lights up the screen. Every screen wake uses power. You've never checked which apps actually need to notify you.

What It Actually Does:
A notification wakes the display, wakes the processor, and sometimes wakes the radio. If you get 200 notifications a day, that's 200 screen wakes. Some apps send notifications for things that don't matter promotional offers, "recommended for you" alerts, streak reminders. Each one costs battery.

The Insider Quote:
"I've audited phones that received 300+ notifications a day. Most were from apps the user didn't even care about. Shopping apps. Games. News apps they never opened. Every notification is a screen wake. Every screen wake is battery. Turn off notifications for everything that isn't a human trying to reach you."

The Before/After:
Turning off notifications for non-essential apps can save 5–8% of battery per day. Your phone also becomes less distracting. You'll check it less. It'll last longer.

How to Fix It:
Settings → Notifications → Go through every app. Turn off notifications for shopping apps, games, news apps, and anything that isn't a person or a critical service. Keep them on for Messages, Phone, Mail, and maybe one or two others.

text:
This Hindu temple stands a thousand miles from India, in what is now central Vietnam.

Built by kings of Champa, it was a maritime kingdom whose Court language was Sanskrit and whose gods were Shiva and Vishnu. Its temple complex at My Son was begun in the fourth century and expanded for a thousand years afterwards. The Chams adopted the Indian cosmology and the Indian Court apparatus because they judged it the best system on offer to a king who wanted to look legitimate at home and abroad.

The same pattern occurs across half of Southeast Asia between the third century BC and roughly the thirteenth century AD. India gave the region its religions, its epics, its scripts and its models of kingship in a peaceful transfer of ideas.

text:
Mt 11:28–12:8

The call “Come to me… and I will give you rest” is not an isolated devotional invitation but a royal‑temple summons. In Klinean architecture, rest is never psychological; it is covenantal. It is the enthronement‑rest of the Creator‑King after His cosmic building work, the Sabbath enthronement that Israel’s weekly observance typologically reenacted. Jesus’ words therefore function as a declaration that the eschatological Sabbath has arrived in His person. He is the finished‑work kingdom.

This is why Matthew immediately moves into Sabbath controversy. The narrative shift is not accidental; it is architectural. The Son who offers rest now walks through grainfields on the Sabbath as the true Davidic king whose men may eat the bread of the kingdom because the king is present. The typology is not merely analogical but escalated: David’s need justified a temporary cultic exception; Jesus’ presence inaugurates a new covenant order. The priestly precedent in the temple further intensifies the point—priests “profane” the Sabbath by laboring in the sanctuary, yet remain guiltless because temple service is Sabbath service. Jesus’ claim “something greater than the temple is here” is therefore a kingdom‑cosmic assertion: He is the final sanctuary, and those united to Him participate in His Sabbath authority.

The climactic statement “the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath” is not a legal ruling but a royal enthronement claim. The Sabbath belongs to the enthroned Son of Man of Daniel 7, the one who receives dominion after passing through judgment. In Klinean terms, Jesus is announcing that the Sabbath’s typological function has reached its eschatological fulfillment. The day no longer governs the Son; the Son governs the day. The sign yields to the reality. The weekly shadow yields to the enthroned king.

Thus the movement from 11:28 to 12:8 is covenantal ascent: the weary are summoned into the kingdom‑rest; the king demonstrates His authority over the typological structures of that rest; and the narrative reveals that the Sabbath is not abolished but transfigured—its meaning now located in union with the crucified‑risen Son who embodies the new‑creation temple.

The Klinean X therefore runs:

Rest → Temple → Son of Man → Kingdom.

The Sabbath is not a boundary marker but a pointer. Its telos stands before the Pharisees in grainfields and synagogue: the enthroned Lord who gives rest by giving Himself.
