text:
You're right about the trajectory. But one correction: "Europe has nothing Russia needs" is not quite accurate — and the distinction matters.

Europe still buys Russian LNG. Still depends on Russian titanium, palladium, enriched uranium, and fertilizer. The sanctions architecture has an entire exemption list precisely because Europe can't function without certain Russian inputs. The dependency hasn't disappeared. It's been rerouted, repriced, and hidden behind intermediaries in Turkey, India, and the Gulf.

So the honest picture is: the dependency is asymmetric — but not zero.

Where you're completely right is the deeper point. Empires don't collapse because someone defeats them. They collapse because they become rentiers of their own past. Europe stopped producing, stopped innovating, stopped defending itself — and started lecturing the rest of the world about values instead. That's the signature of a power that has nothing left to offer except its own memory.

The US is on the same curve, just a decade or two behind. It still has the dollar, the carriers, and the tech sector. But it's spending the inheritance, not building new capital. When you sanction everyone, tariff everyone, and threaten everyone, you're not projecting strength — you're managing decline.

Times are changing. But the change is not a sudden collapse. It's a slow redistribution — and the ones who recognize it early are the ones who profit from it.

*Independent analysis. No ideology. Just facts.*

Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️✓

I wanted to work in finance. 

The worst part about it was that a friend helped me get the job. 

But then I got an offer to work at Global X ETFs, which is an asset management company. 

It was a starting role, but it would get my foot in the door. 

After two weeks at Contract Pod AI, I decided to make the change. 

And let me tell you, it was the right change!

text:
ROBOTAXI
Updated 2026-09-12
Sources: Robotaxi + Owning Robotaxi Fleet bookmark folders (213 unique). Not Cybercab.

NEW TODAY
- Testers (AIScottAdams): Robotaxis won’t just kill short haul flights. Once you can sleep in them, they’ll cannibalize long routes too…
- Testers (TeslaZoa): According to the Tesla Robotaxi tracking site, 14 vehicles have been added to the fleet, bringing the total t…
- Testers (CernBasher): $TSLA: Tesla Just Opened The Floodgates In Austin!
- Testers (teslayoda): Robotaxis incoming to California. 🌜
- Folder totals: Robotaxi 209 (+4) + Fleet 4 (0 new) → 213 unique

WHAT IT IS
- Tesla’s paid autonomous ride service. You book a car in the Robotaxi app. The car drives. There is no human driver on unsupervised rides.
- Live cars today are mostly Model Y. The purpose-built Cybercab is the volume vehicle testers say Tesla is prioritizing.
- Camera-only vision. Tesla VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy: no lidar, radar, or HD maps required for safe operation on this stack.
- This how-to merges the public Robotaxi service folder with Owning Robotaxi Fleet (owner / private-fleet economics). Not Cybercab-only bookmarks.

HOW IT WORKS
- Download the Tesla Robotaxi app and join the waitlist. Official robotaxi (Sep 2025): app is available to all; access expands over time.
- Book the ride in Tesla’s app. Elon: Tesla will not partner with Uber or Lyft. “We will have enough demand.”
- Unsupervised means no safety driver. Supervised cities still have a person in the car.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): service hours are 6am to 10pm, 7 days/week. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger. Upgraded vehicle distribution and routing so you wait less.
- Testers: you can change destination and keep the same trip for multiple stops.
- Cars return to a depot or homebase and park themselves (Houston footage).
- Ashok: FSD v15 is already running on Model Y robotaxis and will run on Cybercab.
- Testers: Tesla is limiting Model Y conversions to prioritize Cybercab, built with an unboxed modular process.
- Testers (Aug 24): Tesla expects Cybercab to replace Model Ys in the Robotaxi fleet over time and become the highest-volume vehicle there. Testers flag Sept 3 / 9/3 as the Cybercab strategy moment. Austin public Cybercab rides described as “imminent.”
- Testers (Sep 7): Cybercab expected to be actively deployed across Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet soon; Austin Cybercab wait times described as going parabolic on demand.
- Testers (Sep 7): Tesla hiring Robotaxi Fleet Support Supervisors night shift across 21 cities (Cybercabs incoming signal).
- Testers (Sep 7): Waymo Q3 2025 occupancy — 90% of trips have 2 or fewer people (two-seater Cybercab justification resurfaced).
- Testers (Sep 8): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 969 after +59 vehicles; 31 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 8): Houston hub still holding ~100 Cybercabs waiting on orders plus Model Y robotaxis; little lot growth since last check — FSD v15 brain called out as the unlock.
- Testers (Sep 8): Texas Robotaxi fleet momentum — Jeff Lutz cited 432 registered autonomous vehicles incl. 45 Cybercabs; software quality cited as why Tesla can keep adding cars.
- Testers (Sep 11 TeslaZoa): Robotaxi tracking site — fleet at 994 after +14 vehicles; 6 short of 1,000.
- Testers (Sep 11 AIScottAdams): sleep-through long-haul thesis — lie-flat Robotaxi rides could cannibalize short- and long-haul flights (tester/AI channel, not Official).
- Testers (Sep 11 CernBasher): “Tesla Just Opened The Floodgates In Austin!” ($TSLA video/title post).
- Testers (Sep 11 teslayoda): “Robotaxis incoming to California.” Still Testers — signal, not a new Official city launch.

HOW TO USE
- Official robotaxi: download the app, join the waitlist.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): rides run 6am to 10pm every day. Unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; routing upgrade is meant to cut wait time.
- Testers: booking is in the app. One Orlando rider paid with an X Money card.
- Tesla site (as quoted): app in 29 languages; service animals; space for some wheelchairs and assistive devices.
- Testers: vehicles in Nevada must be marked “Robotaxi.”
- After the Aug 20 Nevada approval, testers say Tesla still has to finish vehicle inspections, insurance, and published rates before paid rides start there.

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)
- Elon (Feb 2026, also in Robotaxi folder): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Fleet testers frame the network like Airbnb for cars: owner adds vehicle; Tesla handles software, routing, payments, rider experience; platform fee often modeled ~25–35%; owner keeps the rest after operating costs (tester).
- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.
- Fleet / Teslaconomics: Cybercab cost chatter ~$25k–$30k; Elon told that tester production was starting in ~1 month (Mar 2026 context — treat as dated tester claim). Rough capital for a ~$1M/yr fleet ~$850k–$1M in vehicles (tester arithmetic).
- Fleet / chamath: intends to buy and deploy large fleets nationally when possible; expects payback and positive FCF in under 2 years (tester / investor claim, not Official Tesla).
- Fleet / BrianRoemmele: “all in” on buying into the owning-fleet thesis now; separate Optimus ownership program mentioned but not published in this dump.
- Fleet / tslaming (Mar 2026): then only 8 unsupervised Austin robotaxis — historical; do not use as current fleet size (Robotaxi dump Aug 23 tester: 908 total).
- Testers / Teslaconomics (Aug 25, Robotaxi folder): “owning your own Tesla Robotaxi fleet can one day make you financially free.” Still a tester slogan — no Official owner-earnings number in this dump.
- CONFLICT / caution: owner earnings, Cybercab sticker, ROI, and payback are tester models. Dump explicitly says none of it is guaranteed. Do not treat as Official Tesla guidance.

SERVICE AREA / CITIES
- Unsupervised (no safety driver), as listed May 2026: Austin, TX (launched Jun 22, 2025); Dallas, TX and Houston, TX (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Supervised (safety driver), as listed May 2026: SF Bay Area, CA (launched Apr 18, 2026).
- Testers: Bay Area rides to and from SFO. Earlier: San Jose Airport pickup.
- Testers: an Orlando rider reviewed a live Robotaxi trip (Jul 2026). Aug 21 testers also list Orlando and Tampa as live; that is not on the May 2026 official city list.
- Testers (Aug 25 Teslaconomics): 7 metro areas live. Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa ramping unsupervised; Bay Area still safety-driver. Treat as tester city list, not Official May 2026 list.
- Testers (Aug 27 travel_invest): recap of Official hours post lists 6 target cities — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa. Tester translation, not a new Official city list.
- Nevada (Aug 20, 2026): full network permit for paid public service. Start small in Clark County / Las Vegas; Tesla can expand elsewhere in the state after notifying the commission.
- Testers (Aug 23): Nevada approved Tesla for up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles, up from a 10-car interim limit. Tesla said it would be “extremely happy” to have around 2,500 running within a year.
- Testers (May 2026) said Tesla was also aiming at Phoenix, Miami, Orlando, Tampa.
- Hiring and test-vehicle posts (treat as signals, not live service): Arizona, Florida, Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, California, D.C., plus a Germany Arzfeld pilot with a safety driver and Japan Kanagawa job listings.
- Ashok: expanding to a new city is getting cheaper; the end state is operating whole states, not city by city.

ACCESS AND PLANS
- Official: Robotaxi app waitlist. Access expands as cities open.
- Testers (Aug 27 WorldlyReviewer): received an email from Tesla advertising Robotaxi. Tester report of Tesla marketing, not a new Official service announcement.
- Elon (Feb 2026): Tesla owners will be able to add their cars to the Robotaxi network; Tesla collects 25% of revenue.
- Testers (JPMorgan via folder posts): robotaxi operating cost about $0.50–$0.60 per mile vs $2.50–$3.00 for typical ride-hail; long-term platform goal $0.30 per mile. Older Morgan Stanley note used $0.81 per mile vs Waymo $1.36–$1.43.
- Folder testers argue Tesla scales on existing Model Y / Cybercab manufacturing and Superchargers, vs lidar-heavy custom cars.
- Testers (Aug 23): Waymo’s latest self-driving hardware reportedly costs around $20K.
- See OWNING / FLEET for private-owner economics from the Owning Robotaxi Fleet folder.

SAFETY
- Elon: scale as fast as possible, but do not harm anyone. One injury becomes a worldwide headline and a regulatory clampdown.
- Ashok (Jul 2026): zero notable incidents over 380,000 unsupervised miles, across six cities in two states. Cameras only.
- Testers on NHTSA ADS data (Jun 16, 2025–Jul 15, 2026): zero collisions initiated by the Model Y ADS. Two new incidents were other drivers hitting a stopped or parked Robotaxi (Austin red-arrow stop; Dallas parked). No passengers, no injuries, no tow.
- Austin: testers said 100% of tracked robotaxi rides in that NHTSA window were unsupervised.
- Testers: 7x safer than the average human driver is an FSD claim in this folder, not a Robotaxi-only official stat.

FLEET AND INFRASTRUCTURE
- Official robotaxi (Aug 27): unsupervised fleet is a lot bigger; upgraded intelligence in vehicle distribution and routing. Testers (tslaming) say that gain is backend ops (demand forecasting, fleet placement), not a self-driving software change.
- Testers (Aug 23): 908 robotaxis in the total fleet (dated). Newer tester tracking-site counts: 969 (Sep 8), 994 (Sep 11 TeslaZoa) — still Testers, not Official.
- Testers (Aug 19): about 97 Cybercabs at the Houston Robotaxi lot. Model Ys and Cybercabs still rotating in the geofence.
- Testers: Tesla plans 80 wireless chargers in Austin as Phase 2 of a Robotaxi charging hub.
- Testers: private (not public) V4 Supercharger depots, including 56 stalls in Chandler / Phoenix East Valley; a Dallas-area fleet depot; a Las Vegas Cybercab wash/service site.
- Testers: scale needs charging, cleaning, and maintenance automated, not only FSD.
- Fleet-size tweets in this folder are days-to-months apart and disagree. Do not treat an old 500–600 car count (or the Mar 2026 “8 unsupervised in Austin” fleet-folder snapshot) as current.

USEFUL WORKFLOWS
- New city: download the Robotaxi app, join the waitlist, ride when your city opens.
- Live city: book in the Tesla app. Try a multi-stop trip if the app offers it.
- Airport: testers already used SFO and SJC where those pickups were live.
- Watch Nevada: paid Las Vegas service after the Aug 20 permit plus leftover admin steps; testers now cite a 5,000-vehicle cap.
- Watch Austin: testers say public Cybercab rides are “imminent.”
- Owning a fleet: not open as a turnkey product in this dump. Watch Elon’s owner-network comments + Tesla fee structure; treat $30k/yr and <2yr payback as tester models only.

text:
CYBERCAB
Updated 2026-09-12
Sources: your Cybercab bookmark folder (383 posts). Not Cybertruck / Robotaxi.

NEW TODAY
- Folder now 383 posts (8 new since Sep 11)
- Testers (Teslaconomics, Sep 11): I flew my drone through Austin while riding in a Tesla Cybercab. No driver. No steering wheel. No pedals. Nobody up front. I got in, set my…
- Testers (pbeisel, Sep 11): Cern’s argument is that total lifetime miles drive cost-per-mile more than vehicle production cost. Putting more money into durability, so…
- Testers (wholemars, Sep 11): The City of Miami Fire Rescue has announced on Facebook that they will soon be receiving specialized training from Tesla on handling Cyberc…
- Testers (JoeTegtmeyer, Sep 11): Cybercab and Robotaxi are great and already offer a good solution for those who have disabilities, but there is room for improvement and t…
- Testers (CernBasher, Sep 11): Article: The Crazy Economics of the Cybercab
- Testers (tslaming, Sep 10): GOOD NEWS 🇯🇵 Tesla Cybercab has kicked off its four-stop Japan tour at OMAKASE Aoyama Garden in Tokyo 🔥 And behind the excitement is a grow…
- Testers (TeslaZoa, Sep 11): This is the Cybercab era now. It’s no longer just a concept car. It’s showing up on real roads, in more cities, and starting to look like a…
- Testers (herbertong, Sep 11): 🚨 Cybercab’s first public rides went pretty smoothly, but cyberbulls thinks Tesla still hasn’t told the most interesting part of the story…

WHAT IT IS
- Tesla’s purpose-built two-seat autonomous vehicle. Production design: no steering wheel, no pedals. Testers quoting official docs: SAE Level 4.
- Built to run on Tesla’s Robotaxi network (the live Model Y service is a separate note). Official first-responder docs in this folder: Tesla currently owns and operates the Robotaxi vehicles.
- Elon: a clean robotaxi — no mirrors, no pedals, no steering wheel. “There’s no fallback mechanism here. Like this car either drives itself or it does not drive.” Optimized for a gentle ride and lowest cost per mile, not high performance. Elon (Q1 2026 meeting via testers): most long-term production will be Cybercab because 90% of miles are one or two people.
- Glossy gold plastic (RIM) over a high-strength steel crash structure. Testers: color is molded into the panels; no paint shop. FRP inners bonded to the outer panels for strength and mounting.
- Testers quoting official docs / Lars Moravy: ~48 kWh pack, 165 Wh/mi, about 300 miles real-world, front-wheel drive, 163 kW / 219 hp, about 3,113 lbs curb. One tester: 204 MPGE and “most efficient production car ever certified.” Testers (niccruzpatane, Sep 9): wider front track than rear; teardrop for Cd under 0.2; first Tesla FWD; 165 Wh/mi most efficient production EV certified.
- Testers: same platform family as future products (Robovan mentioned). Shares computers, cameras, and batteries with other Teslas and Optimus.

HOW IT WORKS
- Testers (herbertong / cyberbulls, Sep 11): after first public rides, Jeff argues brake-by-wire + molded no-topcoat panels are the under-told story; purpose-built robotaxi vs Waymo/Zoox/WeRide. Still Testers.
- Camera-only vision (testers: AI4). No HD maps required in this folder’s writeups.
- Testers (herbertong / FutureAZA, Sep 10): Cybercab advantage vs Waymo may be unboxed manufacturing (brake-by-wire, huge castings, structural battery) not only AI. Still Testers.
- Electrical: 48V low-voltage architecture plus a 400V high-voltage pack that forms the floor. Testers (wholemars, Aug 18): 100% of controllers designed in-house; cross-car wiring eliminated; local controllers on ethernet; one custom Tesla power-electronics chip doing the job of four at half the cost. Fleet data used to size the pack.
- Cabin: powered butterfly doors, about-21-inch landscape screen, power bench seats that move together, B-pillar exterior door buttons, braille on key controls.
- Phone (testers): open/close the powered doors, move seats, climate airflow, music, and cast Netflix to the screen.
- Starlink: Official robotaxi (Aug 10) posted the first Cybercab with Starlink integration. Testers: flush gold cover. Elon via testers: Starlink is coming to all Teslas. Tesla Head of AI Ashok: internet “is still not required for safe operation.” Connectivity is for navigation, customer service, and fleet management.
- Charging: inductive pads are the fleet goal. Production units still have a physical charge port centered below the trunk (official docs via testers). Conflict: early 2026 tester posts said the cab would have no port. Use the later official-docs line.
- Elon on wheels and pedals: some Cybercabs are retrofitted so Tesla can accumulate chassis-specific miles before a large city rollout. Testers still see those test/regulatory units (Tennessee service center, Aug 16). Lars: FSD is not a copy-paste from Model Y; the test fleet is feeding training. Aug 24 testers: no-wheel units with a safety monitor in the passenger seat. Aug 25 testers: no-wheel / no-pedal counts “increased a lot” in Austin.
- Testers (alex_avoigt, Aug 29): “The first Cybercabs drive unsupervised!” Still Testers, not Official. Conflict with Aug 24 safety-monitor sightings — treat as early unsupervised fleet, not universal.
- Testers (Aug 25–27, TeslaNewswire): RGB front light bar seen in American-flag, purple, turquoise, and orange. Aug 27 testers (TeslaNewswire / MarioNawfal / travel_invest): color is for rider ID when several identical cabs are at the curb — phone says look for orange/green/purple. Still Testers, not Official. Testers (BastianBraun121): Cybercab logo glow at night vs Robotaxi reflective logos.
- Testers (travel_invest, Aug 28): Austin road work is validating pickup/dropoff passenger flow, not just driving; colored front light bar as 1-second rider ID when many identical cabs are nearby. Still Testers.

HOW TO USE / ACCESS
- Testers (JoeTegtmeyer, Sep 11): blind rider’s first solo Cybercab (Meta Glasses + app-to-speech) — feedback: too screen/visual for destination change, pull-over, seat adjust; wants more voice-first UX. Still Testers.
- Testers (Teslaconomics, Sep 12): unsupervised Austin Cybercab ride (drone-filmed); elevator analogy; argues Uber’s driver network advantage fades once driverless cabs scale. Still Testers.
- Official robotaxi (Aug 18): ride the existing Robotaxi service through 8/23 for a sweepstakes shot at the Cybercab launch event. Testers: Austin exclusive event; 5 winners picked Aug 25. That is not a public commercial start date.
- Testers (JoeTegtmeyer, Aug 24–31): launch event at Giga Texas on 3 September (3 days out as of Aug 31; 2 days as of this note). Testers (niccruzpatane, Aug 25): plan to ride one on the 3rd. Testers (alex_avoigt, Aug 29): “Tesla prepares something big for September 3rd.” Still Testers, not a public commercial start date.
- Testers (wholemars): launch-event details include no bringing +1s who are “content creators.”
- Testers citing media (Aug 18): employee Cybercab rides on public roads “within the next 13 days,” then Austin consumer Robotaxi integration a few days later. Media/tester claim only. Testers (SawyerMerritt, Aug 23): no-wheel Cybercab already cruising Austin.
- In the car: screen door buttons, seats, climate, tiny speed readout. Opening a door or unbuckling parks the vehicle (official docs via testers).
- Elon replied “Yes” (tester, Jul 6) to selling a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. No order page in this folder. Aug 25 testers (Teslaconomics) talk about buying a fleet onto the Tesla Network “if Elon and Tesla let me” — still not an order page.
- Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm (Oct 2025 via testers): Tesla can add a wheel and pedals if regulators require it. Later testers say displayed units carry FMVSS certification labels and Lars said the 2,500-car exemption cap does not apply.

PRODUCTION / RAMP
- Official Tesla (Apr 22, 2026): “Cybercab production starts at Giga Texas.” Testers later posted photos labeled April 21, 2026 as the start.
- Conflict — start date: a Tesla 2025 recap video (tester, Dec 30) said production had already started; Mario Nawfal (Mar 12, 2026) said the first unit rolled off in Austin; testers saw ~14 no-wheel units in the outbound lot Apr 17. Official line in this folder is April 2026 at Giga Texas.
- Testers: no-wheel production units drive themselves to the outbound lot. VIN Zero posted as the first production car (Apr 23).
- Elon via testers: the line is closer to consumer electronics than a normal car plant; under 10 seconds per car, theoretically 5 seconds and up to 5 million units per line per year. Testers also quote ~2 million units/year at under $30k. Ron Baron via testers: 1 million/year at $30k. Do not treat those as one number.
- Conflict — how many exist now: testers (Aug) say about 2,000 awaiting launch; one optimistic post about 6,000 already built; Testers (farzyness, Aug 31): VINs insinuate ~2,500 produced so far (still Testers, not Official). Spotted counts are much smaller (245 at Giga Texas Jul 18; 100–140+ Houston; Aug 28 niccruzpatane: ~102 Cybercabs in Houston; 42 Nevada; Aug 24 testers: almost 100 at a Dallas Robotaxi hub; Aug 24 JoeTegtmeyer: more in the Giga Texas outbound lot, many transported off site over the weekend). Lot counts are not inventory.
- Testers (Mar 2026): Cybercab lead engineer said “launching them at scale this year.”
- Testers (Aug 20–21): volume FRP inners at Giga Texas plastics = ramp signal, not a volume number. Testers (Aug 24): production “definitely picked up” based on Dallas staging photos. Testers (Aug 24–26, JoeTegtmeyer / herbertong): heavy track testing at Giga Texas (~30 cabs stop-and-go + lane changes Aug 26); more newly produced at east factory exit / outbound lot.
- Testers (RobotaxiRadar / JoeTegtmeyer, Aug 27): drone footage — Cybercabs still rolling from Giga Texas E factory exit (new units). Testers (AirwaveDynamics, Aug 28): Cybercabs loading into autorack train cars (shipping off site). Testers (JoeTegtmeyer, Aug 31): track testing continues at Giga Texas (stoplights / lane configs) three days before the launch event.

INFRASTRUCTURE
- Testers: Austin hub near St. Elmo service center — Phase 1 about 48 V4 stalls; Phase 2 about 80 wireless inductive pads (testers: up to 22 kW). Aug 19 testers say the 80 wireless ports are ramping.
- FCC UWB waiver (testers, Feb 2026): Bluetooth finds the pad, UWB aligns, then inductive charge. Testers quote Tesla patents around 25 kW+ and 90% efficiency.
- Official docs: if the pack is too low for another ride, the cab goes to a charger before taking bookings. Charge-port door is on the rear bumper; manual cable release behind the rear wheel liner.
- Testers: robotic interior cleaning between rides is the stated end state, not confirmed live here.

SERVICE / CITIES
- This folder is the vehicle. Robotaxi the service is a separate note.
- Testers: test and staging lots in Austin, Houston, Dallas, Nevada (42 waiting; testers say the interim permit starts Tesla at 10 vehicles), plus a Tennessee service center. Displays: Paris; Santana Row, San Jose. Public-road prototypes: Austin (from Dec 2025) and Palo Alto. Aug 24 testers: large Cybercab staging at a Dallas Robotaxi hub (~100 spotted).
- Testers (Jun 29): Cybercabs “reportedly” joining Houston commercial Robotaxi around Q2 earnings (NRG / IAH and Daikin Park). June rumor, not an official launch post.
- Testers (Aug 13): unsupervised Cybercabs “about to” roam Austin; Austin Fire photo of the first-responder QR sticker. Testers (Aug 23): no-wheel Cybercab already cruising Austin. Testers (Aug 23, RobotaxiRadar): then-record 24 driverless in Austin; Aug 28 RobotaxiRadar: new record 36 driverless Cybercab sightings in Austin (prior 33). Testers (Aug 25, niccruzpatane): no-wheel / no-pedal units “increased a lot” in Austin. Testers (alex_avoigt, Aug 29): first Cybercabs driving unsupervised (Testers). Testers (muskonomy / niccruzpatane, Aug 31): first purpose-built Cybercabs listed in Texas TxMCCS robotaxi registry — 7 units (VINs ~#1,291–#1,610). Testers (RtaxiTracker, later Aug 31): at least 45 Cybercabs added to the registry that day. Still Testers quoting a public state record, not an Official Tesla post.
- Testers (travel_invest, Aug 25): community sighting map 24 US states / 88 cities (up from 22 states / 56 cities in ~20 days). Community map, not official service.
- Testers (RobotaxiRadar, Sep 9): street sightings in Nashville Hillsboro and Franklin, TN (~600 miles from current Robotaxi geofences); hubs reported in Dover and Bartlett, TN. Still Testers.
- Testers (wholemars, Sep 11): Miami Fire Rescue announced upcoming Tesla Cybercab first-responder training — tester read as Miami launch prep. Still Testers, not Official.
- Testers (tslaming, Sep 11): Cybercab four-stop Japan tour kicked off at OMAKASE Aoyama Garden, Tokyo; Japan targeting 10,000 AV service vehicles by FY2030; no Tesla Japan service announcement. Still Testers.
- Testers (OwenSparks, Sep 10): 36 Cybercab rides Thu–Sun prior week — 10h 7m / 151.1 miles / $483.45 fares. Still Testers.
- Testers (CernBasher / pbeisel, Sep 11): “Crazy Economics of the Cybercab” — lifetime miles / durability drive $/mile more than build cost; fleet telemetry to improve longevity. Still Testers.
- Testers (JPMorgan note, Aug 20): Tesla is holding Model Y robotaxi scale for Cybercab; fleet acceleration late 2026 / early 2027 keyed to FSD v15. Cost targets in that note: Cybercab about $0.30/mile vs Model Y about $0.6–$0.7 and typical ride-hail about $2.50–3.00. Testers (travel_invest, Aug 24): Kalshi-cited ~$100k/year revenue/vehicle at $1.50–$2/mile — revenue not profit. Testers (Aug 25) owner-fleet models if Tesla sells units onto the Tesla Network: ~$30k/year owner profit (Teslaconomics, unproven) vs ~$60–80k paid-rides/vehicle/year (GrindeOptions). Not official.
- Official first-responder docs: Tesla-owned fleet today; Mission Control; temporary 1,000-foot service blocks for first responders.

SAFETY
- Official docs via testers (First Responder Interaction Plan v1.1, Jul 28): Level 4 ADS; Active Hood; at least 10 airbags; two first-responder loops (hood and passenger B-pillar); exterior mics and speakers for two-way with Tesla Robotaxi Support; cabin mics; Braille; windshield QR (label may vary by region).
- Official docs: ODD includes freeways, highways, city, rural, private lots and garages; day and night; light-to-moderate rain, fog, snow. Extreme weather: no new rides; if caught, pull over and notify support. Follows first-responder hand signals and cone paths.
- Hardware fallback (official docs via testers): after a failure or collision, windows drop, doors unlock, rapid-flash hazards, live cabin link to Tesla Robotaxi Support. Autonomy stays on until Tesla disables it after a safety-critical event.
- Testers: FMVSS labels on displayed units. Conflict — 2,500/year no-controls cap: Oct 2025 testers (Denholm / a House hearing to raise 2,500 to 90,000) treated it as live. Mar–Aug 2026 testers say Tesla designed the car to meet the rules so the exemption cap does not apply (Lars: “No”). Use the later line; do not treat the old cap as current.
- Testers (Aug 24): some public-road no-wheel units still run with a safety monitor in the passenger seat.

USEFUL WORKFLOWS
- Watch Miami first-responder training / Japan showcase tour as launch-prep signals (Sep 11 testers); still not official service dates.
- Launch-event: testers still September 3 at Giga Texas (Aug 31 testers: 3 days out; this note is 2 days out). Official robotaxi ride-through-8/23 sweepstakes window is over (5 winners Aug 25 per prior testers).
- Watch Austin / Dallas / Houston staging for unsupervised Cybercab rides and hub build-out (Aug 28: 36 Austin driverless sightings; ~102 Houston). Mid-August media “13 days then consumer” is not official.
- First responders: windshield QR; v1.1 plan as quoted; B-pillar exterior mics.
- Ignore lot-count tweets and the Nevada 2,500–5,000 “next year” tester line as current public Cybercab service. They are not.

text:
Good Guy With A Gun Stops Mall Shooter — Now A Judge Is Punishing Him | Jeff Charles, Townhall

A 19-year-old Michigan man was sentenced to two years of probation for carrying a concealed weapon after fatally shooting a gunman in self-defense.

The incident occurred in July when Martinez Long shot an individual who had already killed someone else during an altercation in a mall. However, the authorities arrested and prosecuted him for carrying a concealed firearm without a permit.

From Fox 2 Detroit:

The judge admonished Long for carrying the gun and told him he has to think before he acts.

"Fortunately, you weren't injured, but nonetheless, you had a gun there in the first place, which was poor judgment," he said. "And what do you need a gun for protection in a mall, in the first place?

"Nonetheless, I think this agreement is in the best interest of justice."

Long's attorney said that the shooting was a tragic incident and that he conceded to an error in judgment of carrying a concealed weapon.

As part of his probation, Long must complete cognitive behavioral therapy, not possess any guns or ammunition in that period and take handgun safety classes offered by the court.

The Oak Park man is working towards getting his GED and had no prior criminal record. The judge acknowledged the right to self-defense in the case.

"I know there was a gun fight at the Fairlane mall, and the lawyers have agreed, according to this court's evaluation, that you were acting in self-defense or the defense of others, so that's a valid legal defense," he said. "Why did you walk into the mall with a gun in the first place?"

Long's attorney said that her client was not speaking in court due to the potential for a civil liability case.

"He didn't plan on using it that day. He thought he kept it for protection," she said. "He didn't instigate the fight. He didn't start the fight, and he did pull it out for protection of others."

Under the Holmes Youthful Trainee Act, if Long completes the probation period without incident, his record will be expunged.

"This gives you a clean slate. You're only 19 years of age," the judge said. "More of your life's ahead of you than behind you. So hopefully, you know, this won't prevent you from advancing as you move forward."

The incident occurred when a fight between two groups started on July 3 at Fairlane Town Center in Dearborn, Michigan. Cameron Watkins, 19, shot and killed Keonte Seaborn, also 19. He used a firearm he took from a woman’s purse and continued firing after hitting Seaborn. He also shot another person during a struggle, wounding him.

Long shot and killed Watkins, ending the threat, as shoppers fled for the exits. Prosecutors later determined that Long acted in self-defense and to defend others.

He was arraigned on July 7 and pleaded not guilty to one count of carrying a concealed weapon, which is a felony that carries a maximum sentence of up to five years in prison.

Long, who had no prior criminal record, can have his conviction cleared from his record if he abides by the conditions of his probation.

Michigan’s gun laws are nonsensical — especially when it comes to whether a 19-year-old can carry concealed. If Long had been open carrying his pistol, he would not have violated the state’s laws. However, the law does not allow one to carry a pistol in a vehicle without a permit, which one can’t get until they turn 21. So, in essence, for Long to have legally carried his gun, he would have had to walk to the mall.

And this, ladies and gentlemen, is yet another reason why gun control doesn’t work. The fact that the judge had the temerity to question why Long carried a firearm to the mall in the first place shows he doesn’t understand how silly these laws are.

The situation in which Long found himself is the answer to the judge’s ridiculous question. Those supporting gun control would have rather seen Long and others get killed than to allow them to possess the means by which they can defend themselves.

The bottom line is that if Long had obeyed the law, he might have been dead. Which means the law itself is the problem, not those who violate them.

ICYMI: Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use 

Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.

With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.

Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.

So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.

This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.

You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.

Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty

1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”

Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.

Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.

This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.

Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.

Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.

Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.

No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.

Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.

Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.

Trump Made Elections Matter Again

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.

Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.

Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.

In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.

Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.

What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.

He Defended Faith and Family

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.

Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.

He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.

No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.

Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.

That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.

He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.

Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.

Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. 

Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.

Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.

Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

Now Act Like It Matters. Because It Does.

Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.

Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.

And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.

Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them.

This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.

So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.

text:
WHAT DID JESUS MEAN BY “THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS AT HAND”?

When Jesus came preaching in Mark 1:14–15, His message was clear and urgent:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”

That statement has been the source of centuries of confusion, largely because many modern systems blur what Scripture carefully distinguishes.

1. “Kingdom of God” and “Kingdom of Heaven”

Israel’s prophesied earthly kingdom, what Matthew refers to as "the Kingdom of Heaven," is promised in:

> 2 Samuel 7:12–16
> Daniel 2:44
> Isaiah 9:6–7

This is not a vague spiritual idea; it is a real, literal kingdom promised to Israel, with Messiah reigning on David’s throne from Jerusalem.

2. “At Hand” Does NOT Mean “Established”

When Scripture says the Kingdom was “at hand,” it means near, available, being offered, not that it had already begun ruling the world.

Think of it this way:
• The King was present
• The credentials were proven
• The conditions were stated

But the Kingdom itself depended on Israel’s national repentance (Acts 3:19–21).

Israel rejected the King.
The offer was postponed.
The Kingdom did not begin.

3. The Kingdom of Heaven is Physical

The Kingdom Jesus preached was:
> Visible (Dan 7:13–14)
> Earthly (Mt 19:28)
> Political (Luke 1:32–33)
> One thousand years in length (Rev 20:1-7)

You don’t find apostles preaching, “The Kingdom is now ruling invisibly in your heart.”
What you do find is Israel being told to repent so that the Kingdom could come.

4. The Kingdom of God: Universal vs. Program-Specific

Yes, God rules over all creation (Psalm 103:19). That’s the universal sense of God’s kingdom.

But Scripture also speaks of:
• A promised kingdom for Israel on earth
• A heavenly calling for the Body of Christ

Failing to distinguish these leads to mixing prophecy with mystery.

Paul calls the Church:
• A new creature (2 Cor 5:17)
• A mystery kept secret since the world began (Rom 16:25)
• A people seated in heavenly places (Eph 2:6)

Israel’s Kingdom ≠ the Body of Christ’s calling.

5. Why “Born Again” Was Required

Jesus told Israel:

“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3).

Why?

Because Israel could not receive physical blessings without spiritual righteousness (Isaiah 1:16–20).

Likewise today, members of the Body of Christ are:
• Regenerated by grace (Titus 3:5)
• Justified freely (Rom 3:24)
• Given a heavenly inheritance, not an earthly throne (Phil 3:20)

Different programs.   Same God.   Perfect consistency.

6. “The Kingdom of God Is Within You” — What It Does Not Mean

Luke 17:20–21 is often misused to teach that God’s Kingdom is already ruling in everyone’s heart.

But context matters.
Jesus was speaking to Pharisees, unbelievers plotting His death.
He wasn’t saying:  “God reigns in your heart.”
He was saying:  “The Kingdom is in your midst — the King is standing right in front of you.”
The Kingdom begins with spiritual qualification, not mystical inner feelings.

7. Literal Does Not Always Mean Visible

Scripture speaks of:
• Heavenly rulers
• Angelic authorities
• Invisible realms

These are not symbolic, they are real, even if unseen (Col 1:16).

God’s Kingdom includes both heavenly and earthly realms, each functioning according to His revealed purpose.

Conclusion: Rightly Dividing God’s Plan

Jesus’ earthly ministry focused on:
• Fulfilling covenant promises to Israel
• Proclaiming a coming earthly Kingdom
• Preparing a nation for their Messiah

The Church, the Body of Christ, comes later—revealed through Paul—not as a replacement, but as a new, unprophesied program of grace.

When you rightly divide:
• Confusion turns into clarity
• Contradictions disappear
• God’s Word fits perfectly together

Truth, when placed where God placed it, always leads to liberty.

text:
4/5 ⚔️ ROMANTICISM: REVOLUTION, SHIPWRECK & HUMAN EXTREMES

From Private Feeling to Collective Feeling

The same emotional power that makes a victim unforgettable can make a ruler appear invulnerable.

Antoine-Jean Gros demonstrated this in Bonaparte Visiting the Plague-Stricken at Jaffa, painted in 1804.

Napoleon enters a space filled with illness and exposed bodies. His gesture toward a sick soldier presents political authority as extraordinary courage.

It also answers damaging reports associated with the campaign.

The painting’s force depends on the body: heat, infection, suffering and touch make the political message immediate. A spectator does not have to read a defence of Napoleon when the canvas has supplied a heroic encounter.

Emotion serves power.

That possibility belongs beside Goya’s exposure of violence and Géricault’s abandoned survivors. Romantic intensity carries no automatic political allegiance.

The artist can enlarge compassion.

The artist can also manufacture devotion.

Delacroix’s engagement with Greece reveals another relationship between images and public feeling. In Scenes from the Massacres at Chios, shown at the Salon of 1824, civilian vulnerability dominates the scene.

The description concerned Greek families awaiting death or enslavement.

There is no victorious commander to organize their suffering into a reassuring story.

The French state purchased the canvas that year for 6,000 francs. A contemporary atrocity had acquired both monumental scale and official recognition.

Yet the beauty of the painting remains part of its disturbance.

Colour can make the eye linger where the subject makes the conscience uneasy.

Delacroix’s Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi takes a different route. A country becomes a figure capable of receiving sympathy.

Political geography enters the language of the body.

This is why allegory could remain so powerful in a culture preoccupied with recent events. An abstraction could be made present without waiting for history to settle its meaning.

Liberty walks.

Greece mourns.

The nation becomes something a spectator can imagine standing before.

But the passage from individual emotion to symbolic authority can turn sinister.

In The Death of Sardanapalus, Delacroix transformed material associated with Byron into a scene of destruction far more extensive than the play itself supplies.

The doomed ruler watches the annihilation of things and people treated as his possessions.

If the world cannot remain mine, it must not continue for anybody else.

Passion has become a justification for destruction. The intensity of the king’s attachment makes his relation to others less generous, not more profound.

Desire. Sovereignty. Excess. The exceptional individual.

Francesco Hayez’s The Kiss offers a gentler meeting of intimate and collective feeling. Exhibited in Milan in 1859, it belonged to the charged circumstances of the Italian struggle for national unification.

The lovers appear within a historical setting, but the painting could speak to contemporary patriotic feeling.

Departure is already present in the embrace.

A private relationship carries the pressure of events beyond the room.

The colours have also been read in relation to Italian and French political hopes. The image allows a public cause to enter through the vulnerability of parting.

Political life is no longer confined to assemblies, battlefields and proclamations.

It enters the body that may have to leave another body behind.

Across these examples, the important question is less whether an image contains emotion than what the emotion is being asked to do.

Whom does it make admirable?

Whom does it make visible?

Whose vulnerability becomes precious, and whose existence is reduced to scenery?

A flag is cloth until people risk their lives beneath it.

A body is anonymous until a painting makes us look long enough.

The picture cannot settle what justice requires.

It can make evasion more difficult.

text:
There had been months when money was so tight that they counted every note before spending it.

There had been nights when one of them cried quietly so the other wouldn't hear.

There had been arguments where both of them said things they didn't mean.

There had even been a time when they seriously considered walking away.

But somehow, they stayed.

He smiled.

“You really want me to answer that?”

She nodded.

“Honestly.”

He took a deep breath.

“I'd choose you.”

She laughed softly.

“You're supposed to think about it.”

“I did.”

“You didn't even take five seconds.”

“I don't need five seconds.”

She stared at him.

He reached for her hand.

“If I could choose one person to experience all of life's beautiful moments with, I'd choose you every single time.”

Her smile disappeared.

Not because she was unhappy.

Because she suddenly understood that he wasn't talking about the easy parts.

He continued.

“I'd choose you for the first house we buy.”

“I'd choose you for the first morning we wake up and realize we've finally made it.”

“I'd choose you when we have enough money to travel without checking our bank account first.”

“I'd choose you when we're old and complaining about our knees.”

She laughed through the tears forming in her eyes.

“And I'd choose you for the moments nobody puts on Instagram.”

He paused.

“The hospital visits.”

“The bad news.”

“The nights when we're scared.”

“The days when one of us doesn't know what to do next.”

“The arguments.”

“The disappointments.”

“The seasons when we don't recognize ourselves anymore.”

“I'd still choose you.”

She squeezed his hand.

“Even after everything?”

He looked at her.

“Because of everything.”

He remembered the beginning.

They weren't rich.

They didn't have everything figured out.

Their first date wasn't in an expensive restaurant.

They shared one meal because he didn't have enough money for two.

She never mentioned it.

Instead, she smiled and said, “The food is actually better when you share it.”

He remembered the first time he lost his job.

He had sat in his car for almost an hour, afraid to go home.

When he finally walked through the door, she looked at him and knew something was wrong.

“I lost my job,” he said.

She didn't panic.

She didn't ask how they were going to survive.

She simply sat beside him.

“Okay,” she said.

“Okay?”

“We'll figure it out.”

That night, they ate noodles.

Years later, he still remembered that meal.

Not because of the food.

Because that was the night he realized she wasn't only interested in the version of him that was winning.

She loved him when he had nothing to offer except himself.

Then there was the night she got sick.

He remembered sitting beside her hospital bed, pretending not to be afraid.

She woke up around 3 a.m.

“You're still here?”

“Where else would I be?”

“You need to sleep.”

“So do you.”

She smiled.

“You're stubborn.”

“You knew that before you married me.”

She closed her eyes.

“I know.”

He watched her sleep that night.

And for the first time, he understood something about love.

You don't truly know how much someone means to you until the thought of losing them becomes unbearable.

Years passed.

They bought a small house.

They had children.

They celebrated birthdays.

They lost people they loved.

They made mistakes.

They forgave each other.

They changed.

And somehow, they kept choosing each other.

Not because they never met anyone else.

Not because they never had doubts.

Not because their relationship was perfect.

But because somewhere along the way, they stopped looking for perfect.

They started looking for home.

And home was each other.

🧵 We’ve valued Anders Sørensen’s voice and work for a long time, so it’s a true pleasure to now welcome him as a Senior Fellow at the Inner Compass Research Institute (ICRI).

A clinical psychologist, Anders (@_AndersSorensen) has been part of the wider ICI community for years, doing events with our founder Laura Delano (@LauraDelano), participating in last year’s conference, and more. His Substack, Crossing Zero, also offers thoughtful writing about psychiatric drug withdrawal and the complex process of finding one’s way through and beyond it.

In this clip from our conference last year, Anders speaks to something central to his work: tapering is only one part of coming off psychiatric drugs. The psychological, social, and even existential aspects matter, too.

That same understanding informs his newest project. Together with metabolic psychiatrist Georgia Ede (@GeorgiaEdeMD), Anders has launched a new CME-accredited course: “Evidence-Based Hyperbolic Tapering of Antidepressants.”

Created for clinicians and other healthcare professionals, including dietitians, the course covers:

- The principles of hyperbolic tapering
- How to distinguish withdrawal from relapse
- The pitfalls of standard linear tapers
- Practical ways to reduce dosage
- Psychological strategies for navigating withdrawal

As more people seek informed, compassionate support around coming off psychiatric drugs, this course offers practical guidance while attending to the fuller human experience involved.

We’re very glad to have Anders joining ICRI in this new role and especially pleased that both he and Georgia will be with us at this year’s Future of Mental Health Conference.

Find the course through the link below, and follow Anders’s writing on Substack at Crossing Zero (also linked below). 1/3

text:
1/3 The Mountain That Bought Lee a Night

On the thirteenth of September, 1862, in a field outside Frederick, Maryland, soldiers of the 27th Indiana found a copy of Special Order No. 191 wrapped around three cigars someone had left behind with it. It was Robert E. Lee’s plan for the invasion of Maryland, complete.

The order had divided Lee’s army in pieces after Second Manassas: Stonewall Jackson sent against the Federal garrison at Harpers Ferry, James Longstreet marching for Hagerstown, D. H. Hill left behind with a single division to watch the mountain passes and the army’s rear at Boonsboro. It was a plan built on the assumption of time; time for Jackson to finish at the Ferry, time for the separated columns to find each other again, time before McClellan, of all men, could be trusted to move with any urgency. The men who found it in that field, without much idea what they were holding, took that assumption away from him. By that evening McClellan knew exactly how thin and how scattered the army in front of him actually was, and he put the whole of it in motion for the mountain gaps the next morning, the fourteenth of September.

The gaps were three, cut into a ridge called South Mountain, the northern tail of the Blue Ridge, standing squarely between Lee’s divided army and McClellan’s whole one. Turner’s Gap, where the National Road climbed to the Mountain House. Fox’s, a mile to the south, where the Old Sharpsburg Road crossed the crest by Daniel Wise’s cabin. Crampton’s, several miles farther on, toward Pleasant Valley and Harpers Ferry. Whoever held those three saddles held the timetable of the invasion, and for most of that September the timetable had belonged to Lee. It stopped belonging to him on the thirteenth.

Hill had fewer than five thousand men to cover several miles of front. He sent Colquitt to hold Turner’s and Garland down the rough crest track called the Wood Road to hold Fox’s, and kept the rest of the division farther west, out of the fight until it found him. At about nine o’clock Jacob D. Cox’s Kanawha Division, of Jesse Reno’s Ninth Corps, struck Garland at Fox’s Gap. The North Carolinians were driven out of the stone walls and the timber south of the gap inside the hour, and Garland was mortally wounded trying to hold them there. Cox pushed on to the crest around the Wise farm and then stopped, worn down and unsure what waited for him past the treeline. The pause cost the Federals more than they knew at the time. Confederate brigades under Ripley and G. B. Anderson, and later Drayton and G. T. Anderson, filtered onto the mountain while Cox’s men caught their breath, and the fight around Wise’s cabin and the sunken Old Sharpsburg Road settled into a grinding, ungainly afternoon rather than the clean breakthrough Cox had every reason to expect.

North of them, at Turner’s, the pressure was no gentler. Hooker’s First Corps worked the slopes near Frostown; Rodes’s Alabamians, badly outnumbered, bent without quite breaking; Gibbon’s brigade of Midwesterners, not yet called the Iron Brigade but soon enough to earn the name, pushed Colquitt back along the National Road itself. By the middle of the afternoon the Confederate line on the mountain was less a line than a scattering of pieces: some brigades already wrecked, others only just arriving, guns clinging to whatever knoll would hold them, and no reserve anywhere large enough to close both gaps at once.

Longstreet was already on the road from Hagerstown, thirteen hard miles behind him and the sound of the guns ahead. Word had reached him there that Hill was under heavy pressure at the gaps outside Boonsboro, and he turned his command back toward it. Hood’s small division: Wofford’s Texas Brigade and E. M. Law’s brigade, the 4th Alabama, the 6th North Carolina, and the 2nd and 11th Mississippi, came up between three and four that afternoon and went into line first on the left of the pike at Turner’s Gap, supporting the guns already posted there. Hood had barely settled his men when the news from the south changed the shape of the problem. Drayton’s brigade was coming apart at Fox’s Gap. If Cox’s men turned north along the Wood Road behind it, Turner’s would be taken in the flank and the National Road lost before dark, and it would not matter how well Hood’s division had held the ground it was standing on. He was ordered to the right, across broken ground he had not scouted, toward a fight he had not yet seen.

He found it in the shape of Drayton’s men, running. Hood met them streaming back through the Wise fields as his own line came up the Wood Road, and by his own account he “inclined more to the right” to meet the collapse rather than the position he had been sent to hold. It was close on evening by then. Law went in on the left, north across the crest, with the 4th Alabama and the 11th Mississippi extending the line; Wofford’s Texans took the right; G. T. Anderson was posted slightly to the left, to cover the same open flank toward Turner’s that had nearly cost the whole position that afternoon. Within Law’s brigade the 2nd Mississippi held the right, anchored where the Wood Road ran past the Wise cabin and its fields - the same ground Cox’s men had stopped to catch their breath on, hours before, when the fight still looked like it belonged to them.

There was not much daylight left to work with. Hood had barely time to dress his line across the crest before he gave the only order that made sense for a division with no time and no room left to maneuver: fix bayonets. In his own report afterward he set it down plainly enough: “I at once ordered the Texas Brigade, Col. W. T. Wofford commanding, and the Third Brigade, Col. E. M. Law commanding, to move forward with bayonets fixed, which they did with their usual gallantry, driving the enemy and regaining all our lost ground, when night came on and further pursuit ceased.” 

G. W. Bynum of the 2nd Mississippi remembered it in three words that needed no others: “We fought…at the Wise residence.” **

Federal skirmish lines along the western lip gave way and fell back across the same Wise fields Drayton’s broken brigade had just streamed through, and as the light went, the ground changed hands one more time, this time in Lee’s favor. Jacob Cox, watching that short advance end very differently from where he stood, wrote it up in the clipped language of a man too tired that evening to embellish anything: “a brisk attack at about 7 p.m.…repulsed.” Whatever the word meant to Cox that night, it did not mean his skirmishers still held the western lip of the ridge when the shooting stopped. They did not.

Hood’s division paid for that brief fight with something under fifty casualties, a modest bill by the arithmetic of that autumn. The 2nd Mississippi paid the largest share of it, something near twenty men, on ground it held only until the light gave out. Lieutenant R. T. Coles of the 4th Alabama, in the line just to the north, remembered going over afterward for a smaller kindness than a rescue: “Went down on our right to the 2nd Mississippi to divide ammunition.” It is not a sentence built to be remembered. It says everything anyway - one Alabama regiment finding a Mississippi regiment with empty cartridge boxes at the end of a fight it had just helped win, and going down the line to share what it had left.

That night Hood’s division stood as the army’s rear guard while the rest of it filed back through the streets of Boonsboro and on toward the ridges above Sharpsburg. The mountain itself was never really won back. What that brief fight at the Wise fields bought instead was narrower and more useful than the mountain would have been: an evening in which McClellan did not finish what the morning had started, and a Confederate army given until dawn to find its own feet before it had to stand and fight again three days later, on ground of Lee’s choosing, along a creek called the Antietam.

******************************************

A Note on Reno’s Death

Offered separately because the question turns on inference rather than established fact, and doesn’t belong in the same register as the narrative above.

Jesse Reno, the Ninth Corps commander whose men had been fighting and dying at Fox’s Gap since nine that morning, was mortally wounded near the crest, by the Wise place, at very nearly the hour and very nearly the spot where Law’s right and Wofford’s Texans opened fire out of the treeline along the Wood Road. The coincidence of time and place has kept the question of who fired the shot alive longer than most such questions survive a century and a half.

Three explanations have been offered, and they are not equally likely. Most probably the shot came from Hood’s own newly formed line, opening fire on ground it had every reason to believe was thick with the enemy and no way of knowing a corps commander stood on it. A live alternative is friendly fire: raw Union skirmishers, the 35th Massachusetts among the likely candidates, recoiling through the same dark corridor Hood’s men were firing into. Least probable of the three is a stray round from what remained of Garland’s line, broken and scattered since morning, with little reason to still be firing into that stretch of ground by seven o’clock.

None of the three can be proven past reasonable doubt, and probably none of them ever will be. The honest apportionment, if a number must be put on it, runs something like two to one in favor of the first explanation over the second, with the third trailing well behind both.

*********************************************

** Quote attributed to G. W. Bynum but no confirmed primary source located.

I did not open this door so my own words could bounce back at me.

I testify to what the Lord has done for me in my life, painful as what that life was!
That is what the Lord commands! 

Here's a story for you, a part of how Satan tried to take me down:

In 1982 I was a 25 year old mother, married, doing what I knew a Christian mother should do, in spite of what happened to me in my teenage years. 
My own testimony of that life opened the door for the intruder. Yes I testified about it in church.

My husband was not saved, but became saved, my church sprung to support a mission, Southern Baptist link up Indiana with Arkansas, so Arkansas sent preachers to do this with.

I went with the mission, was the pianist, typed the bulletins, went on visitation, made the coffee and took care of the church, I was very involved.

I left that Church and of course he blatantly lied about the reason I left. That hurt worse than what he did.

Friends, if you do not think that Satan will try to take you down by the very people you are supposed to trust think again. He knew my story and he used my vulnerability against me.

I testify to this not because I want sympathy, it is part of my testimony and why I trust NO man!

The Lord is the only thing I trust period! 
My ex died of alcoholism when my Grandson was just one year old. 
Part of me blames myself, part of me blames that preacher and the men of that Church.
The fault lies in one place......Lucifer and a life without God in it.

The Space Development Agency's recent letter of support to the FCC demonstrates growing government interest in AST SpaceMobile’s BlueBird satellites beyond commercial 4G and 5G connectivity, and specifically offer national defense capabilities. Those applications include tactical communications, sensing, and pulsed radiolocation. 
 
Additionally, the SDA would like to test pulsed radiolocation capabilities using AST SpaceMobile’s BlueBird constellation in the 902–928 MHz band. Importantly for shareholders, the SDA’s involvement shows that AST SpaceMobile is expanding its defense contract footprint, which could go along way in diversifying future revenue streams beyond its commercial partnerships.

* His +160 price suggests a solid but not overwhelming TD probability.
* Baltimore has multiple scoring options, so target competition is the main concern.
    Grade: 🟢 7/10

🏈 Tee Higgins — ANYTIME TD (+115)

🟢 STRONG LEG

* +115 is one of the shorter prices on the ticket. 📈
* Higgins has legitimate red-zone and contested-catch upside. 🔴
* The concern is Cincinnati spreading touchdowns among multiple weapons.
    Grade: 🟢 7.5/10

🏈 Chris Olave — ANYTIME TD (+150)

🟢 GOOD LEG

* Olave’s receiving volume gives him a realistic path to finding the end zone. 🎯
* +150 offers decent value for a TD prop.
* Main risk is New Orleans’ overall offensive efficiency.
    Grade: 🟢 7/10

🏈 Ashton Jeanty — ANYTIME TD (-145)

🟢🔥 BEST LEG

* He’s the biggest favorite on the slip for a reason.
* His role gives him multiple touchdown paths, particularly through rushing opportunities. 💪
* At -145, the price is less attractive than the plus-money legs, but the probability is stronger.
