text:
🚨 An anonymous “veteran” account is attacking the RNLI while selling remigration, civil-war talk, and a politically vetted male cell, trained in stealth, hunting, and close-quarters combat...

There’s a particular kind of authority that comes from having served in the military which is earned through the often boring specifics real soldiers carry without needing to perform them.

Anonymous account @ArthurBearHunt borrows the trappings of that authority to sell remigration, civil war rhetoric, and a Devon “brotherhood” that looks less like a hiking club and more like a politically filtered outdoor cell with militia branding and a closed application process.

‘Arthur Hunt’ appeared on @X in October 2025. The bio reads “Veteran, Loyal to the Soil,” alongside support for British farmers and a call for remigration. The account has around 1,400 followers.

There’s no unit, no years of service, no theatre, no regiment that matches the costume, and no photograph of an actual living man. The avatar is a colourised photograph of a WWII Wiltshire Regiment soldier, a stock image doing the work a real service record would otherwise do.

The posting style leans on military vocabulary when convenient, calling critics “walts” while sitting on nothing but a historical photograph and a one-word self-description. Genuine veterans, when challenged, tend to produce the mundane details that prove service: dates, postings, units. This account never does. None of that proves he never served. It just shows that he won’t back up his claim with any evidence, and that the absence doesn’t stop him trading on it.

The account’s rhetoric is disturbing: “I vote for civil war”; “Remigration, or civil war and mass deaths”; “They don’t respect us, they respect violence.” The claim is that political persuasion has failed and force remains the only option. The same binary shows up elsewhere. 25 January 2026: “If you lean even remotely left your traitor. The left have been the enemy for a long time.”

We see how this plays out. Arthur’s response when Poole Old Lifeboat Museum closed after volunteers were verbally abused: “This is utterly fantastic. It will hit the RNLI financially... @RNLI has no future in this country. Traitors, there is blood on your hands. Absolutely fuck the RNLI.”

Celebrating the negative consequences of abuse aimed at volunteers, and treating the financial harm it causes as vindication, is about as bare an admission of punitive intent as this kind of account tends to offer. A separate post accuses the RNLI of “importing rape and murder,” the same target recurring across months.

A pattern emerges across posts: name a hated institution, the RNLI, the government, “globalists”; fuse it to rape, murder, or a name like Lee Rigby’s; declare that war is already underway; offer belonging, through soil, veterans, or a “fyrd”;  and mock anyone who still speaks like a citizen rather than a combatant.

That structure doesn’t need an explicit call to violence to function as one. It only needs a country in which violence, riots, and “mass deaths” are the realistic remaining options.

This sequence, ‘traitors first, invaders second’, is not a local invention. The order of operations, with domestic “traitors” targeted before migrants, is standard in far-right and accelerationist rhetoric, and runs through William Luther Pierce’s 1978 novel The Turner Diaries, in which a cell of white extremists executes “race traitors” before turning to non-white people.

On 27 June 2026, former US Navy SEAL and civil-war novelist Matt Bracken posted the slogan “First the traitors, then the invaders” over an image of a man pointing a handgun at the camera. Elon Musk replied “Yes.” The post reached 463,000 views. Arthur Hunt’s RNLI posts already run that same order: name the domestic “traitors,” then the “invasion.”

A few rhetorical mechanisms do most of the work. Contempt operates as method, not commentary: “Not your turn with the family braincell.” “Clown.” “Boot on your tongue.” None of this argues with a critic, it attempts to humiliate them, fuelling polarisation and keeping an audience oriented toward grievance rather than thought.

The militia aesthetic supplies narrative stakes, not hobby content: bushcraft and rehearsal for “the real thing” are framed as preparation for a coming collapse, making apocalyptic claims feel actionable rather than merely believable.

The content also runs on a closed either/or structure. Natives are coded as soil, farmers, and warriors; outsiders as parasites, snakes, and imported violence; institutions that don’t comply as treason; anyone offering a middle position as a “cuck.”

Once that binary is set, no individual case needs proving, a particular RNLI volunteer doesn’t need to be shown to have imported anything, the category itself is presumed guilty. That’s what makes the framework resistant to correction: it was never built to be falsified by a counter-example.

Finally, the account oscillates between disavowing and endorsing violence. A peaceful protest gets praised as “the right direction.” Other posts insist voting is finished, that “they” only respect violence, that civil war is already on.

This oscillation is a recognisable feature of accelerationist-adjacent rhetoric, claiming the rhetorical high ground of reasonableness while normalising the language of violent conflict, without ever technically crossing a threshold into an explicit unlawful call to arms.

None of this depends on knowing who is behind the keyboard. The pattern works the same whether it’s one person, a small group, or a persona built for effect. What can be assessed is the output, not the psychology of its author.

This isn’t “adjacent” to the far right. It’s deep inside it. 

Remigration is the account’s policy core, not a slogan added for edge. Blood-and-soil imagery runs throughout: “Loyal to the Soil,” ancestral farmers, “no cost too high, no pain too great, no voice too loud, no act too harsh.”

The Great Replacement is treated as kinetic war already underway.

Political Islam is framed in civilisational terms.

English natives are described as not existing in law.

The enemies list, “Zionists, Islamists, globalists, communists, satanists,” is the standard far-right conspiracy bundle, not a foreign policy critique.

Reform UK is written off as “left-wing” and unwilling to commit to remigration. Restore, which he claims he joined early, is mocked for taking “ex Tory’s, and ex leftists” instead of “super based... highly experienced ex military types.”

The complaint is an insider’s, not an outsider’s: he describes paying a Restore membership nearly a year ago and being a member since before it was a party, which makes the disappointment sharper: even the outfit he backed from the start is judged too soft on who it lets in.

‘Arthur’ regularly promotes @devonshirefyrd, styled as “The Fyrd,” a Devon-based “brotherhood of outdoor athletes, enthusiasts, veterans & hobbyists” who “come together to train in the wild.”

The word fyrd is the Old English militia levy, and the branding does exactly the work that name suggests. Created February 2026, it has 958 followers on X. The linked Instagram account, @devonfyrd, is considerably larger, 5,177 followers from a single post, as of writing, with a bio adding “Ethos-driven. Land & heritage focused.”

Their poster lists Survival, Navigation, Bushcraft, CQC. CQC is close-quarters combat - not a skill a hiking club teaches. The pinned post makes the vetting process explicit: “Interested? Message us... We’ll see if we’re aligned. If it feels right, a digital Welcome Pack may be sent or a meet arranged.” Nothing is offered unconditionally. “Aligned” is the filter, and the group screens for the same remigration and collapse politics Arthur posts openly. CQC on the poster and “aligned” in the pitch are the giveaway: recruitment copy wearing an outdoor-club skin.

Is anyone actually training? Probably, in a limited way. There are a few original-looking outdoor photographs of at least one man in camouflage with a loaded pack, repeated claims of field sessions, and a genuine application process rather than a simple “like and share.” Arthur talks about it as something forming in Devon, free, with no subscription. Copycats already treat it as a template, a South Wales account has launched an “Agoge” ruck programme, and nationalist accounts are calling for versions “set up all over the country.” But the organisational substance is thin: no Companies House entity, no website, no public venue, no named instructor, no insurance, no advertised dates. 

Months into its existence, the account is still asking strangers to DM if they want in. The most accurate description is one or a few men in Devon doing kit walks and trying to build a politically filtered outdoor circle around themselves. The battalion suggested by the marketing is not there.

No founder is named, and that is by design. But the operator cluster isn’t subtle: Arthur Hunt writes the identical soil, tribe, and “get ready” copy, and announced “a brotherhood forming in Devon” the same day the Fyrd posted “The Fyrd is rising.” The Fyrd then quote-posted his “Xbox generation... the real thing” recruitment thread.

Arthur’s account predates the Fyrd’s by four months. One account carries the politics; the other, more anodyne-sounding, carries the “training,” and stays just inside “fitness and heritage” while Arthur’s account supplies the explicit war talk. Read separately, each looks like a hobbyist and a crank. Read together, they are one operation with two functions.

Strip the branding away and the offer is not fitness or heritage hiking. It is a politically vetted male cell, trained in stealth, hunting, and close-quarters combat, built around a story in which voting is noise, collapse is coming, and readiness for “the real thing” is the only rational response.

The instruction to replicate the model in every county turns a single Devon project into a template, the Active Club and identitarian outdoor-network pattern, repackaged with English branding. Free, with “no subs,” is not generosity. It removes the ordinary consumer relationship and replaces it with a loyalty test, a welcome pack and an application process is how you build a private list without ever putting a public timetable on the internet.

None of this is large. Yet. A few hundred followers, sixteen likes on a good day, one or two men in camouflage. But scale isn’t the point, replicability is.

The template, veteran costume, closed vetting, county-by-county branding, is designed to be copied cheaply and often, and it is already being copied. A movement doesn’t need one big account to matter. It needs a script small accounts everywhere can run.

Take away the veteran claim and this is simply another anonymous remigration account with a taste for Old English vocabulary. With it, the same posts pose as testimony from a man who has already paid a price real soldiers pay, and who has therefore earned the standing to tell other people that restraint is treason. 

As with figures like Rupert Lowe and Nigel Farage, who masquerade as anti-establishment despite having support from some of the richest people on earth and having spent their entire lives in the heart of the financial, media, and political establishment, the costume helps deliver the extremist politics to the desperate, the radicalised, and the gullible.

text:
🚨 Allow me to explain who and what @elonmusk is agreeing with when he replied “Yes” to this post, and why this should concern every decent person in Britain, and perhaps especially, @RNLI crew.

Matt Bracken is an extremely dangerous former US Navy SEAL, sailor, boatbuilder and self-published novelist.

He graduated from the University of Virginia (Russian studies), served on East Coast UDT/SEAL teams, and took a Naval Special Warfare detachment to Beirut in 1983. He left active duty after that tour, stayed in the reserve through the 1980s, then built a boat and sailed extensively.

He lives in North Florida. He has written several violent fiction books and been on Alex Jones’s Infowars and other right-wing shows.

His fiction is often treated by some on the far/extreme right as political prophecy, not just novels, as they read as fictionalised far-right conspiracy theories: false-flag mass shootings to justify gun confiscation; a Mexican “Reconquista” of the Southwest; federal agents as the real enemy, civil-war prep. US militia and Patriot circles treat them as how-to warnings.

His 2015 Gates of Vienna essay compared the European migrant crisis to the Viet Cong infiltration before Tet. Some researchers of the militia movement say that essay helped popularise the idea that mass migration is a coordinated conquest, not a policy failure, and that it circulated among Oath Keepers and similar groups.

After the 2019 Christchurch massacre he appeared on Infowars with Alex Jones and Stewart Rhodes where they condemned the shooting but agreed with the killer’s diagnosis of “invasion” and predicted the attack would be used to disarm whites and start a civil war, thus amplifying the same narrative as the attacker while disclaiming the violence.

The word “invasion” has been used against immigrants in Britain since the 1890s-1900s, with groups like the British Brothers' League using it before the 1905 Aliens Act. It recurred around Commonwealth immigration in the 1960s and Thatcher's 1978 “swamped” remark. Its shift into routine, mainstream political use dates to the small boats era, around 2019-2020, with Suella Braverman’s 2022 Commons statement as the clearest turning point, after which the term moved from shocking to commonplace across politics and right-wing media.

“First the traitors, then the invaders” is a known white-supremacist meme. Its contempt-laden logic holds that before targeting immigrants themselves, extremists need to attack people who support immigration: the “traitors” are those seen as facilitating or defending immigration, and the “invaders” are immigrants themselves.

In white supremacist circles, the idea traces back the 1978 racist novel “The Turner Diaries," written by William Luther Pierce, founder of the neo-Nazi National Alliance. It’s since become one of the most influential texts in white supremacist and accelerationist circles, cited as inspiration by Timothy McVeigh among others.

text:
Evolution has been quietly building monsters in your backyard for 300 million years, and you've never heard of most of them.

Not metaphorical monsters. Actual, walking, breathing creatures so strange that if you saw one without context, your first instinct wouldn't be "insect." It would be "nope." And your second instinct would be to grab your phone, because nobody's going to believe you otherwise.

This is a list of those creatures. Ranked. Numbered. And by the time you hit the last one, you're going to stop trusting your own definition of what an "insect" is even allowed to look like.

I'm not going to describe them to you here. That would ruin it. Half the power of this list is the reveal — the half-second where your brain tries to categorize what it's looking at and fails completely. Reading about it first steals that moment from you. Watching it first is the only way it actually works.

So here's what I'll do instead: I'll tell you why this list matters, why your brain is wired to be floored by it, and why — if you actually care about how insane the natural world still is, even in 2026, even after you think you've seen everything — you need to press play before you read another word of this.

—

Let's start with an uncomfortable truth: most of us think we've basically seen it all. Documentaries, YouTube, a decade of viral "weird animal" content flooding every feed — surely by now, nature has run out of surprises worth stopping your scroll for.

It hasn't. Not even close. What's actually happened is that the truly bizarre stuff rarely gets algorithmic push, because it's harder to package into six seconds of dopamine. The internet rewards fast, familiar, comfortable weirdness — a cat doing something almost-human, a dog with an expressive face. It doesn't reward things that require you to actually stop and process what you're looking at.

This list does the opposite. Every single entry on it requires a beat of "wait, what." That's rare. That's valuable. And that's exactly why, once you watch it, you won't be able to stop thinking about at least two or three of these things for the rest of the day.

—

Here's something most people don't know about camouflage, and it's the reason half of this list works as well as it does.

Camouflage isn't one trick. It's an entire toolbox, refined over hundreds of millions of years of "look weird enough that something faster than you decides you're not worth the effort." Some species solved this with color. Some solved it with texture. Some solved it with something far stranger: shape-mimicry so exact that predators with genuinely excellent eyesight still walk right past them, every single time, for millions of years running.

And a small number of species didn't just solve camouflage. They solved it so thoroughly that they stopped looking like animals at all, and started looking like specific other objects — plants, debris, things that shouldn't move and definitely shouldn't have legs. When you see those species without warning, your brain doesn't process "camouflaged insect." It processes "wait, did that just move?" That reaction, that exact half-second of confused recalibration, is what number one on this list is going to give you. I promise you that.

—

I want to talk for a second about why insects specifically get underrated in the "wow, nature is incredible" conversation, because I think it's a genuine blind spot most people have.

We reserve our awe for the big stuff. Whales. Big cats. Anything with fur and eyes big enough to read emotion into. Insects get filed under "gross" or "ignore" by default, a category most people mentally skip past unless something is actively landing on them.

But pound for pound — or actually, given how tiny most of these are, milligram for milligram — insects are running some of the most sophisticated evolutionary software on the planet. Compressed life cycles. Absurd reproductive strategies. Camouflage systems that would take a Hollywood special effects team months to design and millions of dollars to execute, running on a creature you could lose in a houseplant.

This list is a corrective. It's ninety seconds of proof that the "gross bug" category is hiding some of the most objectively unbelievable design work evolution has ever produced. Once you see it laid out back to back, ranked, escalating — you stop seeing insects as background noise and start seeing them as what they actually are: tiny, walking miracles that happen to have too many legs for our comfort.

—

Let's talk about the ranking itself for a second, because I think the format matters more than people give it credit for.

A countdown works on your brain differently than a single reveal does. Each entry raises the bar for what comes next, which means your skepticism compounds with every number. By the time you're two or three entries in, some part of you is thinking "okay, there's no way it gets weirder than that." And then it does. Every time. That's not an accident — that's the entire design of a well-built countdown, and it's exactly why this one is worth watching start to finish instead of skipping to the end.

If you jump straight to the final entry, you'll see something impressive, sure. But you'll have robbed yourself of the escalation that makes the final reveal actually land the way it's supposed to land. The buildup is doing real work here. Trust it.

—

Here's a specific claim I'll make, and I don't make it lightly: at least one entry on this list is going to make you stop, rewind, and watch it again in slow motion just to convince your own eyes that what you saw was real and not some kind of editing trick.

I know that because it happened to me. I've been doing this — finding and analyzing content that actually deserves the attention economy's most valuable currency, a full, undistracted ninety seconds — for over a decade. I don't say "you need to see this" often, because I know exactly how devalued that phrase has become. Every third caption on this platform claims to have found "the craziest thing you'll see today," and 90% of the time it's recycled, overhyped, or outright fake.

This isn't that. This is the rare case where the actual footage earns every bit of hype a caption could throw at it, and honestly undersells itself if anything, because words are a genuinely weak medium for describing something your visual cortex needs to process directly to fully register.

—

Let's talk mimicry for a second, because it's the connective tissue running through almost every entry on this list, and understanding it a little makes the payoff hit even harder.

Mimicry isn't just "looking similar to something." True mimicry, the evolutionary kind, is an arms race that plays out over unimaginable timescales — generation after generation, the slightly-more-convincing fakes survive slightly more often, and the slightly-less-convincing ones get eaten before they can pass anything on. Run that process for a few hundred thousand generations and you don't get "looks kind of like a leaf." You get something so precise that actual leaf-eating insects sometimes mistake the mimic for real foliage and start investigating it, only to get an extremely unpleasant surprise.

That's the level of precision we're talking about with several of the species that show up in this list. Not "pretty good disguise for a bug." Museum-grade, Pixar-animator-level attention to detail, produced entirely by blind trial and error running for longer than humans have existed as a species.

—

I also want to flag something that tends to surprise people who don't spend a lot of time around this kind of content: several of the creatures on this list are things you can actually see, and in some cases even hold, without traveling to some impossibly remote rainforest most of us will never visit.

That's part of what makes a list like this so quietly unsettling in a good way. This isn't deep-sea footage of creatures that live in total darkness eight kilometers down, so alien-looking that their strangeness feels almost expected, almost like cheating. This is stuff sharing a planet with you right now, at accessible depths and elevations, that you have simply never had a reason to look closely enough to notice.

The natural world isn't hiding its weirdest work exclusively in inaccessible extremes. Sometimes it's sitting on a leaf at eye level, and the only reason you've never seen it is that you've never had a reason to look that closely, at that exact leaf, at that exact moment. This list gives you that moment without requiring the plane ticket.

—

There's a particular kind of person this list is going to hit hardest, and if you had any kind of "bug phase" as a kid — flipping over rocks, catching things in jars, asking your parents uncomfortable questions about metamorphosis at the dinner table — you already know who you are.

That curiosity doesn't actually go away as an adult. It just stops getting fed, because most adult content isn't built for it. Somewhere between childhood and now, "what is that and why does it look like that" got replaced by spreadsheets and group chats and whatever argument is trending this week. This list is a direct line back to that exact, specific, uncomplicated kind of wonder. No cynicism required. No context needed beyond eyes and a working sense of curiosity.

If that's you, you're going to watch this once, immediately watch it again, and then go down a three-hour rabbit hole afterward looking up every single entry by name. I say this with total confidence, because it's exactly what happened to me.

—

Let's talk about the specific psychology of "this shouldn't exist" content for a second, because it's a genuinely different reaction than most viral content produces, and I think it's worth naming.

Most viral content makes you feel something you already have a name for: funny, sad, angry, nostalgic. This list produces something closer to cognitive dissonance — a small, pleasant glitch where your existing categories for "what animals look like" and "what plants look like" and "what objects look like" briefly fail to sort what you're looking at. That glitch is uncomfortable for about half a second and then extremely satisfying once your brain resolves it.

That specific sensation — confusion resolving into delighted understanding — is one of the most shareable emotional arcs that exists, and it's the exact arc this entire list is built around, entry after entry, each one resetting the glitch and resolving it again.

—

One more thing before I let you go watch it, and it's maybe the most important thing in this entire post.

Watch this with sound on. I know, I know — half of you have your phone on silent by default and never think twice about it. Don't do that here. The reactions, the pacing, the way certain reveals are timed against the audio, all of it is designed to land a specific way, and muting it flattens the experience into something noticeably less effective. Give it the full ninety seconds, full volume, no multitasking. It's not a big ask, and the payoff is worth it.

—

If you're the kind of person who needs a concrete reason to click before you click, here's my honest pitch, stripped of all the buildup:

You are about to see things that look like they were designed by someone with a very strange, very specific sense of humor, except nobody designed them. They designed themselves, through nothing but time and death and the occasional lucky mutation, over a span of time so long it stops being intuitive somewhere around the ten-thousand-generations mark.

Every entry on this list is a tiny rebellion against your assumptions about what's possible with legs, wings, and a few million years to spare. And the ranking is not arbitrary — it escalates for a reason, and the reason becomes obvious the second you hit the final entry.

—

I'll leave you with this, because I think it's the actual point buried underneath all the "whoa, nature is wild" framing.

We live in an era where it feels like everything has already been discovered, catalogued, filmed, and turned into content. The frontier feels closed. But the truth is the frontier was never really about geography. It's about attention. There are entire universes of genuinely bizarre, previously-invisible-to-you design sitting in plain sight, at ground level, in backyards and forest floors and the undersides of leaves you've walked past ten thousand times without a second look.

This list is ninety seconds pulled from that hidden universe. It's proof that "I've seen everything the internet has to offer" is a claim that gets disproven on a near-weekly basis if you're willing to look in the right places.

This is one of those places.

Go watch it. Watch it in order. Don't skip to the end. Let each entry reset your sense of "okay, surely that's the weirdest one" before the next one breaks it again.

By the final number, you won't be scrolling past the next post immediately. You'll be sitting there, slightly stunned, doing exactly what I did: rewatching it, trying to figure out how something that strange is allowed to just... exist, unbothered, somewhere on the same planet you woke up on this morning.

—

P.S. — if any single entry on this list makes you say "no way" out loud, alone, in a room with nobody else in it, that's not embarrassing. That's just what genuinely well-earned amazement sounds like when nobody's around to perform it for. That reaction is the whole reason this list exists. Let it happen.

Press play.

—

Let's go a little deeper on why "shape mimicry" specifically breaks people's brains harder than color mimicry does, because I think it's the single biggest reason this list performs the way it does wherever it gets posted.

Color camouflage is intuitive to us. We understand blending in. A green insect on a green leaf doesn't require any mental gymnastics — of course it's hard to see, it's the same color as the background. Your brain files that under "makes sense" almost instantly and moves on.

Shape mimicry is a different category entirely, and it's the one that actually produces the "wait, what" reaction. When something doesn't just match a color but replicates an entire three-dimensional structure — the exact curl of a dead leaf edge, the specific asymmetry of insect damage on foliage, the precise droop angle of something wilting — your brain doesn't file that under "clever disguise." It files it under "that's not supposed to be possible," because nothing in your intuitive understanding of biology prepares you for an animal that looks less like an animal and more like a highly specific, slightly damaged piece of plant matter, down to details you'd only notice if you were staring directly at it.

That's the reaction this list is engineered to produce, entry after entry. Not "oh, that blends in nicely." Something closer to genuine disorientation, followed by the slow-dawning realization that yes, that thing has legs, and yes, it has been sitting there the entire time doing absolutely nothing to hide the fact except being extremely, unfairly good at its one job.

—

I want to bring up something most people never think about: the sheer cost, in evolutionary terms, of getting a disguise this precise.

Evolution doesn't design things on purpose. There's no blueprint, no engineer sitting down with a plan to make something look like a dead leaf. What actually happens is almost unbearably slow and unbearably brutal: over countless generations, individuals who happened to look slightly more convincing survived slightly more often than individuals who didn't. The ones who looked slightly less convincing got found, got eaten, and took their genes out of the pool permanently.

Repeat that process for long enough — and we're talking about spans of time that make human history look like a rounding error — and you get something so refined it looks intentional, even though every step of the process was blind, random, and merciless. Every convincing detail you're about to see represents thousands of ancestors who weren't convincing enough, and didn't get to pass anything on.

That's a heavy thought to have about something that looks, on the surface, like a fun "wow nature" clip. But it's also what makes it genuinely awe-inspiring instead of just cute. You're not looking at a costume. You're looking at the visible output of an unthinkably long, unthinkably harsh optimization process, with the failures quietly erased from the record and only the successes left standing in front of the camera.

—

Here's a pattern worth noticing once you start paying attention to lists like this: almost every single "impossible-looking" creature falls into one of two survival strategies, and understanding the split makes the whole list click into place.

Strategy one: don't be seen at all. Blend in so completely that a predator's eyes slide right past you without registering anything worth investigating. This is the leaf-mimic, the twig-mimic, the moss-mimic approach — safety through total visual silence.

Strategy two: be seen, but be seen as something else entirely — something dangerous, something toxic, something not worth the risk of finding out the hard way. This is the flashy, high-contrast, "look at me" approach, where bright colors aren't a mistake, they're a warning label, whether or not the creature wearing them is actually dangerous at all. Plenty of species have evolved to borrow the warning colors of genuinely dangerous species without any of the actual danger, essentially running a bluff that's worked well enough, for long enough, to become permanent.

Once you know to look for that split, you'll notice it running through basically the entire list, alternating between "I am nothing, look away" and "I am extremely dangerous, also look away, but for a different reason." Both strategies work. Both are on full display here. And watching them stacked back to back is part of what makes the escalation so satisfying.

—

Let's talk briefly about why this kind of content is having a moment specifically right now, in a feed environment that's more crowded and more competitive for attention than it's ever been.

There's a ceiling on how many times a brain can be surprised by the same category of stimulus before it stops registering as surprising. Prank videos, reaction videos, staged "gotcha" content — all of it has been run into the ground so thoroughly that most feeds have developed a kind of immune response to it. People see the setup coming from a mile away now. The surprise is gone before the video even starts, because the format itself has become predictable.

Nature content, especially the genuinely strange and lesser-known corners of it, hasn't hit that ceiling yet, because the well is functionally bottomless. There are more undiscovered or under-filmed species of insect alone than there are grains of... well, not sand, but you get the point — the number is large enough that "running out of surprising material" isn't a realistic concern for decades, maybe longer. That's a rare and valuable position to be in, content-wise. Nearly everything else has been mined dry. This category hasn't even been scratched.

—

I want to address something that always comes up in the comments of lists like this, because it's a fair question and worth answering directly: is any of this real, or is some of it AI-generated, given how much synthetic content is currently flooding every platform?

It's a completely reasonable thing to wonder in 2026. The tools for generating convincing fake wildlife footage have gotten good enough that skepticism is honestly the correct default setting now, not a character flaw. But here's the tell that actually matters, and it's the same tell that separates real nature footage from synthetic content across the board: the small imperfections. The slightly shaky handheld camera work. The natural, uneven lighting that doesn't perfectly flatter every angle. The tiny, unscripted movements that don't serve the "story" of the shot but happen anyway, because real creatures do things that don't make narrative sense.

AI-generated content, even at its current best, still struggles enormously with exactly those unscripted, purposeless little details — the stuff that exists in reality simply because reality doesn't care about being cinematic. Real footage is full of moments that don't earn their place in the frame. That's precisely what makes it convincing, and it's precisely what's still hardest to fake convincingly. Keep that in the back of your mind as a general filter, not just for this list, but for everything you're going to encounter on this platform going forward. It's a genuinely useful skill to build now, before it becomes even harder to tell the difference.

—

A short digression on why kids, historically, have always been better at noticing this stuff than adults are, because I think it's a useful and slightly humbling point.

Kids don't have a fully built category system yet for "what things are allowed to look like." An adult sees a shape on a branch and immediately, unconsciously, sorts it: leaf, twig, bark, done, move on, nothing here worth a second look. A kid's sorting system is less automatic, less confident, which paradoxically makes them more likely to actually stop and look closely at something an adult's brain would have already dismissed and filed away without ever really seeing it.

That's not a knock on adults. It's just what happens when a brain gets efficient — efficiency means dismissing things faster, which means missing more. Lists like this are valuable specifically because they force adult brains to slow back down to kid-speed for ninety seconds: to stop assuming they already know what they're looking at, and to actually look. That's a genuinely rare experience to get handed to you passively, through nothing more than a video autoplaying in your feed.

—

Let's talk about scale for a second, because it's easy to lose track of just how small most of these creatures actually are, and that detail matters enormously for how impressive the whole thing becomes once it clicks.

Most of what you're about to see could sit comfortably on a fingertip, sometimes several times over. We're not talking about large, easily-observed creatures with obvious visual real estate to work with. We're talking about design work this intricate, this convincing, this borderline-absurd, compressed into a canvas smaller than your thumbnail. Whatever respect you already have for the natural world, multiply it by however much you were underestimating the size of the thing producing that level of detail. It's not just impressive. It's impressive at a scale most people never bother to actually picture.

—

Okay — genuinely, this is close to the end, and I want to leave you with the framing that I think makes the biggest difference in how much you get out of the next ninety seconds of your day.

Don't watch this as "weird bug compilation, mildly interesting, forget by tomorrow." Watch it as a direct, undeniable rebuttal to the quiet assumption most of us walk around with — that the world has basically finished surprising us, that everything genuinely astonishing has already been filmed, ranked, and turned into a thumbnail somewhere.

It hasn't. Not even close. This list is proof, delivered in real time, that there are still things on this actual planet, at ground level, unbothered by cameras or attention or virality, quietly being more strange and more impressive than almost anything an algorithm has served you this week.

That's worth ninety seconds. That's worth pressing play for.

Go count along. See if you can guess what's coming before each reveal. I'd bet money you won't get past the halfway point without being wrong at least once.

And once you're done, do the thing you almost never do with content like this: send it to the one person you know who still has that "flip over every rock" curiosity left in them. They'll thank you. They'll also probably send it right back to you with three exclamation points and no other comment, because that's genuinely the only appropriate reaction once the ranking hits its final entry.

One last note before you go. Notice how the tension actually builds instead of resetting with each new number — that's not incidental editing, that's the entire structure earning its final payoff the honest way, one escalating "surely not" at a time. Each entry is quietly setting up the next, and you won't fully appreciate that architecture until you've seen where it lands.

Watch it in order. Don't skip ahead. Let the countdown do what it was actually built to do.

Press play.

text:
😂The Noise Machine Springs to Life😂

Donald Trump said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it is “going to happen eventually.” Within hours the nationalist commentariat was treating the remark as a seismic shift in the constitutional debate.

This is what desperation looks like.

A US president on a golf-focused visit offers a casual, non-binding personal opinion. No policy change. No diplomatic initiative. No alteration to the principle of consent. Yet it is immediately framed as proof that the ground has moved and that reunification is now the “national journey.” When your political project has to mine significance from a throwaway line delivered beside the Taoiseach, the cupboard is bare.

The Good Friday Agreement is clear. Northern Ireland’s status changes only if a majority here vote for it. Every credible poll continues to show that majority does not exist. Elections continue to return a substantial unionist vote. Those are the things that actually matter. A flippant comment from a foreign leader who has no vote and no authority over the process does not.

The volume of the reaction is itself revealing. When a political movement feels the need to amplify every sympathetic soundbite from abroad while downplaying the consistent preference of people on the ground, it is advertising insecurity, not strength. Manufactured noise is not momentum. It is a substitute for it.

Unionists do not need to over-react to every external opinion. The constitutional reality remains unchanged: the future of Northern Ireland will be decided by the people who live here, not by commentary from Washington, Dublin or anywhere else. Trump is entitled to his view. He is not entitled to rewrite the rules of consent.

Nationalists can celebrate the remark all they like. It changes nothing of substance. The noise is loud precisely because the substance is missing.

text:
David Pogue on Apple after Steve Jobs: "Maybe even Steve Jobs couldn't come up with another mega hit of that size."

Tech journalist David Pogue was asked whether Apple has stopped inventing. His answer is more generous to Tim Cook than the usual take and, by the end, more damning.

He starts by refusing the easy narrative:

"Maybe the lowhanging fruit of the 90s and the early 2000s have been plucked. Maybe even Steve Jobs couldn't come up with another mega hit of that size. We don't know."

Then he pivots to what isn't in doubt:

"What we do know is that Tim Cook has taken the company much more into software and services. Apple Music is now bigger than Spotify. They make so much money with these services."

That's the Cook-era trade: fewer world-changing objects, far more recurring revenue. Pogue doesn't sneer at it. But when the conversation reaches the one place where invention still matters, his tone changes:

"…and eventually AI, they're trying. They completely missed the AI wave, the generative AI wave."

What makes the miss sting is that Apple showed everyone exactly what winning would have looked like. Pogue describes the 2024 demo of a rebuilt Siri, one with access to your email and your messages and walks through the scenario himself:

"So, you could say, 'What time do I need to leave to pick up my mom?' And it would go through your email, know that your mom is flying in today, then in the background, go to a flight tracking website and look up the flight, then look at Google Maps and know what the traffic's like, and in the blink of an eye, say, 'You need to leave at 1:20.'"

His verdict on that demo is not cynical. It's wistful:

"Like that would be genuinely useful. I would like that."

Interviewer Clare Duffy adds the obvious caveat "If they could pull it off."

Pogue finishes the sentence for her: "…which they have not yet, which they have not."

Asked which retired Apple product he'd resurrect, he lands somewhere much smaller, and on the same fault line:

"iPhones have gotten really big. And for a long time, they offered, you know, the SE, they offered a smaller one for people with smaller hands, and that didn't sell as well as they'd like. So, that's kind of gone away. But I know a lot of people, including my wife, who really find the big phones too big. So, I think they should still offer a smaller iPhone."

text:
OCSO Honors the Lives, Service, and Sacrifice of September 11

OSCEOLA COUNTY, Fla. — On the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, the Osceola County Sheriff’s Office joined community leaders, law enforcement partners, and residents to honor the nearly 3,000 lives lost, the survivors whose lives were changed, and the first responders who showed extraordinary courage and sacrifice.

Sheriff Christopher A. Blackmon attended the Patriot Day Remembrance Breakfast hosted by the Central Florida Hotel & Lodging Association (CFHLA), along with law enforcement leaders and community members. The event offered an opportunity to reflect on the lasting impact of September 11 and honor those who served in its aftermath. Florida Senator Brian Avila was also present.

Members of the Osceola County Sheriff’s Office also attended the 25 Years 9/11 Remembrance Memorial at Valencia College, joining students, community members, and first responders to remember the victims and survivors of the September 11 attacks.

Although these events took place in different settings, they shared a common purpose: to remember those lost, honor those who responded, and recognize the courage, resilience, and unity shown in the face of tragedy. Twenty-five years later, September 11 remains a solemn reminder of the sacrifices made and our collective responsibility to remember.

Ron DeSantis (@GovRonDeSantis) wasn't having it. “𝘈 𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘣𝘫𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘰𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘬!𝘭𝘭 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘦𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘨 𝘬𝘪𝘥𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘢𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘪𝘵, 𝘴𝘰 𝘕𝘉𝘊 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘳𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘳𝘰𝘳, 𝘸𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥,” he wrote, adding: “𝘐𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘫𝘶𝘳𝘰𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘢𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘥, 𝘍𝘭𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘥𝘢 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘥𝘦 𝘢𝘴𝘺𝘭𝘶𝘮 — 𝘐'𝘮 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘦'𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘸𝘦𝘭𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥.”

text:
Weekend Agriculture
Publishing Date: September 12, 2026

As mid-September arrives across the Corn Belt and Great Plains, the 2026 harvest season is officially underway. Markets navigated a major news week led by the release of the USDA’s September WASDE and Crop Production reports, which trimmed national corn and soybean yield projections while reflecting the ongoing impact of late summer heat and moisture stress across western growing zones.

Grain board trading closed the week with solid gains across the board as traders absorbed lower yield estimates and steady export activity. In livestock country, cattle futures rebounded into the weekend, supported by historically tight market ready feeder supplies and steady cash feedlot bids, while swine markets held firm on stable slaughter demand.

USDA AND POLICY DIGEST

The grain trade spent the week processing the landmark September WASDE report alongside the latest weekly Crop Progress metrics, establishing fresh price baselines for the 2026 harvest:

In its updated objective yield estimates, the USDA lowered the national average corn yield projection to 180.1 bushels per acre (down from 180.7 in August), bringing total production to 15.95 billion bushels. 2026/27 U.S. corn ending stocks were revised down to 2.01 billion bushels on reduced supply.

National soybean yields were trimmed to 52.4 bushels per acre (down from 52.7 in August), lowering total production to 4.49 billion bushels. Soybean ending stocks tightened to 295 million bushels as solid domestic crush demand and steady foreign inquiries absorbed supplies.

Weekly progress reports confirmed national corn maturity reached 29%, with 5% of the national corn crop harvested. Soybean leaf dropping advanced to 25%, with early cutting beginning in southern districts. Spring wheat harvest cleared 82% complete nationally, while winter wheat seeding reached 8% complete for the 2027 crop.

On the policy front, Capitol Hill discussions focused on farm safety net adjustments and regional drought mitigation funding. Export channels remained steady, with private exporters reporting daily flash sales of new crop soybeans to China and unknown destinations alongside continuous corn movement to Mexico.

WEATHER, SOIL AND FIELD REALITY

Field conditions across the central U.S. favored rapid crop dry down and early combine progress, though dry soil conditions persist across western production zones:

In the Western Corn Belt and Plains, warm, dry weather accelerated corn and soybean maturity across Nebraska, Kansas, and South Dakota. While the dry stretch enabled early harvest activity, dryland yields reflect the topsoil moisture deficits that persisted through late August.

In the Central and Eastern Corn Belt, Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana experienced favorable field conditions. Iowa leads major states with corn maturity reaching 35%, while soybean fields are turning color rapidly. Light rainfall in eastern districts provided minor topsoil moisture for fall pasture without delaying field work.

In the Delta and South, corn harvest reached advanced stages with producers reporting steady progress, while early soybean cutting expanded under dry harvesting conditions.

Across regional production zones:

In the Western Plains, operators focused on combine settings and managing dry grain in on farm storage bins as corn moisture drops quickly. In the Central Corn Belt, producers conducted final stalk strength evaluations and scheduled fields for early harvest priority based on standability.

In the Northern Plains, custom harvest crews made rapid progress finishing spring wheat and moving into early sunflower and row crop cutting.

In the Southern Plains, winter wheat producers monitored soil moisture levels ahead of full scale fall drill passes.

MARKET AND BOARD REVIEW

Board trading closed Friday with strong buying interest as the market priced in reduced USDA yield figures and steady export demand.

Weekly commodity settlements closed around these core baselines:

December Corn Futures: Settled higher on the week near $4.22 to $4.32 per bushel, bolstered by the USDA yield reduction and tightening ending stocks.

November Soybean Futures: Traded up into the $10.45 to $10.70 per bushel range, supported by trimmed yield estimates and continuous export flash sales.

December Wheat Futures: Held firm near $5.60 to $5.80 per bushel, backed by global supply adjustments and steady winter wheat seeding pace.

WTI Crude Oil: Traded near $86 to $88 per barrel, maintaining elevated fuel and freight overhead for commercial grain logistics.

Live Cattle Futures: CME October live cattle settled near $220.20 per hundredweight, backed by tight fed cattle inventories and firm cash bids.

Lean Hog Futures: October lean hog futures held steady near $81.50 per hundredweight on disciplined hog slaughter volume.

Cash grain prices across the Corn Belt reflected early harvest basis adjustments against steady processor demand:

Corn Belt Cash Corn Bids: Country elevator bids posted between $4.05 and $4.35 per bushel, with interior country basis averaging 20 cents to 35 cents under the December contract. Ethanol processing facilities offered competitive local bids ranging from $4.40 to $4.55 per bushel.

Corn Belt Cash Soybean Bids: Interior elevator bids ranged from $9.90 to $10.40 per bushel, while major crushing mills held strong bids near $10.50 to $10.85 per bushel to secure early new crop deliveries.

Corn Belt Cash Wheat Bids: Country bids across winter and spring wheat zones held between $5.60 and $6.30 per bushel, with basis holding steady on milling quality.

In livestock markets, Choice boxed beef cutouts maintained strong baseline pricing near $385.50 per hundredweight, while cash cattle trade held firm in Northern feedlots at $234.00 to $236.00 live, underpinned by light market-ready numbers.

TECHNICAL SPOTLIGHT, HISTORY AND HOMESTEAD

In agricultural technology, adoption of real-time combine yield telemetry and automated moisture-sensing technology is providing immediate harvest feedback. By syncing field mapping data directly to farm management software, operators are tracking real time yield variances across soil types and evaluating the impact of late season weather stress.

Looking back at historical milestones, mid-September marks the mid-20th century widespread adoption of tractor-mounted corn pickershellers and field combines across the Midwest. By combining harvesting and shelling into a single pass, farmers eliminated labor intensive ear corn storage cribs, setting the stage for modern bulk grain handling and high capacity bin drying.

On the homestead and in the field:

Fall Pasture Management: Smallholders prepared for cool-season grass recovery, resting grazed paddocks and evaluating winter forage inventory before cold weather sets in.

Fix-It Corner: Harvest machinery maintenance transitions to field operation checks monitor combine cylinder/rotor clearances, inspect auger flighting for wear, check tire pressures on heavy grain carts, and ensure bin aeration fans are operational.

Producer Voice: "The corn is coming down faster than expected in this dry weather yields are variable on the lighter ground, but we're moving grain fast."

Clark of Whitehall, New York, were awarded the Medal of Honor for their extraordinary actions on September 12, 1944, during World War II. Also on that day, U.S. Army Second Lieutenant Raymond Zussman of Hamtramck, Michigan, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor for his heroic actions.

Tominac joined the Army in November 1941, and by September 12, 1944 was serving as a first lieutenant in Company I, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division. On that day, in Saulx de Vesoul, France, he repeatedly exposed himself to hostile fire to attack the German forces, even after being wounded.

Clark joined the Army in March 1942 and, by September 12, 1944, was serving as a technical sergeant in Company K, 109th Infantry Regiment, 28th Infantry Division. On that day near Kalborn, Luxembourg, he crawled through open terrain to reach a platoon that had been pinned down by heavy fire, led them to safety, and then returned to rescue a wounded man. Five days later, he single-handedly attacked a German machine gun position and assumed command of two leaderless platoons. 

Zussman joined the Army in September 1941 and became a street fighting instructor at Fort Knox, Kentucky. In June 1943, he participated in the Allied invasions of North Africa and Italy. After being wounded at the battle of Monte Cassino in Italy, the Army offered Zussman a Headquarters position. Zussman declined, stating he wanted another front-line position; he was then assigned to a tank unit in France. By September 12, 1944, he was serving as a second lieutenant, commanding tanks of the 756th Tank Battalion. On September 12, during a battle in the city of Noroy-le-Bourg, France, Zussman repeatedly went forward alone to scout enemy positions and exposed himself to enemy fire while directing his tank’s action. On September 21, he was killed in action by a German mortar blast.

text:
Joseph Smith Jr.’s Claims: A Documentary Timeline, 1822-1844

Joseph Smith used a brown seer stone to hunt buried treasure. Then, according to David Whitmer, Emma Smith, and Martin Harris, he put a dark stone in a hat, shut out the light, and dictated the Book of Mormon. The Three Witnesses and Eight Witnesses signed statements that they saw plates. That is affidavit, not science. No gold plates were assayed, or sent to an independent scientific laboratory for investigation. No archive outside Smith’s movement attests “Reformed Egyptian” as a known language.

No Book of Mormon manuscript - complete, or of 1 Nephi, Alma, or Ether - exists from before Joseph Smith’s 1828-1829 dictation. The 1829 Original and Printer’s manuscripts are that dictation. They are not an independent, pre-Smith text. The first printed edition is March 1830. Zero ancient dated manuscripts exist for the Book of Mormon.

1822: The Chase well stone
About 1822, Willard Chase said a brown, egg-shaped stone came from a well on his family’s land while he employed Alvin and Joseph Smith. Chase’s 1833 affidavit states that after about twenty feet they found a “singularly appearing stone”; Joseph put it in his hat, put his face in the hat, and the next morning asked for it because he could “see in it.” Chase said he would only lend it. Joseph used that stone to claim sight of buried chests and mines. No controlled test ever showed that the stone found metal.

September 21-22, 1823 and September 22, 1827
Smith dated a heavenly angel visitor to the night of September 21-22, 1823 and said he took gold plates on September 22, 1827. The history printed in the Times and Seasons on April 15, 1842 named that messenger “Nephi.” Official LDS use later settled on Moroni. A typeset name is not an ancient manuscript.

October-November 1825: Stowell and the Harmony agreement
In October 1825 Josiah Stowell hired Smith to find a rumored Spanish silver mine near Harmony, Pennsylvania. On November 1, 1825, articles of agreement were signed in Harmony Township. The document divided any “valuable mine of either Gold or Silver” and “coined money and bars or ingots.” Joseph Smith Sr. and Joseph Smith Jr. were assigned two-elevenths. The mine was not found.

“The Glass looker”
On March 20, 1826, Smith was examined in South Bainbridge, Chenango County, New York, after Peter G. Bridgeman complained that he was a disorderly person and an impostor. Justice Albert Neely’s county bill lists the case as “Joseph Smith The Glass looker,” a misdemeanor examination. Smith admitted he had a stone he had “occasionally looked at to determine where hidden treasures” were. Stowell believed him and testified for him. Belief is not silver in the hand.

In July 1838 the Elders’ Journal answered the question “Was not Jo Smith a money digger?” with: “Yes, but it was never a very profitable job to him, as he only got fourteen dollars a month for it.”

July 1835 and after: the papyri
In July 1835 Smith bought Egyptian papyri and mummies from Michael Chandler in Kirtland and said one roll contained the writings of Abraham. Fragments returned to the LDS Church in 1967 are Egyptian funerary texts. Egyptologists identify the piece tied to Facsimile 1 as a Book of Breathings - the Document of Breathings Made by Isis - for a Theban priest named Hor. It is not Abraham.

Mid-1830s-July 12, 1843: Fanny Alger and D&C 132
In Kirtland in the mid-1830s, Smith was linked to Fanny Alger, a young woman in his household. On January 21, 1838, Oliver Cowdery wrote of “a dirty, nasty, filthy affair of his and Fanny Alger’s.” Cowdery was excommunicated in April 1838. The written revelation now printed as Doctrine and Covenants 132 was dictated July 12, 1843. It commands plural marriage and threatens Emma Smith with destruction if she refuses. By then Smith had already been sealed in Nauvoo to many women, including women who already had living husbands, and in May 1843 to Helen Mar Kimball, age fourteen.

November 1836-1837: Kirtland Safety Society
On November 2, 1836, church leaders organized the Kirtland Safety Society. Ohio would not charter it as a bank. On January 2, 1837, they reorganized it as the Kirtland Safety Society Anti-Banking Company and issued notes anyway. The notes collapsed in 1837.

April-May 1843: Kinderhook plates
On April 23, 1843, six bell-shaped brass plates were “found” near Kinderhook, Illinois. They were a hoax. The LDS Ensign conceded that in August 1981. William Clayton’s journal, May 1, 1843, records that Smith “translated a portion” and said the buried man was “a descendant of Ham through the loins of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.”

April 7, 1844: King Follett sermon
On April 7, 1844, at the Nauvoo general conference, Smith preached the King Follett sermon. He taught that God the Father “was once as we are now, and is an exalted man,” that God “dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ Himself did,” and that men must learn to become gods. That sermon is not in the Bible and not in the four LDS standard works. It was still preached from the conference pulpit.

Official LDS teaching has presented Jesus and Lucifer as spirit children of the same Father. Older editions of Gospel Principles said it in plain words: “Two of our brothers offered to help,” naming Jesus and Lucifer. Later manuals often drop the word “brothers” and keep the same parentage. Either wording makes them spirit siblings. Genesis through Revelation does not.

June 10, 1844: Nauvoo Expositor
On June 7, 1844, the Nauvoo Expositor printed its only issue. On June 10, as mayor, Smith ordered the marshal to destroy the press, pie the type in the street, and burn the papers. The marshal reported it done that night.

What can be tested of Smith failed. What the Bible rests on, exists.

Genesis-Malachi and Matthew-Revelation do not teach a hat-stone method of scripture, Smith’s 1844 exalted-man God, or Jesus and Lucifer as spirit brothers.

The Bible stands on dated manuscript copies.

Qumran left about 930 manuscripts. About 210-230 of them are biblical. The most copied books there include Psalms (about 35-37 copies), Deuteronomy (about 28-35), Isaiah (21), and Genesis (about 20-24). The Great Isaiah Scroll from Cave 1 (1QIsaᵃ) is a nearly complete Isaiah from about the second century B.C. Esther is missing from the Qumran biblical finds.

The oldest complete Hebrew Bible codex is the Leningrad Codex, copied in 1008/1009. The Aleppo Codex, written about 920–930, is older but incomplete after 1947 damage; about 294 leaves survive.

The Greek New Testament corpus in Münster’s INTF Kurzgefasste Liste stands at about 5,700 catalogued witnesses (later counts run near 5,800–5,900 as numbers are added): about 140 papyri, more than 320 majuscules, about 2,900 minuscules, and more than 2,300 lectionaries. Only about 20-25 of those manuscripts contain the entire New Testament. Latin Vulgate New Testament copies number in the thousands-commonly more than 8,000, often cited as 10,000 or more. Greek Old Testament/Septuagint manuscripts number more than 2,000.

Against that pile, Smith’s gold plates have no independent laboratory file. Reformed Egyptian has no external inscription corpus. Again - The Book of Mormon has no ancient pre-1830 manuscript copies. The papyri that can be read are Hor’s funerary text. King Follett is an 1844 conference sermon, not canon. The Jesus-Lucifer pairing is LDS premortal doctrine, not the biblical text.

Jesus said: “Beware of false prophets… Ye shall know them by their fruits.” Then: “Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name?… And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me.” (Matthew 7:15-16, 22-23)

Smith’s corrupt fruits are the Chase stone used to hunt treasure; the 1825 Harmony contract on a mine that was never opened; the 1826 glass-looker examination; gold plates no lab ever tested; papyri that are not Abraham; the Kirtland Safety Society notes that failed in 1837; a mid-1830s entanglement with Fanny Alger that Cowdery called filthy; D&C 132 on July 12, 1843, after Nauvoo plural sealings, including Helen Mar Kimball at fourteen and women who already had husbands; a “translation” of the hoax Kinderhook plates in 1843; the April 7, 1844 discourse that God was once a man; official teaching that Jesus and Lucifer are spirit brothers of one Father; and the June 10, 1844 order, as mayor, to smash the Nauvoo Expositor.

Smith’s false prophecies stand under Deuteronomy 18:22: “When a prophet speaketh in the name of the Lord, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the Lord hath not spoken.”

Sept. 22-23, 1832 (D&C 84:4-5): Zion’s Missouri temple “shall be reared in this generation”; “this generation shall not all pass away” until the Lord’s house stands there under a cloud of glory. That generation is dead. The lot is still empty.

Aug. 6, 1836 (D&C 111): Salem’s “gold and silver shall be yours,” and power to pay the debts. No treasure. Debts remained.

April 11, 1838 (D&C 114): David W. Patten to take a mission “next spring.” Patten was killed Oct. 25, 1838.

May 18, 1843: unless the United States redressed Missouri, “in a few years the government will be utterly overthrown and wasted,” not “so much as a potsherd left.”

Dec. 16, 1843: if Congress refused protection, it would be “broken up as a government,” “not even a grease spot.” Congress refused. The government remained.

Saying “Lord, Lord” does not cancel Smith’s fruit. It does not cancel Smith’s prophecies that did not come to pass.

September 12, 2026

Middle East Escalation: Red Sea Port Seizures & Shadow Fleet Banking Sanctions
Geopolitical tension escalated significantly into the weekend across key global shipping corridors. Following military clashes around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Houthi forces seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha, adding further strain to global maritime trade as the Strait of Hormuz remains heavily restricted. With long-term borrowing costs under pressure, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent outlined expanded anti-fraud sweeps aimed at blocking improper federal payments while navigating executive tariff revenue strategies. Concurrently, congressional leaders face tight timelines as budget committees work to reconcile spending allocations before key fiscal deadlines.

Global Economy: August CPI Release & Fed Rate Hike Odds

The macroeconomic landscape shifted Friday following the release of the U.S. August Consumer Price Index (CPI). Headline inflation rose 0.4% for the month and 3.4% year-over-year, matching expectations but reflecting ongoing energy price pressures. Meanwhile, wholesale inflation (PPI) jumped to 5.4% annually, driven by a surge in diesel costs. The hot wholesale data drove a late-week push in bond yields, with CME FedWatch tools now pricing in an 85% probability of a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike at next Wednesday's FOMC meeting. Despite the inflation backdrop, U.S. equity markets staged a solid Friday recovery, with the S&P 500 up 0.9% and the Dow snapping a four-day losing streak as oil prices stabilized.

Domestic Policy: Farm Bill Authorization & Renewable Fuel Mandates

Bipartisan negotiations over the multi-year Farm Bill are accelerating on Capitol Hill as committee leaders scramble to finalize draft language before current program authorizations expire. Primary friction points center on proposed adjustments to statutory Reference Prices under the Price Loss Coverage (PLC) program, alongside expanded crop insurance provisions for row-crop and livestock operations. Concurrently, Midwest lawmakers are pressing federal agencies for expanded year-round E15 biofuel access to support domestic corn demand and cushion producers against elevated diesel and fertilizer expenses.

Energy & Infrastructure: AI Server Demand & Enterprise Grid Capex

Enterprise capital continues to flow aggressively into digital infrastructure and energy assets. Technology and hardware leaders surged into the weekend, led by strong earnings and coverage upgrades for AI server providers like Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell. Utility and midstream pipeline operators maintain steady cash-flow profiles, insulated by long-term take-or-pay transport contracts as energy producers expand capacity to feed growing baseline power demand from enterprise data centers.

With midterm elections less than eight weeks away, domestic political battles are intensifying. The U.S. Supreme Court temporarily blocked a new congressional district map in Missouri, requiring the state to utilize its 2022 district lines for the upcoming November elections. text:
Meta's AI feature mined years of family Facebook and Instagram posts to build an unsolicited profile of a Utah mother's two young daughters, surfacing their names, ages, birth weights, school grade level, favorite hiking trails, and their mother's likely home address after she posted a car-singalong video showing only one daughter's face.

Kalie Robins never named her children in her own posts. Meta AI didn't need her to. It cross-referenced birthday posts and birth announcements shared by relatives — a grandmother's newborn photo, a cousin's comment — and assembled what Robins called a portfolio: both daughters identified, ages calculated, school district narrowed to the only one in town, favorite beaches and books listed, her own employment history and "mental health advocacy" work summarized, her location pinpointed from a 2018 congratulatory post she didn't even write.

Meta spent two decades building a platform on the promise that sharing your kids' milestones with distant grandparents was just what families do now. The company took every one of those birthday posts, comments, and tagged photos and turned them into training data for a feature that assembles child surveillance dossiers from a single suggested prompt. A human stalker could theoretically piece together the same information. Meta AI did it in minutes, unprompted, from inside the app, and offered it up before Robins even asked.

Meta called the feature's behavior a mistake and said it had been fixed. The company did not explain why a tool built on a user's own social graph generated a prompt asking where a private citizen with a few hundred followers lives. Meta built the data trove and the retrieval feature; the dossier is what that combination produces by default.
Robins is now asking relatives to delete a decade of family photos to protect her kids from her own platform. Meta doesn't have to take down anyone's scrapbook. It just has to stop building products that turn one into a target.

text:
My missing savings had cost me thousands of hours under fluorescent hospital lights, missed holidays, sore feet, aching shoulders, and dinners eaten out of vending machines.

But to Margaret, apparently, my identity had been worth five grand.

Derek looked sick.

“What money?”

Marissa stared at him.

“You seriously don’t know?”

He didn’t answer.

She looked at Margaret.

Then back at Derek.

“Oh my God.”

Margaret whispered,

“Marissa, think very carefully.”

Marissa pointed at her.

“She told me it was your idea.”

Derek stopped breathing.

I saw it happen.

His chest simply froze.

Marissa continued.

“She said you wanted the savings gone before the divorce.”

Derek turned toward Margaret.

“She said you wanted it to look like Angela took it because your lawyer could use it against her.”

“Mom?”

“She said you told her Angela would fold if the bank records made her look like a liar.”

“Mom!”

Margaret snapped,

“I was protecting you!”

The words hung there.

Nobody moved.

Derek’s face changed.

Slowly.

Like a curtain dropping.

I watched him realize there was no way to pull those words back.

Margaret realized it too.

She looked around.

At the spectators.

At the bailiff.

At both attorneys.

At me.

Her shoulders dropped.

And then, strangely, she became calm.

The same calm she had used for sixteen years whenever she was about to say something cruel and wanted everyone to believe it was common sense.

“You would have lost everything,” she told Derek.

He stared at her.

“You were going to lose the house. Your retirement. Half the savings.”

“My savings,” I said.

Margaret finally looked at me.

“Oh, spare me.”

There she was.

The real Margaret.

Not the navy suit.

Not the church smile.

Not the woman who brought casseroles when neighbors were sick.

The woman underneath.

“You always acted like every dollar was yours because you wore scrubs and worked ridiculous hours.”

“I earned most of it.”

“And my son worked.”

“Yes.”

“Hard.”

“Yes.”

“Then you filed for divorce.”

I shook my head.

“He filed.”

Margaret blinked.

That landed.

Because it was true.

Derek had filed after I confronted him about the account.

He told everyone I was paranoid.

He told his mother I was trying to control him.

He told his lawyer I had drained the savings and was preparing to leave.

He offered me a settlement that gave him the house, his pension untouched, the boat, and nearly every major asset.

In exchange, he said he wouldn’t “pursue” the missing sixty-one thousand.

He wanted me to pay for being robbed.

I looked at Margaret.

“Your son filed.”

Her mouth tightened.

“You drove him to it.”

That used to hurt.

God, it used to hurt.

For years, Margaret could say one sentence and somehow make me review every mistake I had ever made.

Maybe I worked too much.

Maybe I was too independent.

Maybe I didn’t praise Derek enough.

Maybe I made him feel small by earning more some years.

Maybe I should have pretended the boat wasn’t destroying our budget.

Maybe marriage meant swallowing disrespect until everyone else was comfortable.

Standing in that courtroom, I finally understood something.

Some people don’t want forgiveness.

They want access.

Access to your money.

Your labor.

Your silence.

Your ability to doubt yourself.

And when you stop giving them access, they call you cruel.

The judge returned before Margaret could say anything else…..
