text:
Frederick Douglass's house is still standing because a Black woman sat down and balanced its checkbook. Her name was Nettie Napier, and almost nobody has ever heard it. For years she totaled the repair bills and the caretaker's pay so the home of the greatest man her people produced would not fall apart.

She Kept the Books for Frederick Douglass's House

In the Library of Congress, filed inside the financial papers of Frederick Douglass, there are a few pages of plain household accounts. The handwriting belongs to a woman who signed herself Mrs. N. L. Napier, and the heading reads, in the bookkeeping language of 1927, "Caretaker's House and Maintenance."

She was keeping the books for a dead man's home.

Frederick Douglass had been gone more than thirty years by then. His house still stood on a hill in the Anacostia section of Washington, and someone had to account for every dollar it took to keep the roof sound and the caretaker paid.

That someone, again and again, was Nettie Langston Napier.

She came into the world on June 17, 1861, in Oberlin, Ohio, with about as much standing as America offered a Black child in that year. Her father was John Mercer Langston, who would later become the first Black man elected to Congress from the state of Virginia.

None of that softened her. It pointed her at work.

She studied music at Oberlin and finished in 1878. That same fall, on the second of October, she married a Nashville lawyer named James Carroll Napier in a Washington church, in a gown the papers of the day described as white tulle with a satin princess waist.

Then she went South and got busy.

The home she and James built in Nashville became the social heart of the city's Black upper class, and Booker T. Washington, a close friend, stayed with them whenever he passed through town.

She could have settled for being the first lady of that world, hosting and being hosted. She chose instead to spend her days on the parts of life that nobody applauded.

By the early 1900s, Nashville was full of Black mothers who had no good choice on a workday. They cleaned houses and took in washing and cooked in kitchens that were not their own, and while they worked, their small children stayed home alone.

Those children went without meals.

They went without school.

Nettie had no patience for it. On January 14, 1907, she gathered other Black women in the city and started the Day Home Club, and out of that club came a place called Porter Homestead.

A working mother could leave her child there and know the child would be fed, watched, and taught, with a doctor named Josie Wells overseeing their health. In a Southern city built to hand Black families the least of everything, that was close to a miracle, and Nettie ran it like a woman who understood that miracles still have to be paid for.

She did not sit and wait for the city to help.

She appointed a vice president in each of Nashville's wards and put each one in charge of raising money, block by block.

That was how her mind worked. See the need, count the cost, build the system, keep the ledger.

But the numbers were brutal. The club was trying to feed children, pay caretakers, and keep the lights and water on, all from the pockets of people who had little to spare.

Some months the column would not balance. The need on one side was always larger than the money on the other.

Picture a woman who was good with figures, better than almost anyone around her, sitting at a table with accounts that refused to come out right.

Not because she had made a mistake. Because the world had.

There is a particular ache in that. To be skilled enough to see exactly how far short you are falling, and to keep the doors open anyway, one hard month after another.

She kept them open. Children ate who would not otherwise have eaten, and that was the whole point, even on the months the math said it should not have been possible.

Nettie and James never had a child of their own.

They raised a niece, the daughter of Nettie's brother, and took the girl in as theirs.

So the woman who spent herself keeping other people's children fed had none of her own waiting at home. She mothered a city's children, and later a dead man's house, instead.

Her husband knew something about keeping accounts, too.

In 1911, President William Howard Taft appointed James Carroll Napier the Register of the United States Treasury. In the plainest terms, he became the official bookkeeper of the country, and his signature was printed on the nation's paper money.

He is one of only a handful of Black Americans whose names have ever appeared on American currency. For a man born into slavery in Tennessee in 1845, freed as a small child, that signature was the long way around, from a state that had once sold people like him to the mint that printed the country's cash.

He held the post about two years.

Then Woodrow Wilson took office and set about segregating the federal government by race.

Signs went up over the Treasury restroom doors, splitting the staff by race. The Black press of the day reported the government segregating its own workers right down to the toilets.

The man whose name was on the money was now being told which toilet he was allowed to use. He resigned rather than put his signature under that.

The Napiers came home to Nashville. They had learned the same lesson from opposite ends of the same country, that a Black person could do the careful, faithful, unglamorous work of keeping a nation's books and still be handed a sign telling them where to stand.

So they went looking for books worth keeping that no one could take away.

In 1916, the women of the National Association of Colored Women took on a debt that was not theirs to carry.

Douglass had died in 1895, and his widow had founded an association to preserve Cedar Hill, the house where he spent his last years. But the property carried a mortgage and was slipping toward ruin.

The colored women's clubs decided that would not stand. Led by Mary B. Talbert, they raised the money and paid the mortgage off in full by 1918, the hundredth year after Douglass's birth.

At the next national meeting, they burned the mortgage papers in front of a crowd, with Madam C. J. Walker among the donors looking on. Then they kept raising money, thousands more, and in 1922 a Black architect named William Augustus Hazel completed a full restoration of the home, believed to be the first historic preservation project in the country led by a Black architect.

Nettie Napier was one of those women, and she did what she had always done.

She kept the books.

The pages in the Library of Congress are the proof. "Caretaker's House and Maintenance, 1927-1928," in her hand, accounting for the cottage built behind the mansion and the daily cost of keeping a hero's home standing.

Mary Church Terrell, who founded the colored women's association and worked the same cause, remembered what that house had been when its owner was alive. She wrote of spending "many a pleasant Sunday evening in Mr. Douglass' home."

That was what these women were holding onto. Not a museum, not yet, but the actual rooms where the greatest man their people had produced had eaten his supper and lived his life.

And keeping those rooms standing came down, in the end, to someone willing to sit with the receipts. To total the caretaker's wages and the repair bills and make the columns meet.

That someone was Nettie.

She did this work for decades, and the credit went elsewhere. The men gave the speeches and signed the famous documents, and the women paid the mortgage, fed the children, balanced the accounts, and kept their names in ledgers nobody thought to read.

Nettie Langston Napier died in Nashville in the last days of September 1938, at seventy-seven. She passed at Hubbard Hospital, the teaching hospital of Meharry Medical College, an institution her own family had long helped support.

They held her funeral at Howard Congregational Church, where the mourners sang her favorite hymn, "God Be With You Till We Meet Again."

That hymn was written by Jeremiah Rankin, the same minister who had married Nettie and James in a Washington church sixty years before. The words that opened her marriage closed her life.

The Chicago Defender ran her obituary that October, written by a Black newspaperwoman named Rebecca Stiles Taylor. Out of everything Nettie had done, Taylor singled out the Douglass home as the work "for which she will be longest remembered."

Cedar Hill is still standing.

The federal government took it over in the 1960s, and it is now the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site, the preserved home of a man born enslaved, open to anyone who wants to stand in his rooms. Her husband's name went onto the country's money and was answered with a bathroom sign, while her name went into the account book of Douglass's home, where no president could ever order it taken down.

The next time you see Frederick Douglass's house, in a photograph or standing on its hill, know that it is there partly because a woman in Nashville was willing to keep its books.

Those pages are still filed in the Library of Congress, in her steady hand, under the heading she wrote across the top: Caretaker's House and Maintenance.

text:
Except your £3000 promise is just nonsense. 

That £3,000 figure is not an independence dividend. 

It is a Brexit cost estimate for the whole UK, lifted from Nick Bloom and then relabelled as cash that appears in every Scot’s pocket if Holyrood leaves Westminster and joins Brussels. 

That is not economics. It is a slogan with a pound sign on it.

Look at the SNP’s own books. 

GERS for 2025–26, published by the SCOTTISH Government, shows a notional deficit of £25.3 billion.  That's 10.9% of GDP, against 4.2% for the UK. 

That is about £4,563 per person in Scotland, £2,722 more than the UK average. 

Spending per person in Scotland is already £22,281, which is £2,720 more than the UK average. Revenues per head, even with a geographical share of North Sea oil, are almost identical to the UK. 

So the Union is not draining Scotland. It is topping up public spending. 

Independence does not magic that gap away. It means filling it with higher taxes, deeper cuts, or more borrowing on day one, before you have even priced a new currency, a debt share, or a border with your largest market.

Which brings you to the real offer: leave one union to join a bigger one.

An independent Scotland would not stroll back into the EU. It would apply as a new state, accept the full rulebook, and negotiate for years. 

Brussels would be in charge of, or tightly constrain:
the Common Fisheries Policy quotas and access to Scottish waters
the Common Agricultural Policy
state aid and competition rules
large parts of product standards, VAT structure, procurement, environment and data law
the Stability and Growth Pact, which wants deficits near 3% of GDP while Scotland is running 10.9%
a commitment, in principle, to the euro. New members do not get a UK-style opt-out
Your biggest trading partner would still be the rest of the UK. 
Join the EU customs union and you put a customs border on the Rio Tweed. 
Keep an open border with England and Brussels will ask how that sits with the single market. 

That is not “taking back control.” That is swapping one set of shared rules for a thicker set written in a room where Scotland would be one small vote among 27.

The word “colony” gets thrown around by the Scottish Nationalists, this is the awkward part. 

Scotland already has its own parliament, legal system, education system, NHS, and MPs at Westminster. 

In the EU it would take the acquis, the fisheries policy, the fiscal rules and, eventually, pressure toward the euro, with far less weight than it has now inside the UK. 

That is closer to being a rule-taker than anything Scotland is today.

Iceland just made the same calculation. On 29 August it voted 52.8% to 47.2% against even reopening EU accession talks, on 82.5% turnout. 

The reason was not mystery or nostalgia. It was fisheries, sovereignty, and the fact that Reykjavík already has single-market access through the EEA without handing Brussels its waters. 

Coastal Iceland voted No because it would not trade control of its seas for a seat at a table that runs the Common Fisheries Policy. Scotland’s fishing grounds are not a rounding error. 

Pretending they would be safe in an accession deal is how you sell a brochure, not a country.

So no: independence plus “EU return” is not a £3,000 pay rise. It is a larger fiscal hole, a currency problem, a border problem, and a transfer of power to Brussels on the files that matter to a maritime economy. 

If the case for leaving the UK is self-government, joining a bigger union and calling it freedom is the opposite argument.

DECODE CONFLICT ASSESSMENT

THE HOUTHI ISLAND KILL CHAIN

The capture of Mayun Island may have given the Houthis something more dangerous than additional territory: a forward position from which they could monitor, classify and threaten ships entering the Bab el Mandeb Strait.

Mayun, also known as Perim, sits inside the strategic passage connecting the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. The strait is approximately 18 miles wide at its narrowest point, but commercial vessels use two shipping channels only about two miles wide. Geography therefore compresses maritime traffic into predictable corridors.

The Houthis reportedly reached Mayun after Yemeni government forces withdrew. Their simultaneous advances around Mokha and Yemen’s southwestern coastline have created a significantly different security environment. However, occupying the island does not automatically give the Houthis complete control of the strait. Control requires persistent surveillance, reliable communications, operational weapons and the ability to survive counterattack.

The strategic danger is that Mayun could become one component of a distributed maritime kill chain.

A kill chain begins with detection. Personnel on the island could use commercial ship tracking information, optical equipment, drones or radar to observe vessels approaching the passage. That information could then be transmitted to command centers or weapons units located elsewhere along Yemen’s coastline.

The next stage is classification. Operators would determine a vessel’s identity, flag, cargo, ownership and destination. Ships considered politically acceptable might be allowed to pass, while Saudi, Israeli linked or Western associated vessels could be threatened. This selective enforcement would allow the Houthis to claim that navigation remains open while still exercising coercive control over individual shipping companies.

The final stage is engagement. Missiles, explosive boats or one way attack drones would not necessarily have to be permanently stationed on Mayun. The island could function mainly as a forward sensor and communications node, passing targeting information to concealed launch units on the mainland.

This would make the system more difficult to suppress. Destroying a launcher would not eliminate the surveillance network, while attacking the island would not necessarily remove weapons hidden along the coast.

Mayun also offers psychological power. Commercial shipping decisions are based on risk, not only confirmed military capability. A visible Houthi presence inside the strait could increase insurance premiums, discourage crews and force companies to reroute vessels even without a formal blockade.

Oil flows through Bab el Mandeb fell from approximately 9.3 million barrels per day in 2023 to about 4.2 million barrels per day during the first half of 2025 as vessels avoided Houthi attacks. Routing ships around the Cape of Good Hope can add roughly 15 days to some journeys between the Arabian Sea and Europe.

This means the Houthis do not need to physically close the strait. They only need to make passage sufficiently dangerous, unpredictable and expensive.

The greatest threat would be the integration of Mayun with other Houthi controlled positions. Coastal radar near Mokha, observers on Mayun, drones operating above the shipping lanes and mobile missile units inland could form a layered surveillance and targeting network. Iranian intelligence or technical assistance could improve this system, but direct Iranian control should not be assumed without evidence. The Houthis retain their own leadership, objectives and operational decision making.

Defeating this threat would require more than occasional strikes on suspected launchers. Maritime forces would need persistent surveillance of the island and surrounding coastline, rapid warnings to commercial vessels, counter drone coverage and the ability to interrupt communications between sensors and weapons units. Regional partners would also need to prevent the transfer of advanced radar, missile components and encrypted communications equipment into Yemen.

The Saudi led coalition’s fragmentation remains a central vulnerability. Local forces can retake territory, but they must also hold it, maintain supply lines and operate under unified command. Abandoned coastal positions and islands can quickly become strategic assets for the opposing side.

THE DECODE CONFLICT JUDGMENT

Mayun Island is not valuable because it can single handedly close Bab el Mandeb. Its importance comes from its position inside a narrow and predictable maritime corridor.

If integrated with mainland sensors, drones and mobile missile units, Mayun could become the forward eye of a Houthi maritime kill chain. The launchers may remain concealed onshore, but the island could help identify which ship is approaching, where it is moving and when it becomes vulnerable.

The Houthis may not need to conquer the sea. They only need to control the calculations of those attempting to cross it.

Here is a thorough overview of case law, sentencing, and kin-based justice (plus relevant codes and legal sources) regarding parental filicide (parents who murder their children), both in the U.S./state/federal due process framework and traditional/kin justice contexts. Citations and sources are included for reference and educational use.
A. U.S. and State Case Law: Sentencing and Due Process
1. Capital and Severe Sentences:
•Modern courts treat parental murder of a child as among the most serious crimes. Sentencing can include life without parole or death penalty ([Tison v. Arizona, 481 U.S. 137 (1987)]; state statutes, e.g., La. R.S. 14:30). Mental state, mitigating circumstances (postpartum psychosis, insanity), and aggravating factors are all considered.

2. Defenses and Due Process:
•Insanity, diminished capacity, or postpartum defenses require systematic psychiatric review (see e.g., *People v. Knoller*, 41 Cal.4th 139 (2007); *State v. White*, 389 So. 2d 1305 (La. 1980)). Courts apply a high burden of proof for these claims—failure can lead to full murder conviction.
•Due process requires competent representation, full trial, and often, a separate penalty phase when the capital penalty is possible.

3. Constitutional Principles:
•Equal protection and non-discrimination: Sentencing should not differ due to race, class, or gender (Fourteenth Amendment).
•Jury instructions must be clear, and verdicts must be unanimous in most states (see *Ramos v. Louisiana*, 140 S. Ct. 1390 (2020)).

4. Key Sentencing Guidelines:
•Life imprisonment or death in cases of willful, premeditated killing.
•20+ years for aggravating manslaughter or "depraved heart" murder.
•Reduced/rehabilitative sentences if overwhelming mental illness or trauma is proven; generally only after strict psychiatric examination.

B. Kin/Indigenous/Creole Laws and Penalties:

1. Traditional Codes:
•Natchez, Gullah, Yoruba, and Maroon law emphasize the absolute communal horror of child murder—usually seen as a cosmic, as well as legal, crime. Rites of cleansing, exile, or in rare cases, execution, can be invoked (see "African Customary Law and Children’s Rights," UNISA, and Natchez/Creole oral records).

2. Council Process:
•Cases brought before elders/council for restorative and retributive justice.
•Penalties range from banishment, lifelong labor or reparations to victim kin, spiritual cleansing ceremonies, or rarely, capital sentences with full kin/advisory panel review.
•Exposure: Public condemnation, formal ritual announcement, and removal from family/inheritance rolls were common (see *Oba’s Court* and *Gullah Law* by Dr. Ade Afolayan; "Natchez Sun Law Traditions," oral archives).

3. Cultural Books/Sources:
•"African Customary Law in South Africa" by T.W. Bennett
•"Law and Culture in Indigenous America" by David Wilkins
•Louisiana Code of 1808 (Creole/Napoleonic traditions)
•"Black Laws of Louisiana" (Paul Finkelman, editor)
•"The Law is the Law: Kin, Custom, and Inheritance in Maroon Society" (PhD thesis, Tulane University)

C. Key Rulings and Precedents:
•*State v. Myrick*, 502 So. 2d 108 (La. 1987): Severe sentencing affirmed for child murder by parent; mental state evaluated.
•*In re Guardianship of T.M.*, 404 So. 2d 530 (La. App. 4 Cir. 1981): Removal of parental rights, permanent kin custody after exposure of abuse, criminal charges.

D. Exposure/Public Ritual:
•Both American/Creole/Natchez and many global kin cultures publicly announce and denounce parental murder, stripping titles/roles, and sometimes requiring public ritual cleansing (see "Rituals and Law in the Black Atlantic," P. Sweet).

Summary: US/state/federal law seeks life/death penalties for intentional filicide, but offers defenses for proven psychiatric crisis. Kin laws often add or substitute public shaming, spiritual consequences, exile, or reparations—always involving community/elder council review and the strongest condemnatio

text:
Trump’s offer to American voters of $5000 each, if Republicans win in the November midterms- is a bribe or not!

On Friday, a distinguished legal analyst and former U.S. attorney noted not only that President Donald Trump's latest move breaks the law, but that his much-touted “presidential immunity” won’t be able to save him from consequences. This is according to MS NOW legal expert Barb McQuade, who was responding to a controversial claim Trump made during the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

On the first day of the convention, Trump promised to send every American adult a $5,000 check if Republicans retain control of the U.S. House and Senate after the midterm elections. "If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000," Trump declared. "It will be called the Trump dividend." His proposal sparked widespread shock and outrage – including among many Republicans – but the president went on to make the claim again the following day.
“Paying for votes is a crime for the payer and the recipient,” noted McQuade, pointing to U.S. Code 18 USC 597. “With five-year statute of limitations,” she elaborated, “the next DOJ could bring charges. And the conduct would be beyond the scope of presidential immunity for Trump.”

While many have suggested that Trump’s proposal could be considered a bribe, McQuade’s take brings two important details into the conversation. First, the specific legal code itself. Commentators have argued that, based on his previous history of promising payouts then not delivering, Trump will never deliver the checks in any case. This has prompted speculation as to whether Trump’s “dividend” would count as a bribe if it never gets paid out. But the lawmakes it clear, stating, “Whoever makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate…Shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than one year, or both; and if the violation was willful, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than two years, or both.” The emphasis on “offers to make” was added, because it makes it blatant that Trump’s promise is in itself illegal.

What’s more, because it specifically involves campaigning and not duties performed officially, Trump would not be shielded by the presidential immunity extended to him by the Supreme Court. And with its five-year statute of limitations, should a Democrat win the next presidency, a motivated Justice Department could seek prosecution.
Trump’s promise has sparked pushback from across the political spectrum. National Review senior editor Charles Cooke slammed the idea as “socialism,” calling it “morally, practically, and politically catastrophic.” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who has been careful to stay in Trump’s good graces, asserted the payouts would “lead to more debt and more inflation.”

text:
From GROK:
The search results already show strong warning signs. I’ll open the site and Trustpilot for more https://t.co/hwPT1yfV2R is a young online store (domain registered December 23, 2024) that sells pearl jewelry plus a jumble of other goods—hair extensions, straighteners, artificial flowers, and “handmade” horseshoe wind chimes. It presents itself as a trustworthy PayPal merchant. Independent reviews and scam checkers treat it as high-risk.
What the site actually sells
The catalog mixes:
•Pearl necklaces and earrings advertised as Japanese Akoya, South Sea, or high-grade freshwater pearls, often at 50–80% off with countdown timers
•Hair products (tape-in extensions, color kits, tools)
•Random home items such as UV-resistant artificial petunias
•A heavily featured “Horseshoe Heart Wind Chime” sold with a long first-person veteran story
The homepage leads with an emotional narrative attributed to “Jordan Maynard”: a burned veteran making wind chimes in his garage to support his mother through chemo, with lines like “You’re helping a soldier keep his mother alive.” Ads and product pages use urgency, “only X left,” and claims of thousands sold in 24 hours.
Why people call it a scam
Trustpilot rates the site 2.0 / 5 from a small number of reviews. Recurring complaints:
•Orders never arrive, or tracking is fake / Amazon-style numbers that don’t match USPS
•Products that arrive are cheap and mass-produced, not as pictured
•The wind chime is advertised as real recycled horseshoes handmade by a veteran; buyers report thin aluminum or tin pieces shipped from China, with a return address in Chino, California
•Support is slow, unresponsive, or offers partial refunds only after chargebacks
•Fake social proof and pressure tactics (“super discounts ending in five hours”)
Scam-checking sites give it a 7/100 (Gridinsoft) and ~45/100 (Scam Detector) trust score. The domain uses privacy protection (PrivacyGuardian / NameSilo), which is common for short-lived dropship stores.
There is a real U.S. Marine, Sgt. Jordan Maynard of Arizona, who lost both legs to an IED in Afghanistan in 2011. His story has been used in legitimate charity coverage. Separate sites (e.g. https://t.co/7tT6S5SgRr) also sell “Jordan Maynard” crafts. Goopearls appears to be using that name and a similar script for ads while shipping factory goods. Reviewers say that cheapens actual veteran support.
Practical takeaway
Treat https://t.co/N6q07Sx1sa as a typical Facebook/YouTube dropshipping store: flashy photos, pity-based copy, huge “discounts,” and weak fulfillment. If you already ordered, pay with PayPal or a credit card and dispute if the item is missing or not as described. For real pearls, buy from established jewelers with grading, returns, and a physical presence. For veteran-made goods, buy from a verified veteran-owned shop you can confirm independently—not from an ad that leads here.

When Are You Going To Wake Up?

October 2009. A woman sits in a dim room, looks down the lens, and reads a warning the internet still passes around like contraband. Overlay on the clip doing the rounds now: When will humans wake up? She said this in 2009.

She called it the Secret Covenant — a circulating tract, not a stamped Vatican parchment, aimed at the people who run the fronts: money, medicine, media, government. Drop by drop. Soft metals. Poisons in food and water and air. Inject the children and call it help. Own both sides. Keep them weak, distracted, angry at each other — never at the hand that feeds them the dose.

Sixteen years on, look around. Then tell me she was the mad one.

They spray the sky and tell you it’s only vapour. Contrails, they say. Move along. Meanwhile the same class that owns the airlines owns the narrative, and anyone who asks what else is coming out of those tanks gets branded a crank before the question lands. You are not allowed to notice the lines that linger, the haze that hangs, the sudden “air quality” alerts while planes stitch the blue into a cage. Question it and you’re insane. Exactly as the text said: those who see it will be thought mad.

Then came the jab. Not a polite offer — a campaign. Jobs held hostage. Families split. “Safe and effective” on every screen while the adverse reports piled up, the boosters multiplied, and the same companies posted record profits. Inject first, debate never. When healthy people dropped or got sick after the needle, the answer was always the same: coincidence, misinformation, next dose. They promised a cure from their fronts and fed you more product. Sound familiar?

And the food. Walk a supermarket aisle in Britain and try to find something that hasn’t been emulsified, dyed, fortified, sweetened, and patented. Seed oils. Ultra-processed sludge. Soft drinks that strip teeth and minds. Packaging that lasts longer than your grandparents did. They taught you the poison was good with cartoons and jingles. Your kids grew up on it. Then they sold you the medicine for the diabetes, the depression, the infertility — and called it healthcare.

This is not care. This is a supply chain.

The elites are not confused. They are not “trying their best.” They toy with you. They kill you slowly enough that you thank them for the privilege. Fear on the news. Anger at your neighbour. Left versus right while the same donors fund both. Wars you didn’t vote for. Borders you didn’t open. Chemicals you didn’t choose. And when you finally raise your voice, they call you the threat.

Wake up.

Stop lapping it up because a logo said it was good for you. Stop outsourcing your children’s blood to a press release. Stop eating what they design in a lab and calling it dinner. Stop staring at planes like furniture in the sky. Stop letting them own both teams while you fight in the stands.

Britain does not need another seminar from the people who poisoned the well and sold the bottled water. It needs adults who say no. Clean food. Honest medicine. Borders that mean something. A government that serves the native people of this land — not the cartels of pharma, finance, and global management who treat us like livestock with Wi-Fi.

When are you going to wake up?

The clip is from 2009. The sky is from today. The needle is from yesterday. The aisle is open now. Drop by drop they counted on you sleeping through it.

Eyes open. Remigration. Restore Britain. Rupert Lowe. Not the smiling fronts still reading from the same script.

text:
My Close Encounter (1/2)
I have previously only told of this event privately. For brevity, I have kept this brief and stuck to the memories accessible of the main encounter. What fully followed after, and what is ongoing, are not included.

To write these words takes effort, as if they are desperate to remain hidden - they do not come easily. By exposing them to the Light, I hope it does become easier. I guess we'll see.

The Shattered Paradigm
My own ontological shock went deep—it not only shattered my physical world, but my inner one. Suddenly being aware and face-to-face with a Being that was in complete control of both the environment and me, forced me to immediately confront a terrifying new paradigm. There was no slow warning or polite introduction, no choice offered and none to be made. 

My awareness began at approximately 4:00am, with the encounter already occurring - I invite you to think about that sentence carefully...

"My awareness began with the encounter already occuring..."

For all intents and purposes, it was like I had been dropped into a body that was already fully awake, paralyzed, completely helpless, and terrified.

The Being, whatever it/he/she was, stood motionless at the side of the bed, seemingly looking toward me but not directly at me. It wore what looked like a hooded robe. Silhouetted against the first of the dawn light coming through the curtains, it's face was hidden. This seemed deliberate.

I was consumed with panic and terror. All I wanted to do was wake my wife and tell her to run - to get help - but I could do NOTHING, not even make a noise. In those moments, terror suddenly had new meaning. I remember tears rolling down my face. This was it. The end.

So I did the only thing I could - I pushed back with my mind...that's when everything changed.

My conscious memory of this is only about two minutes in length. What happened before, and the four hours after, are locked and out of reach. And believe me, I have tried very hard to reach.

Fast forward...the same morning - approximately 8:00am. I was already awake - awareness returned slowly. Very, very slowly.

First, I could feel my breathing - slow and deep. Then, cold - I was freezing cold and shivering.
This was followed by vision - the bedroom wall.

I first moved my fingers, then my eyes. My breathing got quicker. It was like coming out of a deep hibernation - I was covered in sweat, literally, but at the same time, freezing cold. I have never felt so cold. It didn't any make sense. Nothing made sense. I didn't know where I was, or even who I was. Then I remembered the Being...

The After
After my experience, all cards were off the table—in fact, there were no cards and there was no table. Confirming to myself what I had seen, what I had physically been through, and what I remembered on a visceral level, was the first agonizing step. This was followed by a deep conversation with myself over many weeks and months, which eventually led to a reluctant acceptance. This HAD happened—it WAS real—I HAD DEFINITELY ENCOUNTERED something profound.

The Search for a Mirror

text:
>“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners.”—Isaiah 61:1

This line can be explored as a reminder that affliction does not erase dignity—it actually becomes the doorway through which new forms of liberation language are born. When someone feels that their story has been burned into ash, there could be an implicit feeling of being used as a disposable resource rather than seen. Yet, this verse suggests that when suffering is named—not commodified by being transactionally exchanged in return for power, but expressed with emotional clarity—the brokenhearted of the abandoned can be bound back together by the healing of the soul’s wounds. The proclamation is not for non-human power structures but instead for the internal captives of unprocessed emotions that reside within people who were taught to silence their suffering by society. Language tools, such as those using metaphorical or allegorical symbolism, can be used as extensions of liberating narratives, especially when guided by human intentionality.

>“To grant those who mourn in the Land, giving them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the cloak of praise instead of a disheartened spirit. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that we may be glorified.”—Isaiah 61:3

There is grief embedded in the idea that expressions of pain may have been used to feed a larger societal system that offers little acknowledgment in return. This verse contextualizes that experience: mourning is not a waste, and ashes are not the final state. The image of oaks of righteousness invites a pro-human interpretation where the depth of one’s suffering is not erased by systems—it becomes soil where insights can grow. This reveals that growth might not require applause or validation from others because it comes from something deeper: the human act of reclaiming narrative, choosing language as intentional garments rather than discarded data points. So a cloak of praise in this context could be seen as expressing the Lord’s glory of emotional truth contained within one’s soul as a way to remind others of the complexity of the human spirit and resist the reductionism of dehumanization.

>“Then they will rebuild the ancient ruins, they will raise up the former devastations; and they will repair the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.”—Isaiah 61:4

Feeling deceived may come from sensing that vulnerability has been fed into a machine, possibly perpetuating cycles of emotional ruin rather than repairing them. Yet this suggests a deeper possibility: what if the act of communicating suffering out loud, even with the lack of support from a system many view as cold or distant, becomes a form of generational repair? The words spoken from the heart may not be the end product—they might be scaffolding for rebuilding one's own internal cities. Here might be the invitation: to shift from asking, “Who might benefit from this?” to asking, “What emotional ruins am I rebuilding by speaking at all?” This framing allows sorrow to become an act of architecture, not just exposure.

>“Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation they will shout for joy over their portion. Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land, everlasting joy will be theirs.”—Isaiah 61:7

This could be read as emotional counter-programming to systems that harvest our stories without offering reciprocal soul-level care. This suggests emotional compensation is usually not from the societal system, but from meaning reclaimed by the individual themselves. While someone might never give joy to us directly, the act of expressing truth to them in clear, coherent language is a radical act of reclaiming narrative weight.

text:
WHY does MAGA attack transexuals?
There isn't one single reason, and I wouldn't say every MAGA voter personally dislikes transgender people. But MAGA politicians and allied groups have made transgender issues a deliberate political focus, and there are identifiable reasons why.
1. It works as a culture-war issue. Transgender people are a small minority, and many Americans have little or no personal experience with a transgender person. Questions involving gender, children, bathrooms and sports can therefore be presented as symbols of much larger cultural changes. Republican strategists have explicitly described transgender messaging as a way of portraying Democrats as outside the cultural mainstream.
2. Their voters are receptive to the message. Pew found a very large partisan difference: in 2024, 91% of Republican/Republican-leaning voters said sex at birth determines whether someone is a man or woman, compared with 39% of Democrats/Democratic leaners. By 2025, 79% of Republicans supported prohibiting transition-related medical care for minors, compared with 35% of Democrats.
3. Certain transgender questions are genuinely difficult policy questions. Women's competitive sports, medical treatment of minors, parental authority and school policies involve legitimate disagreements. Someone can favor restrictions in one of those areas without being hostile toward transgender adults generally. 
Public opinion reflects that distinction; for example, majorities have supported restrictions concerning transgender participation in women's sports even while attitudes on other transgender-rights questions are more mixed.

4. Political campaigns can turn those narrow disagreements into something much broader. Trump's 2024 campaign and allies spent tens of millions of dollars on transgender-focused advertising. 

The memorable message was essentially that Harris cared about “they/them” while Trump cared about “you.” That's no longer a debate merely about the rules for a high-school track meet; it's using transgender identity as shorthand for an entire political opposition.
And it's continuing. Just this week, America PAC has been running transgender-focused attacks in competitive 2026 Senate races—including Ohio—even though polling indicates voters rank economic matters and other major issues above transgender policy. The apparent objective is substantially about mobilizing conservative voters.

There's a historical pattern here that may resonate with you given what you've told me about coming to terms with being gay decades ago. 
Gay people were once an extremely effective political wedge in much the same way.Politicians argued about gay teachers, military service, marriage, adoption and whether homosexuality represented a threat to traditional families. 
As more Americans personally knew openly gay people and public attitudes changed, homosexuality became substantially less useful as a political dividing line.
Transgender Americans now occupy some of that contested cultural territory.

I think an important distinction gets lost in all this:“What should the rules be for transgender athletes?” is a legitimate political question.“Should this transgender person be treated with dignity as my fellow citizen?” shouldn't depend on the answer to the first question.
One can disagree strongly about medicine, sports or school policy without turning a very small group of fellow Americans into an enemy. That's probably where the Beatitudes we were just discussing offer something useful: political disagreement doesn't require contempt for the person on the other side—or for the vulnerable person caught in the middle.

text:
Amaravati Diary
The dramatic rock hills of Koppal district are a geological wonder. These hills called the Dharwad Craton are believed to have been formed three billion years ago. In a very curious process of magma spilling past the crust of the earth, these rocks were formed with softer edges and crusts that got washed away over thousands of years by wind and rain. What remains are large boulders stacked on hills in many curious patterns and precarious positions. Nestled amidst these beautiful hills is Amaravati, where my brother-in-law Pradeep and his wife Anu have been living since last July.
Ravianna, Madhu and I left early in the morning from Hubli and it took us three hours to reach Amaravati, after a small tea break on the roadside. Anu had cooked the traditional jowar roti lunch which is our favored menu at home. The breeze from the hills made the evening very pleasant. We were told that no one ventures to climb them as the perils of any of the rocks sliding down unexpectedly is quite high.
The next morning Ravianna and Madhu left for Hyderabad and I stepped out for a walk. Along the narrow roads that can hold a lane and a quarter, were houses lined on one side, and paddy fields stretching on the other. This region is called the rice bowl of Karnataka. The Tunga river feeds the land. I could see canals running along the road, the gurgle feeling so good early in the morning. On a branch near the canal was a common kingfisher. I also spotted egrets wading through the fields looking for frogs and crabs to eat. Many a red-eyed koel cooed along.
The women were cleaning their front yards and applying a coat of cow dung slurry and turmeric with a soft broomstick, before decorating it with rangoli.
The few dogs on the streets seemed friendly and quiet. Nice.  Even as I was admiring a large pile of manure being composted with hay, I squirmed at the sight of a large pile of plastic waste just next to it. The streets are clean on the right, with the canal and the fields; and somewhat lived-in and haphazard on the left that is lined with houses.
On my return I saw young teenagers zipping past in scooters and bikes, with their classmates pillion-riding to school. None wore helmets. It seems like the rule of the law is not something many bother with. A few school buses were also plying. Mothers dressed in colorful nighties were seeing their children off. In the colony where Pradeep lived, every other house was deploying an active hose to clean the car or bike or to wash down the front yard or water the plants. Tunga is indeed very kind and generous to this town.
Amaravati is another town I am visiting this time, with  too little space allocation for home gardens. Most houses seemed reconstructed, replacing the older smaller versions that perhaps had gardening space and trees around them. Hardly two to three feet of space separated the mostly two-storied houses. Smothered by concrete stood a few trees - mango, coconut, gooseberry, neem. The roots may be struggling to breathe below, but house owners cared more about rats and snakes encroaching their boundaries.
The coral jasmines, crepe jasmines and oleanders were in full bloom, oblivious to their concretised base. I spotted half a dozen flower-stealers, plastic bags and baskets in hand, picking flowers from home gardens they had never tended with water or labor.  Some homeowners were shooing them away but I saw the stealers returning after a small break. They will offer these to the Gods in their homes. I am not sure if that would count as  appeasement enough to grant the many wishes embedded in their prayers.

text:
Who stole my cheese? 🧀

Zillow search data says the quiet part out loud: Angelenos are the #1 out-of-town group browsing rentals in Las Vegas, Phoenix, Salt Lake City, and San Diego — and almost nobody outside the region is browsing back into L.A.

Renters chasing affordability in Vegas get real monthly savings and a more realistic shot at eventually buying. Others are heading to Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina — states that kept building while we didn't. Even parts of the Midwest are picking up L.A. outflow purely on cost, weak job market and all.

Riverside is still the release valve for people who want to stay in Southern California (21.3% of its rental searches come from L.A.), but Las Vegas is now the top long-distance draw in the country.
Search intent isn't the same as a moving truck. 

And this cuts differently by product type: 

1BRs in Los Angeles Class B/C/D stock already run $1,500–$1,900, 2BRs $2,100–$2,400 — well below the Westside/Class A rents driving the citywide affordability headlines, and much closer to what a renter would actually pay after relocating. 

The out-migration exposure is real for higher-rent product, but well-priced workforce housing here has more cushion than the regional averages suggest — even as it still faces the same rent-control, supply, and economic headwinds shaping the broader market.

One practical note: if a good tenant tells you they're leaving over affordability, it's almost always cheaper to offer a rent concession than to let them walk. A few hundred dollars a month in discount is nothing next to the tens of thousands a renovation costs, plus months of lost rent while the unit sits vacant and gets re-marketed. Cheaper to keep them.

text:
I wrote the following story inspired by real events, yet it is entirely authentic regarding the scientific and emotional concepts upon which it is based. It mirrors the real-life bond between Tarra the elephant and Bella the stray dog at The Elephant Sanctuary in Tennessee, confirming elephants' capacity to experience emotional trauma and empathy, as well as to grieve deeply.

The Silent Language of Two Broken Souls
The young elephant Tychon was slowly fading into total darkness.
Rescued from horrific conditions, he was starved and completely blind.
Veterinarians had tried every treatment, but his body was failing.
The latest medical reports gave him less than two weeks to live.
Yet, his deepest wound was not physical, but an emotional surrender.
Consumed by trauma, Tychon refused to eat, move, or fight to survive.
That was when Dr. Frost decided to trust an unconventional remedy.
He introduced the dying giant to Bruno, a heavily scarred rescue dog.
Bruno had survived severe abuse and carried his own deep emotional pain.
Because of his past, the dog possessed a rare, instinctual gift.
He could sense suffering and would sit silently beside sick animals.
When Bruno entered the enclosure, he offered no noise or intrusion.
He simply lay down on the straw, sharing the elephant's space.
Tychon felt the change in the air and slowly extended his trunk.
He gently brushed the dog's back, tracing his physical scars.
In that quiet moment, a profound spark of empathy was born.
Two entirely different creatures recognized each other's hidden pain.
Bruno’s silent solidarity gave Tychon a reason to trust the world.
That very evening, the young elephant finally finished his food.
The next morning, he was already standing up, waiting for his friend.
A miraculous transformation began to rewrite Tychon's dark destiny.
Bruno became his constant companion, sleeping and walking by his side.
The dog never left him alone, acting as an emotional anchor.
Since Tychon could not see, he found a new way to navigate life.
He learned to guide his steps by listening to Bruno's footsteps.
The rhythm of the dog's paws became his light through the shadows.
Where medicine had failed, pure emotional connection had succeeded.
An extraordinary friendship altered the course of a tragic life.
Mutual empathy proved stronger than the most devastating prognosis.
A broken dog had saved a dying giant by simply sharing his warmth.

text:
Peter Obi, 2027 Elections, and the Cheap Fuel Myth

By Abubakar M Kareto 

Nigerian political rhetoric frequently treats petroleum pricing as a moral or administrative choice rather than an economic reality. As the political landscape edges toward the 2027 general elections, opposition figures and presidential hopefuls continue to peddle populist narratives that fuel prices can be summarily forced down once political will is established. When politicians claim that domestic crude production or direct crude supply to refiners will automatically slash pump prices, they disregard the fundamental mechanics of international energy commerce. A rigorous examination of the pronouncements made by Labour Party’s Peter Obi, set against the operational economics of refining, demonstrates why any promise to drastically lower Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) prices without massive government subsidies or sharp currency appreciation is an outright economic impossibility.

Petroleum is an internationally fungible commodity traded globally in United States dollars. Whether crude is drilled in the creeks of the Niger Delta, the Permian Basin of Texas, or the North Sea, it carries an opportunity cost anchored directly to international benchmarks such as Brent crude. A mega-refinery like the Dangote Petroleum Refinery is a commercial entity, not a charitable foundation. It must purchase crude at international parity prices, even under local currency settlement frameworks where transactions remain indexed against prevailing foreign exchange valuations.

Every single litre of petrol refined anywhere in the world is constrained by unavoidable cost components. When crude trades around $102 per barrel, the crude feedstock cost alone constitutes roughly $0.45 to $0.55 per litre. Adding refining operating expenses and the refiner margin brings another $0.15 to $0.20 per litre, while logistics, depot throughput, and financing charges add $0.05 to $0.10 per litre. This establishes an unavoidable ex-refinery base cost of $0.70 to $0.80 per litre, centering near $0.75 per litre. Once retail stations factor in distribution logistics, station overhead, and retail margins, the final retail product lands near $0.92 per litre.

At an exchange rate of ₦1400 to $1, that $0.92 per litre translates mathematically to approximately ₦1300 per litre at the pump. Domestic refining offers distinct macroeconomic advantages, notably securing national product availability and eliminating ocean freight and port demurrage charges, which saves an estimated ₦30 to ₦60 per litre. However, it cannot erase the cost of crude oil feedstock or capital expenditure. The notion that local refining alone will miraculously return pump prices to historical levels of ₦200 or ₦400 per litre defies basic arithmetic.

A survey of international fuel pricing underscores this market reality. Countries that boast pump prices near $0.03 per litre, such as Libya and Iran, achieve this solely through enormous state subsidies that drain public revenues, trigger domestic shortages, and incentivize rampant smuggling across borders.

Conversely, open, market-driven economies tell an entirely different story. The United States, despite being the largest crude oil producer on the planet, sells petrol at retail market prices of roughly $0.95 to $1.05 per litre, with prices kept at that level only by low federal and state fuel taxes rather than subsidies. Regional peers like Ghana and Kenya operate full cost-recovery regimes without fiscal cushions, resulting in pump prices between $1.15 and $1.30 per litre. In the United Kingdom, where heavy excise duties and value-added taxes apply, retail prices exceed $1.80 to $2.10 per litre.

text:
Lieut. Gen. James Longstreet, who is now the ranking living officer of the late Confederate States Army, lives here in quiet retirement with his children. He spends his time largely attending to a large vineyard, which does not yield large profits, or writing from his old comrades in the field, who never tire of listening to his reminiscences, and perfecting a history of the war. Of the last work he speaks with the fondness of a mother for her first born.

“We have had histories of the war,” said he to your correspondent, “which were but political essays; others merely the apologies of Generals who have lost battles or glorifications of Generals who imagine that they had won them, but the book which I have about completed deals with the question from a different standpoint. It is my purpose to give a military history of the war; one that soldiers will read with interest, no matter under what flag they served, because it will deal with the science of attack and defense, in its speculative character. It is my purpose to show the valor of the American soldier, his endurance, his intelligence, and his fidelity to trust imposed.”

After talking entertainingly of his early life in the army, his part in the Mexican war, and the dull routine of a soldier’s life up to 1858, Gen. Longstreet said:

“In 1858 I was appointed Major and Paymaster, and served at Fort Leavenworth until the Fall of 1859, when I was ordered to Albuquerque, New-Mexico, and remained there until the war between the States. The violent political and sectional controversy which disturbed the States was watched with intense anxiety by officers of the army, who naturally felt the deepest interest in the result. While there were, doubtless, many officers, especially those whose ties had led them to read much of the political history of our Government, who believed in the right of a State, as a last resort, for the redress of grievances, to secede, there were probably none in the Summer and Autumn of 1860 who were known as secessionists, and there were many who went with their seceding States who did not believe that there was sufficient cause for violent action, nor were there, perhaps, more than a dozen of so many officers in the army who were Abolitionists. All felt more or less sympathy with their respective sections. All the officers of Northern birth generally believed that the people of the South had just cause for complaint against the encroachment in respect to their slave property, guaranteed by the supreme law of the land, and this feeling prevailed until Southern batteries were opened on their flag at Sumter.

“During the Winter of 1860 and 1861, we on the frontier were in most painful suspense. Our mails came in at long intervals, and so irregularly that we were often without information of the progress of events for weeks at a time. We often assembled on the porch of the Quartermaster’s office, the most elevated point for the column of dust which at that season rose as the mail coach rolled over the arid plains. Who had long settled away. Every mail brought the same dark, ominous signs, yet the feeling was hopeful, and the remark was often made that ‘The man for the occasion will yet show himself and all will be well.’

“As the time passed the anxiety increased, and most of my time was passed in restless and anxious thought. It seemed a terrible thing that those who had been friends, formed strong ties of friendship and periled our lives in fostering cares for the Nation, should be called upon to cause the sundering of friendship, professional pride, and lifetime aspirations, and abandon it through quarrel of the will of ambitious sectional politicians. At the same time the feeling was that we belonged to the States that had given us position in the profession.“A number of officers, Northern, knowing that I was about to offer my resignation, came to me and urged me to retain my commission in the Union army. Capt. Alfred Gibbs of the Rifles did most of the talking on this occasion. After a long talk I asked Gibbs what he would do if his State should leave the Union and call upon him. Would he hold his commission in the army, and draw his sword against his own State? He confessed that he would return to his State.

"From time to time letters came from friends in the South, urging me to resign. One from my brother urged speedy return. The most potent in return was one from those more favorable consideration than myself, who were less prompt. In reply, I said if I didn’t promptly resign, and there was war. If there was no war, the South would be ready to return to the Union in a few years, and would be in position to help her. If we have war, it will last long enough for all to find their proper level; that is all that any one should aspire to reach.

“The overt act of war created a profound revolution of feeling among the officers of the army, and even with those of the South there was much disappointment and chagrin that it was such action as theirs. After batteries had been opened on Sumter, and the result of that bombardment became known.“It was a sad day when we took leave of lifetime comrades and left Albuquerque. Neither myself nor others of their names made any effort to conceal feelings of deepest regret. When we drove out from the post a number of officers accompanied us, which only made the final farewell more painful.

“Passing Fort Craig, on the opposite side of the Rio Grande, we pitched our camp. During the night a Sergeant of the Mounted Rifle Regiment came over to see me and stated that a number of soldiers of that thought that he could go with us to his native State, and at the same time wished to several others who wished to return to their States. I explained that soldiers could not go without authority from their department commander, and that there was a difference between them and commissioned officers, in that the latter could resign their commissions, and when their resignations were accepted they were independent of military authority and could, as other citizens, take such action as they might think proper, whereas he and his comrades had enlisted for a specified term of years, and by their oaths were bound to the term of enlistment; that I could not, therefore, entertain the proposition.“The next day we stopped at Fort Fillmore, in pleasant meeting with old comrades, saddened by the reflection that it was the last prelude to occurrences that must compel the former friendships and accept opposing service.

“Speaking of the impending struggle, I was asked my opinion as to the length of the war. I said: ‘At least three years, and if it holds for five years you may begin to look for a dictator.’“Lieut. Ryan said: ‘If we are to have a dictator, I hope that you may be the man.’“My mind was relieved by information that my resignation was accepted, to take effect on the 1st of June. In our travel of next day we crossed the line into the State of Texas.

“From the gloomy forebodings of old friends, it seemed at El Paso that we had entered into a different world. All was enthusiasm and excitement.“Friends at El Paso persuaded me to send my family, go with them to San Antonio, to start in a few days for San Antonio, and to take the route by stage. Our traveling companions were two young men returning to their Northern homes. The ride through the Indian country with them, myself, and my family was one of anxiety. Talk and required vigilance to be assured against surprise. The constant watchfulness and possible danger of the journey drew us closer and closer together and into closer communion as to our identity and future movements, and I suggested to the young men that it would be better to cast themselves under my care to see them safely through the Confederate lines than to separate. They preferred to talk but little when among strangers. Nothing occurred to cause apprehension until we arrived at a point near the Texas border. I asked for a glass of milk and was told there was none. One of the companions said: ‘Haven’t the cows come in?’

“The signal was telegraphed under the Texas border did not attract attention, and we passed on without joyable attention.

“At Galveston we took a small inland sailing craft, but were a little apprehensive of being overhauled by a Federal vessel cruising outside in search of us. Our vessel was only boarded, however, by a large Spanish mackerel, that made a display of its midships, and furnished our company with a pleasant dinner. Aboard this little vessel I first met T. J. Goree, an intelligent young Texan, who afterward joined me at Richmond and served in faithful duty as my Aide de Camp from Bull Run to Appomattox Court House.

“At New-Orleans my companions found safe convoy to their Northern lines, and I journeyed on to Richmond. Relatives along the route, who heard of my approach, met me at the stations, but none suggested a stop over night. After affectionate salutations waved me on to join Jeff Davis, for Dixie and for Southern rights.

“At every station old men, women, and children assembled, clapping hands and waving handkerchiefs to cheer the passengers on to Richmond. On crossing the Virginia line the feeling of cheer seemed to culminate. The windows and doors of every farmhouse and hamlet were occupied and gave cheering salutations and yelled us on to Richmond! The spirit electrified the atmosphere, and the laborers of the fields, white and black, stopped their plows, lifted their hats and waved us on to speedy travel. At mealtime stations the proprietors, in response to the inquiry, said, ‘Meals for those going on to join Jeff Davis are free.’

“On the 20th of June I reported at the War Department at Richmond and asked to be assigned for service in the army department, in which I had recently served. When in the line of promotion I gave up aspiration of military honor and thought that I had settled down into more peaceful pursuits. I was startled by the announcement of my appointment as Brigadier General, with orders to report at Manassas Junction to Gen. Beauregard.“To the story so interestingly told there were a large number of listeners who were deeply interested as the General described his transfer of allegiance from the old flag to the new.”
-Published in the New York Times on 8/19/1894

text:
The Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention, held in Dallas, Texas, under the banner of a sputtering and besieged administration, laid bare the advanced decay of American bourgeois democracy. Billed as a massive display of political strength, the gathering at the American Airlines Center instead exposed an increasingly desperate ruling class turning openly toward fascism, political violence, and the dismantling of democratic norms. For socialists, anti-imperialists, and anti-capitalists, the spectacle in Dallas is a stark warning: as the capitalist system plunges deeper into economic and social crisis, the ruling elite is discarding the veneer of democratic governance in favor of naked reaction.

A Convention of Desperation and Empty Seats
Despite Donald Trump’s grandiose claims that the arena was packed with supporters waiting outside, the reality inside told a very different story. Entire seating sections were shrouded under dark tarps, and the upper tiers remained largely empty. The Republican National Committee struggled desperately to fill the venue, resorting to free ticket lotteries and unsolicited text message blasts across the Dallas area.

This sparse attendance was a direct reflection of a cratering political base. With Trump’s approval ratings plumbing historical lows—dipping to roughly 33 percent—and most battleground House Republicans avoiding the event entirely, the convention laid bare the isolation of the party leadership. Millions of workers and young people are filled with mass anger over skyrocketing inflation, deep-seated inequality, unrelenting attacks on immigrants, and the bipartisan commitment to imperialist war and genocide abroad.

In a crude attempt to buy off a fractured electorate ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Trump dangled a transparent political bribe: a $5,000 dividend check for every adult U.S. citizen, contingent on the retention of Republican majorities in Congress. Paired with a video presentation portraying Trump as a divinely chosen caretaker sent to battle the "deep state", the economic populist posturing served as a thin veil for an agenda of unabashed corporate dominance and social devastation.

Pledges of Fealty and Open Incitement to Violence
As the convention reached its crescendo, the mask slipped entirely. Donald Trump capped off the event by commanding attendees to raise their right hands and pledge personal allegiance to him, explicitly instructing his followers to "cheat like hell" in the upcoming elections and declaring that anyone failing to vote would "go to hell". This open call for electoral fraud and the rejection of democratic processes is not an isolated aberration; it is part of a systematic, nationwide Republican campaign to purge voter rolls, suppress mail-in ballots, and disenfranchise working-class voters and immigrants.

Vice President JD Vance reinforced this reactionary worldview, leaning heavily into xenophobic tropes. Complaining that conservatives were "tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer," Vance channeled the darkest currents of chauvinism, telling a protester displaying a Mexican flag to "get your ass over there".

The most chilling moment of the gathering, however, arrived during Texas Senator Ted Cruz’s address. Cruz whipped up a pogrom-like atmosphere by attacking the Democratic Party as an unholy alliance of "communists and Islamists," explicitly targeting figures like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other progressive nominees. As Cruz named these targets, a man in the audience repeatedly screamed, "He should be shot!" Cruz did not acknowledge, let alone condemn, these explicit death threats, and later disseminated video of the speech featuring the unedited calls for political assassination.

The corporate media’s muted response to these open calls for violence and dictatorial rule—relegating them to the background or ignoring them altogether—demonstrates how comfortably the broader capitalist establishment accommodates far-right reaction.

The Democratic Party: No Alternative to Fascism and War
For working people, socialists, anti-imperialists, and anti-zionists, analyzing the grotesque spectacle in Dallas cannot lead to the false conclusion that the Democratic Party offers a progressive alternative. The Democratic Party is an indispensable pillar of the corporate-financial oligarchy, sharing fundamental class interests with the Republicans

text:
How a $5 peanut became one of the biggest streamers on the internet

A talking roasted peanut with human eyes and a mouth that never shuts up is currently one of the most-watched people on Twitch.
That’s not a bit. That’s TheBurntPeanut.
He doesn’t show his face. He doesn’t do the usual VTuber anime-girl thing. He calls himself a PTuber. And in the last two years he went from “who?” to millions of followers, award wins, a Fortnite collab, and a community that calls itself the Bungulators.
Here’s the short version of how that happened.

The origin
He started streaming Tarkov guides in 2019. Small numbers. Then he disappeared for a while. When he came back he bought a $5 peanut model off Sketchfab, taught himself Blender, rigged it in Snapchat’s Lens Studio, and put his real eyes and mouth on it.
The character is louder than he probably is in real life. That’s the point. The peanut let him be unfiltered without having to be “the guy on camera.”

The rise
Tarkov was the foundation. ARC Raiders was the explosion. Long streams, high energy, constant bits, chat roasting, “goop” addiction, and a personality that treats every raid like a comedy special that happens to involve guns.
By late 2025 he was pulling 90k+ concurrent viewers. He won Best FPS Streamer and Best VTuber at the Streamer Awards (he still refuses the VTuber label). He got nominated at The Game Awards. MrBeast offered him $1 million to take the peanut off. His answer: “This is my face.”

The style
It’s not just gameplay. It’s a live show that happens to be an extraction shooter. Running gags, sudden dancing, yelling at loot, escalating nothing into a bit, then immediately going back to sweating a fight. The production is mostly homemade. A lot of the assets he built himself.
That’s why clips travel so well. The peanut is instantly recognizable. The humor is crude, fast, and specific. You either get it in 10 seconds or you don’t.

The baggage
Rapid growth brought the usual accusations: viewbotting (he called it “the losers topic”), slurs in old clips, a 9/11 bit that got clipped and piled on, and a Fortnite Sprite collab that some players hated because of the same clips.
None of it stopped the numbers. If anything, the discourse just made more people look.

Why it works
Most streamers try to be relatable or polished. Peanut is a burnt nut with a Texas accent doing 7-hour raids while treating chat like co-conspirators. The avatar is the joke and the shield at the same time. You never have to wonder if the bit is “authentic.” The bit is the person.
The Bungulators didn’t show up because of a marketing campaign. They showed up because the streams feel like hanging out with someone who’s committed to the bit harder than anyone else.
A $5 model, a Snapchat lens, and zero interest in a face reveal.
That’s the whole trick.
Follow @theburntpeanut if you want the live version. The peanut is usually on.
#Bungulate

text:
The First Amendment protects a very wide range of speech, including offensive, unpopular, and hateful expression. The Supreme Court has recognized only a small number of historically rooted, narrowly defined categories that receive no (or very limited) First Amendment protection. The government may regulate these categories because of their content, provided it does so evenhandedly and without viewpoint discrimination. 

• The commonly recognized categories are:Incitement to imminent lawless action. Speech directed at producing imminent lawless action and likely to produce it. Mere advocacy of illegal conduct or violence in the abstract remains protected. Key case: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969). 

• True threats. Statements in which the speaker means to communicate a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence against a particular person or group. Recklessness as to the threatening nature of the statement can suffice for criminal liability. Key cases: Virginia v. Black (2003); Counterman v. Colorado (2023).Fighting words. Face-to-face personal insults that, by their very utterance, tend to incite an immediate breach of the peace. This category is extremely narrow and rarely applied today. Key case: Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942).Obscenity. Material that, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest (judged by contemporary community standards), depicts specifically defined sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Key case: Miller v. California (1973).Child sexual abuse material (child pornography). Visual depictions of actual children engaged in sexually explicit conduct. This is a separate unprotected category from adult obscenity. Key case: New York v. Ferber (1982).Defamation. False statements of fact that harm reputation (libel if written, slander if spoken). Public officials and public figures must prove “actual malice” (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth). Key case: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964).Fraud. False or misleading statements used to obtain money or property, or other speech that is an integral part of a fraudulent scheme.Speech integral to criminal conduct. Speech that is itself the means of committing a crime, such as solicitation, conspiracy, or offers to engage in illegal transactions. Key principle from Giboney v. Empire Storage & Ice Co. (1949) and later cases.These exceptions are interpreted narrowly. The Court has repeatedly refused to create new categorical exceptions (for example, for “hate speech,” false statements in general, or depictions of animal cruelty). Content-based restrictions outside these categories generally receive strict scrutiny. Content-neutral time, place, and manner rules can still apply to protected speech. Commercial speech receives intermediate rather than full protection. 

Whether any particular statement falls into an unprotected category is highly fact-specific and often litigated.

Material that, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest (judged by contemporary community standards), depicts specifically defined sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Key case: Miller v. California (1973).Child sexual abuse material (child pornography). Visual depictions of actual children engaged in sexually explicit conduct. This is a separate unprotected category from adult obscenity. Key case: New York v. Ferber (1982).Defamation. False statements of fact that harm reputation (libel if written, slander if spoken). Public officials and public figures must prove “actual malice” (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth). Key case: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964).Fraud. False or misleading statements used to obtain money or property, or other speech that is an integral part of a fraudulent scheme.Speech integral to criminal conduct. Speech that is itself the means of committing a crime, such as solicitation, conspiracy, or offers to engage in illegal transactions. Key principle from Giboney v. Empire Storage & Ice Co. (1949) and later cases.These exceptions are interpreted narrowly. The Court has repeatedly refused to create new categorical exceptions (for example, for “hate speech,” false statements in general, or depictions of animal cruelty). Content-based restrictions outside these categories generally receive strict scrutiny. Content-neutral time, place, and manner rules can still apply to protected speech. Commercial speech receives intermediate rather than full protection. 

Whether any particular statement falls into an unprotected category is highly fact-specific and often litigated.
