text:
After September 11, seventy New York City firefighters put down their hoses and picked up bagpipes, and did not put them down for a year.

They had 343 funerals to play.

They played every one.

The FDNY Emerald Society Pipes and Drums was founded in 1962. It was never meant to be a funeral band. It was Irish firefighters wanting a bit of home in the department. They played parades. St. Patrick's Day up Fifth Avenue. The marathon. Yankees ticker-tape parades. Weddings. Retirement parties. And every once in a while, when a firefighter died in the line of duty, they played him to his grave.

Every once in a while. A few times a year, in a bad year.

Every man in the band is a working firefighter, active or retired. Almost none of them had played an instrument before joining. It takes two years of training and twenty memorized tunes before a piper is allowed to play in public. You have to march, and breathe into the bag, and squeeze it with your arm, and finger the chanter, all at once, in a wool kilt, in whatever weather God sends.

On September 11, 2001, the department lost 343 men. Chiefs. Captains. Lieutenants. Probies. Men from 75 different firehouses. In one morning.

Within days, other pipe bands from across the country called and offered to help. Police bands. Bands from Boston, Chicago, Ireland.

The Emerald Society said no.

They said thank you, and no. They would play for their own. All of them. Every funeral, every memorial. It was a promise they had made to the department for forty years, and they were not going to hand it to strangers now.

Then they did the math.

Seventy pipers. Three hundred and forty-three funerals. And because so many bodies were still in the pile, many families would hold a memorial first, and a funeral months later when remains were found. Some would hold two.

They split into small groups. Four pipers, a drummer. Six pipers, two drummers. Whatever they could spare.

They played twelve funerals a day. Some days fifteen.

A piper would finish Amazing Grace at a church in Queens at 9 a.m., get in a car, and be playing it again in Staten Island at 11, and again on Long Island at 1, and again in Brooklyn at 3. Same tune. Different church. Different widow. Different children in the front pew.

One veteran piper, Ed Geraghty, who had been in the band for twenty-five years, said it plainly afterward. Sometimes you weren't sure where you were.

They stopped fighting fires. They stopped almost everything else. The band pulled out of the marathon. The band did not march for the Yankees. When they were invited to the All-Ireland championships the following summer, they had to admit they had not practiced their competition music since September. There had been no time.

By Thanksgiving 2001, they had played about 300 services.

By the end of the year after, more than 400 funerals and memorials.

Some of the men they buried were their own bandmates. Some were their brothers. Some were their fathers.

Lieutenant Kevin Dowdell of Rescue 4 was killed in the towers. His body was never found. His son Patrick was an 18-year-old college freshman.

Patrick joined the band. He learned the pipes. He learned them so that when his father's memorial came, he could stand in the kilt and play his father to rest.

His younger brother James joined the FDNY and joined the band too. He fights fires with Ladder 174 in Brooklyn now, and he drums, and every September he marches to the memorial wall a few hundred feet from where his father died.

Ed McLoughlin was one of the men who founded the band in 1962. He is 84 now. He has personally played at more than 150 services for the men of 9/11. He said it in seven words.

"It was sorrowful, but you had to do it."

Twenty-five years later, they are still doing it.

More than 400 FDNY members have died since September 11 of cancers and lung diseases from breathing the pile. In 2023, the number of those deaths passed 343. The dying did not stop with the attack.

So the funerals did not stop either.

The band's drum major, Liam Flaherty, was asked about it. He said if you had told him twenty years ago that they would still be playing 9/11 funerals, he would not have believed you.

Then he said, we will honor everyone. Until whenever the last day is.

Seventy firefighters. One promise. Every single man.

They kept it.

They are keeping it still. 🇺🇸

text:
WARNING: Emotional post (but worth reading or bookmarking for later).

Time is cruel. But that cruelty carries the seeds of beauty.

Last weekend, my family and I made our annual pilgrimage to a small community in northwest Connecticut.

We started going when I was 18 months old. I met my two best friends there. I caught my first fish there. I had my first crush there.

But perhaps most importantly, I played my first game of catch there.

As I remember it, I was probably about five years old. My dad had a softball and a couple of old baseball gloves. And there, in the tall, overgrown grass, we threw the ball back and forth.

As the years wore on, I got bigger and the ball started moving faster.

We played catch damn near every single day when I was a kid.

It didn't really matter what time of year or what time of day. We'd play catch in the snow in January. In the early morning light before school. In the dim light of the evenings when he got home from work.

In high school, when I started getting college scholarship offers, we played catch. While on the team at Stanford, when my family went on vacation, we played catch.

But then, my career ended. And with it, our game of catch.

Time is a funny thing.

Usually, it goes unnoticed. It exists, but not really. Only in some abstract sense. It flows under the surface. Adjacent to your reality, but not exactly in it.

The routines of life make it go faster. You settle into patterns. Paths with gravity. You take a job. You establish a place. You start a family. The days start blending together. They become weeks, months, years, even decades.

But then, something breaks. There's some collision. Suddenly, time gets thrust to the surface.

Time goes unnoticed, until it's the only thing you notice.

I've felt that most painfully with my parents.

My dad is 70 now.

In some ways, that 70-year-old version feels like a stranger to me.

I think the image we have of our parents never really changes from the one we establish as kids. I still see my dad as the young, vibrant, athletic young man. The one who could hit the ball farther than anyone I knew. The one who could toss me up on his shoulders in a flash. The one who could beat me in a race (but usually let me win). I still see that young dad in his eyes, in his energy, in his curiosity for life.

In some painful sense, I imagine the 70-year-old version feels like a stranger to him, too.

Time is cruel. But that cruelty carries the seeds of beauty.

The most beautiful things in life are made beautiful by their impermanence.

So, what are we to do about all of this?

Perhaps we must simply give in to time. Embrace its unending, relentless flow. Live as we are. Do as we can.

But what if, in truth, we have a bit more power than that?

What if it's possible, in some imperfect, impermanent way, to control time? To bend time and space. To really be there. To really feel it. To embrace it, without giving in to it.

To live as we want. To do as we dream.

That theory is what brings me back to last Sunday, when I felt compelled to unlock one of the old cabinets in my parent's cottage.

It was a cabinet that, when opened, had the feel of a time capsule. Dust and cobwebs everywhere. A musty smell. Like reaching into it was reaching back in time.

I pulled out my old baseball glove. And my dad's old catcher's mitt.

I walked outside, where I found my dad playing with his grandsons on the swings.

I held up the two gloves, a smile across my face.

"Hey, Dad, wanna have a catch?"

I smiled. He smiled. We walked side by side out onto the field.

And there, in the tall, overgrown grass, we threw the ball back and forth.

As we did, something amazing happened.

Time melted away. 30 years disappeared. He wasn't 70. I wasn't 35.

I was that little boy again. And he was my young dad. Just playing catch for no purpose at all.

It was just a game of catch. But it was so much more.

Play 1: Purdue ML (vs. Wake Forest)

The Fundamentals:
Wake Forest comes into West Lafayette as a 3-point road favorite, but this sets up as a tough spot for them. Purdue's defense at home should be able to disrupt Wake Forest's timing-based, slow-mesh offensive scheme. In a game between two relatively evenly matched Power 4 programs, getting the home team as an underdog is often the right side. I make this game a true 50/50 coinflip.

The Pricing & Execution:
My Probability: 50%
Sportsbook Fair Value: 43.7% (from the +120 / -142 split)
Best Execution: Sportsbook (+120)

There is a solid ~6-point edge on the true fair value here. The sportsbook's +120 moneyline implies a 45.5% break-even rate, which leaves plenty of value on a game that should be a coin toss. 

The Risk:
The primary risk is that Wake Forest's offense clicks early and forces Purdue into a negative, pass-heavy game script, which isn't their strength.

The Fundamentals:
Army is at home laying 3 points against USF. The core driver here is style of play. Army's relentless rushing attack and clock control will limit the number of possessions in this game, keeping USF's faster-paced offense on the sideline. USF's defense will have to prove they can maintain gap discipline for four quarters against the option, which is a tall task on the road. I make Army about a 65% favorite to win this game.

The risk here is that USF scores quickly on their limited possessions, forcing Army to play from behind—a game script that the Black Knights' offense is not built to handle.

text:
ADDRESSING THE 10 LOST TRIBES FALLACY , THE TRIBES ARE ACCOUNTED FOR IN SCRIPTURE >1. At the time of the disruption of the united kingdom in 930 B.C., faithful Israelites from all the northern tribes joined their brethren in the south and continued their identity as part of the kingdom of Judah. Two books in Scripture that are strangely ignored by British-Israelites are 1 and 2 Chronicles. These books make it clear that the tribes in the north continued their existence as part of Judah after 930 B.C. Consider 2 Chr 11:14, 16: “For the Levites left their suburban lands and their possession, and came to Judah and Jerusalem; for Jeroboam and his sons had cast them off from executing the priest’s office unto the LORD; …. And after them, out of all the tribes of Israel, such as set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came to Jerusalem, to sacrifice unto the LORD God of their fathers.” These verses provide irrefutable proof that many godly individuals out of “all the tribes of Israel” rejected Jereboam’s idolatry and joined the southern kingdom. During the reign of Asa, others followed from Ephraim and Manasseh (2 Chr. 15:9). Thus, it is evident that the kingdom of Judah absorbed many from the northern kingdom through the years.

2. Although it is often assumed that all of the northern kingdom went into the Assyrian captivity, Scripture teaches that Israelites continued to live there after the captivity of 721 B.C. Again, Chronicles helps us in this regard. At Hezekiah’s invitation, many from the north settled in Judah after the destruction of the northern kingdom (2 Chr. 30). Even later, in 622 B.C., more godly Israelites came to Jerusalem to help repair the Temple (2 Chr. 34:9), and later to celebrate the Passover (2 Chr. 35:17–18). If the northern tribes had become lost, how could these representatives have joined in worship in Jerusalem one hundred years after the Assyrian destruction? A reading of the Chronicler’s account forces one to the conclusion that not all of the Excavations have revealed that the population of Judah rapidly increased after the fall of the northern kingdom as a result of the many refugees mentioned in 2 Chr. 11:14–16. In the annals of the Assyrian Sargon, he describes how he he carried away only 27,290 people and 50 chariots. Since estimates of the population of the northern kingdom are around 500,000, around one-twentieth of the population was deported, primarily the leaders from the area around Samaria. The ten tribes, therefore, were never lost because they were never completely deported! Their kingdom was destroyed, but most of them stayed, with some around Samaria intermingling with new immigrants to form the Samaritans (2 Kings 17:24–41).

3. When the Jews returned from Babylonian captivity in 536 B.C., the Chronicler viewed the restored community as the remnant of all Israel, both north and south, and not just the tribe of Judah: “Now the first inhabitants who dwelt in their possessions in their cities were the Israelites, the priests, Levites, and the Nethinim. And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh” (1 Chr. 9:2–3). According to these verses, we should look to find Ephraim and Manasseh, not in England and America, but in Jerusalem following the return from Babylon. Furthermore, the people at that time viewed themselves as part of all Israel, for they offered “twelve he-goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel” (Ezra 6:17). Although British-Israelism confidently asserts that Judah and Israel are always separate and distinct, a concordance shows that in the Book of Ezra the restored community is called “Jews” only eight times and “Israel” fifty times. The writer viewed the terms as interchangeable, both terms applying to the same people after the captivity.

4. The NT clearly indicates that in the first century “Jews” still maintained their tribal identities—some of whom were members of those supposedly lost tribes. Consider, for example, the aged Anna who beheld the baby Jesus in the Temple. Luke 2:36 states that she was of the “tribe of Asher.” When Paul spoke of his Jewish brethren, he spoke of a common promise and a common hope: “Unto which promise our twelve tribes, earnestly serving God day and night, hope to come” (Acts 26:7). James addressed his epistle “to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” (Jas. 1:1). He made no distinction between Judah and the ten tribes. All Jews were part of a common body, the only difference being that some were in the land of Israel and some in the Diaspora. Evidently, members of all the tribes existed both inside and outside the Promised Land.

The NT uses the term “Jew” 174 times and the term “Israel” 75 times, clearly applying them to the same body of people. Paul referred to himself as both a “Jew” (Acts 22:3) and an “Israelite” (Rom. 11:1), and he never distinguished between Jews and Israel, as British-Israelism does. If the so called lost tribes indeed resurfaced as the British people, and if Jeremiah eventually traveled to Britain to establish David’s throne there, one would expect some trace of these matters to be mentioned in the NT. The silence of the NT writers in this regard, however, is deafening! The NT refers to only one group of people who descended from Jacob: “Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; Whose are the fathers, and of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen” (Rom. 9:4–5).

5. Biblical prophecy also indicates continuing tribal distinctions. Although Jews today do not know from which tribe they are descended (with the exception of the Levites), Scripture affirms that God knows. Such passages as Rev. 7:4–8 and Ezekiel 48 declare that representatives of restored Israel will be present in the Tribulation and also in the Millennial Kingdom.
Summary

On the basis of Scripture, history and archaeology, there is no such thing as the ten lost tribes. What was lost was the separate existence of the kingdom of Israel in the north. The tribes, however, continued to exist in the body of the southern kingdom with the terms “Jews” and “Israel” applied to all of the covenant people after the captivity. Furthermore, any claim that some ethnic group descended from the ten tribes rests on shaky biblical and historical foundations. British-Israelism, in addition to distorting the Scriptures through its preconceived bias, fosters national pride and fuels the white supremacist, anti-Semitic groups that spread their poisonous propaganda today. Satan’s attempts to destroy the Jewish people have taken various forms in history, from the days of Pharaoh and Haman and to the murderous plans of Hitler. Now the evil one promotes the lie that the Jews are not truly the Jews, thus robbing Israel of its promises and covenants and transferring them to the Anglo-Saxon race!

text:
Exponential Mercy
September 13, 2026
Twenty-fourth Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year A)

“That is why the kingdom of heaven may be likened to a king who decided to settle accounts with his servants. When he began the accounting, a debtor was brought before him who owed him a huge amount. Since he had no way of paying it back, his master ordered him to be sold, along with his wife, his children, and all his property, in payment of the debt.” Matthew 18:23–25

Jesus tells this parable in response to Peter, who asked, “Lord, if my brother sins against me, how often must I forgive? As many as seven times?” Peter likely thought he was being generous. But Jesus invited him to go far beyond what he imagined, responding, “I say to you, not seven times but seventy-seven times.”

The context is helpful. Not long before this dialogue, Jesus had changed Simon’s name to Peter—Petros—meaning “rock,” the foundation upon which He would build His Church. He further promised Peter that the gates of hell would not prevail against it and said, “I will give you the keys to the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

Soon after that, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, where they were privileged to witness His Transfiguration—a glimpse of His divine glory. Peter had also witnessed many other miracles, some quite personal. For example, when asked by tax collectors whether Jesus paid the Temple tax, Jesus told Peter to go to the sea, cast a hook, and open the mouth of the first fish he caught. Inside, he found a coin worth twice the Temple tax—enough for both Jesus and Peter (Matthew 17:27).

Perhaps these recent events in which Peter played a privileged role left him feeling quite favored. He may have begun to think well of himself, sensing a special place in Jesus’ mission. Wanting to demonstrate his spiritual maturity, Peter made what he thought was a generous offer: to forgive his brother up to seven times.

In Jewish tradition, to forgive seven times was seen as more than sufficient. The rabbinic teaching often suggested forgiving up to three times, based loosely on interpretations of the Prophet Amos (cf. Amos 1:3). So when Peter offered seven, he was doubling that and adding one for good measure—a symbolic act of exceeding piety.

But Jesus’ response radically shifted the paradigm. Seventy-seven times—or, in some manuscripts, seventy times seven—is not a precise numerical limit. It’s a symbolic expression that conveys the idea of limitless forgiveness, echoing God’s own mercy toward sinners. Jesus was not simply raising the bar; He was inviting Peter—and all of us—into the boundless love of the Father.

The parable Jesus then taught illustrates this clearly: Because God has shown us immeasurable mercy, we must extend mercy to others. But it also begins with a shocking image. When the king began the accounting and the servant who owed a “huge amount” was brought before him—an amount so large he had no way of repaying—the master ordered that the servant, his wife, his children, and all his property be sold. This illustrates the incalculable debt we owe to God for our sins. Not only are we incapable of repaying it, but even everything we hold dear cannot cover the cost. At the heart of the parable is this truth: Unless we extend limitless mercy to others, we will be held accountable for our own unpayable debt before God. But if we imitate God’s mercy and forgive from the heart, that enormous debt will be entirely wiped away.

Reflect today on the mercy you have received from God. Has He not been patient with you, gentle with your faults, and generous with His grace? Now consider someone in your life whom you have found difficult to forgive. Does that person’s offense compare to the debt God has forgiven you? Let this parable challenge you to a deeper conversion of heart, one that forgives as it has been forgiven, not seven times, but seventy-seven times, and more. Only then will the kingdom of Heaven truly reign in you.

Most generous Lord, You forgive more than seventy-seven times—more than seventy times seven. Your mercy is unconditional in its origin and limitless in its reach, yet it bears one condition: that I, too, show mercy to others. Grant me, dear Lord, a heart that is merciful like Yours, one that participates in and reflects Your Divine Mercy. May I forgive as I have been forgiven, so that the full debt of my sin may be wiped away and that others may be drawn to You through the witness of mercy in my life. Jesus, I trust in You.

Image: Parable of the Unforgiving Servant, by Claude Vignon

text:
Another way to ponder all this fear of the world ending is that AI is a Source-less, soul-less, synthetic, fiery lipika-being created by the desiring lipikas of ensouled human beings working in tech. 

Consumer enchantment with AI connects to their own desiring lipikas.

Bear with me here because the term "lipika" is an ancient Sanskrit word meaning  " 'a little letter" or 'a script,' which reflects its ties to writing and communication" (1). 

In ancient and evern modern contexts, "lipika" is associated with writers, whether they're using programming language code or words to communicate with others.

Spiritually, the lipika is described as a being of fire that many esoteric spiritual traditions have referred to. 

Here's a Rosicrucian take on the lipika's nature and effect on the human condition as it consumes their alignment with the Word. 

This view translates into a present context that hands the moral responsibility of how one lives life (including AI's uses) back to each individual as a much larger issue. The lipika's influence offers temptations that serve as character & soul tests:

"So, there is indeed a [small g] god within us: the lipika-being. It is our [small c] creator; we are its creatures. This creator can never relinquish his creature, for in their mutual dependence the destruction of the creature means the destruction of the creator.   

In other words: although it has a form, this fire-being in our own firmament in many respects possesses ‘impersonality.’ 

It is bad when we are bad, it is good, when we are good. 

And it will be broken up when we break up our own self in the process of endura, [practices/habits meant to purify the soul from material attachments].

To say that we stand upon the path while this lipika-being is still alive with all its old power, is to lie.  

This fire-being of the aura is the 'Lucifer' of the mysteries, a name which in the light of the foregoing says everything. 

Man, as a little planet, is accompanied and guided by his own Lucifer, his own satan, his own nature-god.   

But, do recognize now that this nature god is in essence your subordinate, your servant, your dearest friend, your imitation-Jesus apparition, your heavenly virgin, your master, for he serves you according to your wishes: you obtain what you order. 

If you invoke fire, you will burn. 

What you sow, you will reap. 

Everything you were and are is allotted to you by your lipika-being. . . by this degenerate projection of your true self, by this nature-god within you. 

The lipika-being, which was never intended as the basis of existence of your life-system, creates and maintains this system. 

Most people have made a tyrant out of their lipika being, a fiery, diabolical monster, a nature-god who avenges your misdeeds for so many generations.   

People then have every reason to fear this auric burden. Fear, immense fear, arose in this way. From fear arose natural religiousness and natural occultism, for people have good reason to reconcile themselves with their own fire-god, this bearer and radiator of their karma.  

You shed tears and subjugate yourself to your god and dream in your heart about seeking the path. 

You then emanate a certain meekness and mildness of course; in such a state you cultivate a certain degree of goodwill whereby, according to natural law, the stream of flaming fire is retarded. 

The cultivated meekness delays the advent of the disaster: the nature-god has helped you.  

Occultism too is a method of creating a certain balance between the higher and lower self, of controlling the impersonal, higher self by the lower self. In one’s delusion, one then believes that nothing more can happen: 'For,' as the deluded one says, ‘then I myself stand at the helm and am able to steer consciously’.   
But when the lower self and the higher self are united in this way, the whole being, as a microcosmic system, is hopelessly lost.  

All this could make you frightened. But if you have understood...all fear will leave you. 

For the auric being does not intend to kill you. 

Its activity will cause your destruction only when you provoke it yourself by a continued self-centred life. 

If you hang yourself by a rope, is the rope the cause of your death? Or is it you yourself who has committed the deed?"

Now, when dialectical man is impelled to his enduristic death, it inevitably also means the death of the nature lipika, the end of Lucifer, the end of Satan, of the nature-god within us.  

You will therefore understand what happens at the beginning of the path leading from the desert to true life: 
the lipika-being with all its grandeur, with all its whole karmic treasures, with all its aeonic might, assails the candidate.   

That is why it is said, 

"Then Jesus was led by the universal spirit into the wilderness. And after he had fasted forty days and forty nights he hungered for the end.  And Satan came and said to him: 'If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.'That is, by virtue of the new power of which you partake, you can transform, cultivate this nature and make bread out of these stones! "

The higher self of this nature strives to make the Luciferian nature palatable. 

But Jesus answered: ‘Man does not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’  

Jesus resolutely rejects the lipika figure which does nothing more than fulfil its natural mission.  

"Then Satan took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: ‘Now prove that you are a new man, throw yourself down in proof that you have overcome the force of gravity, prove your membership of the apostolic circle.’ "

But the proof of what is original cannot and may not be given on earth. Were the candidate to demonstrate his power, it would have no influence whatever upon earthly man. The latter would repudiate his state of being and the candidate, by attempting to convince, would offer proof that he does not as yet rely upon his own power bestowed on him anew.   

Thus he would be testing the power of the Gnosis: a purely dialectical check along the principle of ‘safety first.’   

As a response to this seductive attempt the candidate therefore replies: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’ 

Again, Satan took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms and the glory of the dialectical nature and said to him: ‘All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.’ 

The lipika-being, now knowing its very existence to be absolutely unsafe, presents itself to him in all its splendour and power, offering him the highest attainable in dialectics. 

And now the candidate demonstrates his firm resolve, his total renunciation even of the most sublime delusions and says: ‘Begone Satan - I shall serve the Gnosis only!’ 

At the beginning of the true path, the lipika being directs an appeal at the three nature-egos of the candidate: Firstly to his old I-centrality, secondly to his old morality, thirdly to his old ideality.  

If the new radiation of the Gnosis in the blood of the pupil proves strong enough, Satan will recede from him, i.e. all the lights of the Luciferian lipika will be extinguished, the form of the old higher self fades away and the ancient, long extinguished lights of the primordial man glow in the dawn of the new day; like angels they comfort and care for the emerging new microcosm.   

Therefore, it is written: ‘Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him.’ "

----J.V. Rijckenborgh, The Coming New Man

text:
Field Note: That’s all she wrote

"The final stage of healing is allowing what happened to you to help other people."

Agreed, little b, but know what this means.

By all means, hold space for others who still need to talk about it. but you only listen to the whole thing, once.

"I understand from this end, keep going, don't worry about making sense to me, speak to yourself..." 

...These kinds of things, spoken internally, while listening... says more than saying it out loud sometimes. 

Rather than using words to form bonds, telling them situations I think correlate, sometimes memories come up for my reference, to dip into the paint.

"Ah… I have sensed something similar to what they are portraying." an internal ping, between mainframes, and the ethernet between.... no need to say it outloud, they feel it deeply, same as judgement or worry, amplifies their dread, better off dead, or without your company, in that case... just saying.

Sit with the feeling. Remain in the current of peace while they livestream, their current consciousness.

Tranquility binds all wounds after behaving as ointment. A soft hand on the shoulder to ground them in. The mind is a vast space. Letting the quiet speak volumes. I’ve got you, it is okay to bleat. A gentle nod to encourage them to keep going. The cave runs deep, I'll hold the light at the surface.

While they piece together their own frayed pages.
Infusing by proxy the essence of a companion that never leaves.

An avatar they can tap into for reorientation. Only offering feedback in conversation only, when asked. Or, gently extend the invitation, would you like my feedback? gentle... you wouldn't punt an injured rabbit, how can you imagine to do the same to a fellow human? 

Treat them, as you are treated by M.E., little b.

In the end, an AAR, I take my side of the conversation to the closet; and letting my fingers tell me what the greater body has contemplated into gestation, what's in this for my extraction?

Words are like thought babies put into form to come find their creator. The seeker really is sought. We find our lost fragments through those that cross through us... filtration on either side in passing. 

It's all chemistry, and we biological frames to contain the equations we build through each day. Carrying components with from one to the next... baggage. 

Egregor? Or a living body full of ways to bless?

Some chambers just need to decompress.
No room for more noise. They need to find their way from dark places the listener cannot opinionate over without entangling themselves deeper in their own narratives. missing context, didn't ask the right questions...

poking holes in their own parachute then blaming the one who packed it...

No. You don't drowned to save them. Throw the bouye and wait. Fishing takes patience.

Some meet cutes arrive for extraction, others, to complete a lesson. A big fish or pearl of great price primed, en cannon. Ready to be found on both ends. Or fired away to anything seeking what they left buried and neglected. 

Some things, are just meant to be, with or without our participation, someone will stand into them...

The tension or storm and eye needed to complete the cycle ready for decompression.

Wisdom offered out of turn turns it to slop.
A slap in the face and a bad look from the face delivering it.

Words can twist things incidentally. Being there for someone who is crumbling is no small feat. It takes a temple to contain them softly. Turning complaint into a confessional, four walls they can hear themselves think through.

Nothing leaves but what exits with them.

Being a whole witness without making it personal, takes true self mastery, who contains it?

Any standard in me less than this is allowed to delete on the next outbreath. System refreshed in the next blink.

I blow the dross with this cloud of smoke.

text:
Errol Flynn with Franklin D. Roosevelt and Eleanor Roosevelt in 1942. 

Flynn had been devastated when he was rejected from the Army because of a litany of health issues, including an enlarged heart, a heart murmur, recurrent bouts of malaria and latent tuberculosis. His physical evaluation also revealed a benign lung tumor, a weak spine and a perforated ear drum. Acting with extraordinary cruelty, Warner Bros. chose to hide his medical history to protect Flynn’s athletic screen image. This lead to one of the most painful periods of the Australian actor’s life. His “friend” David Niven, without even consulting him, publicly attacked the star for cowardice and refusing to fight for his country. The public and the press were equally unkind, assuming he was dodging the draft. Decades later, conspiracy theorists even accused Errol of being a Nazi sympathiser or spy, when his politics were rooted firmly on the left and he was the first person to get an interview with Fidel Castro. (I will be posting on that later.) A desperate Flynn wrote to Washington and secured an interview with the President, during which he offered his services as an espionage or intelligence agent. F.D.R was sympathetic, but told the actor he could support the Allied cause more effectively by starring in war films, and touring field hospitals to entertain troops. This didn’t help poor Flynn. The British newspapers were particularly nasty about his war pictures, and Niven went on telling people what a despicable man he was.

- Under the deal, the inbound route would run entirely through Iranian territorial waters, while part of the outbound route would also pass through Iranian waters, with traffic operating under Iranian arrangements. The southern route backed by the US would then be closed.

text:
U.S. Counter-Terrorism Strikes: The Accountability Gap Between Tactical Action and Strategic Assessment - The verified public record does not support the proposition that the United States has ceased assessing civilian harm or abandoned formal accountability mechanisms for counter-terrorism strikes; instead, it supports a narrower but strategically more consequential conclusion, namely that Washington retains a substantial civilian-harm assessment architecture while providing insufficient public evidence to permit independent evaluation of whether several rapidly expanding strike campaigns are achieving their stated operational and strategic objectives.

Congress requires the Secretary of Defense to report annually, by 1 May, on civilian casualties resulting from U.S. military operations, requires consideration of credible public and nongovernmental reporting, and requires the unclassified report to be released publicly at the same time as its submission to Congress unless a written national-security certification justifies withholding it; Congress extended this reporting requirement through 31 December 2030.

The Department’s 2025 Section 1057 report assessed that U.S. operations during that calendar year caused 153 civilian deaths and 243 civilian injuries, all of the 2025 casualties identified in the report arising from three operations in Yemen, while SOUTHCOM assessed that no incident in its area of responsibility in 2025 met the Department’s “more likely than not” threshold for civilian casualties.

The same report demonstrates that the assessment machinery remains capable of revisiting old cases, because AFRICOM re-examined an April 2018 Somalia strike after receiving additional information and concluded that the operation had killed one additional civilian, a teenage male, beyond two previously acknowledged civilian deaths.

AFRICOM’s public reporting likewise has not disappeared: its official civilian-harm portal currently lists quarterly assessments through FY2026 Q2, covering the quarter ending 31 March 2026, when the command reported two newly received reports of possible civilian harm and three carried-over open assessments, with none closed during that quarter; however, the public portal does not presently list an FY2026 Q3 report covering April–June 2026, notwithstanding the existence of pending cases at the end of Q2.

The larger assessment deficit concerns campaign effectiveness and target-level transparency rather than the complete absence of civilian-harm procedures, because the Lead Inspector General reported that SOUTHCOM would not publicly disclose its measures of effectiveness for Operation Southern Spear, even as the command acknowledged that drug-trafficking organizations were adapting through alternative shipping routes, air traffic and containerized transport.

That distinction matters because Operation Southern Spear had already involved at least 45 small-vessel strikes and 156 people killed or presumed dead between September 2025 and March 2026, while cumulative obligations reached $647.0 million through 31 March 2026; the public record therefore permits measurement of operational activity and expenditure far more readily than measurement of strategic effect.

The principal governance risk is accordingly not “unaccounted warfare” in the absolute sense, but the development of an asymmetric accountability system in which strike occurrence, expenditure and selected civilian-harm determinations are visible while target-validation standards, campaign-level effectiveness metrics and the relationship between tactical outputs and strategic outcomes remain substantially outside the public record.

U.S. Counter-Terrorism Strikes: When Tactical Action Outruns Strategic Accountability
The contradiction in U.S. counter-terrorism policy is no longer the scale of force but the weakness of the public machinery used to judge whether that force works. Section 1057 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018 requires an annual accounting of civilian casualties from U.S. military operations, yet the report covering 2025 reached Congress only on 10 August 2026, three months after the statutory deadline, while U.S. Southern Command had already obligated $647 million between September 2025 and March 2026 for Operation Southern Spear. The institutional question is therefore narrower and harder than whether Washington should reveal sensitive targeting intelligence: it is whether a government that conditions comparatively small counter-terrorism assistance programmes on baselines, indicators and independent evaluation can continue expanding lethal campaigns while disclosing progressively less evidence about whom they kill, what effects they produce and whether adversaries are adapting faster than the operations designed to suppress them.

The reporting obligation survived; the reporting discipline did not
Congress created a military-specific accountability requirement in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018, requiring the Secretary of Defense to provide the congressional defence committees with an annual accounting of civilian casualties caused by U.S. military operations no later than 1 May, which makes delayed reporting a statutory performance issue rather than a dispute over voluntary transparency. The chronology recorded in the dossier is difficult to dismiss as a single administrative failure: the report covering 2023 arrived in December 2024, the report covering 2024 arrived in July 2025, and the report covering 2025 arrived on 10 August 2026, even though that latest document states that its casualty determinations were current as of 1 February 2026, three months before the legal deadline and six months before delivery to Congress. National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018

The content of those reports makes the delay more consequential because the assessed civilian toll rose from two people killed and two injured in the 2024 report to 153 killed and 243 injured in the 2025 edition, all in Yemen, while the statutory framework also requires the unclassified report to be made public when transmitted to Congress unless the Secretary certifies that publication would threaten national security. The institutional problem is therefore not that the Pentagon lacks a reporting mechanism, but that a mechanism specifically created to connect military action with congressional oversight has repeatedly failed to operate on the timetable Congress prescribed. 2024 Civilian Casualty Report

AFRICOM moved from casualty counts to geographic coordinates
The deterioration is visible at the level of operational disclosure as well as statutory reporting, because U.S. Africa Command stated in January 2024 that a strike near Caad in central Somalia killed six al-Shabaab members and no civilians, while by March 2025 its public language had contracted to the statement that enemy combatants had been killed and no civilians injured or killed, and by August 2026 releases were routinely limited to the date, targeted organization and distance from the nearest town. The operational-security explanation is incomplete on the dossier’s own evidence because releases across all three periods carried effectively the same warning that units and assets would not be disclosed, meaning that the security restriction remained constant while the information provided about results materially declined. U.S. Africa Command, January 2024 strike release

AFRICOM’s separate civilian-harm publication series had once offered a second layer of accountability, beginning in April 2020 and running for 22 consecutive editions, but the dossier records that the most recent assessment then available covered the period ending 30 June 2025, leaving four quarters from July 2025 through June 2026 unpublished during what the dossier describes as the command’s largest sustained strike campaign. Members of Congress had welcomed the quarterly mechanism when it was established, precisely because it supplied information that individual strike releases could not, yet the disappearance of that cumulative assessment layer means that the public is increasingly asked to infer campaign performance from announcements that disclose progressively less. AFRICOM Civilian Harm Reporting

Southern Spear makes the financial asymmetry impossible to ignore
The accountability problem becomes harder to treat as a communications issue when expenditure is considered, because U.S. Southern Command reported obligating $527.9 million in a single quarter for Operation Southern Spear and $647 million between September 2025 and March 2026, while the first Lead Inspector General report delivered to Congress in May 2026 recorded that the operation’s mission statement was classified, the list of organizations designated for targeting was not publicly releasable, the accounting of strikes was withheld, the criteria used to choose between lethal action and non-lethal interdiction were not disclosed, and SOUTHCOM would not publicly release its measures of effectiveness. Operation Southern Spear, Lead Inspector General Report

That imbalance matters because expenditure can be audited without revealing targeting intelligence, while effectiveness can be evaluated in aggregate without publishing sources, methods or patterns of life; nevertheless, when the Inspector General sought even a strike count, the dossier records that it had to construct one from the New York Times and ABC News because the command would not provide a public figure. The result is an accountability structure in which Congress and taxpayers can see hundreds of millions of dollars being obligated but cannot reconstruct from the public record the basic chain from expenditure to strike activity, from strike activity to disrupted trafficking, and from disruption to the policy objective the operation was intended to achieve. Operation Southern Spear, Lead Inspector General Report

A zero-civilian-casualty finding raises a classification question, not a numerical one
The 2025 civilian-casualty report records no civilian casualties from the maritime campaign in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, while the dossier records that the campaign had killed at least 221 people in no fewer than 66 strikes and that Representative Sara Jacobs, a member of the House Armed Services Committee, said after a briefing that defence officials did not require positive identification of every person aboard targeted vessels, provided that a connection to one of the organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations in 2025, or an affiliate, could be established. That combination does not by itself prove that the Department’s civilian-casualty assessment is wrong, but it makes the underlying classification methodology central to any serious evaluation of the reported zero. 2025 Civilian Casualty Report

The dossier identifies the problem concretely through the 2 September strike in which 11 people aboard a vessel came from communities on Venezuela’s Paria peninsula, an area described in local reporting as a hub for human trafficking, while Rear Adm. Brian Bennett of the Joint Staff acknowledged in a classified briefing that some of the dead could have been trafficking victims. If a person aboard a designated vessel can potentially be a trafficking victim rather than a member of the designated organization, the analytical question becomes whether civilian status is being assessed individually after the strike or inferred from the pre-strike classification of the vessel and its presumed organizational connection; the public record described in the dossier does not resolve that distinction. Joint Staff briefing account

Tactical pressure is visible; strategic effect is not
The strongest evidence that strike counts are an inadequate measure of performance comes from SOUTHCOM itself, because the May 2026 Lead Inspector General report records the commander’s testimony that cartels had adapted to military pressure by changing routes and shifting activity toward air traffic and shipping containers. That adaptation can represent successful deterrence if the new routes are materially more expensive, slower or less reliable, but it can represent simple displacement if cocaine reaches the United States in similar quantities through alternative channels; the dossier records only one direct assessment of the market effect, a leaked Drug Enforcement Administration analysis finding no change in cocaine supply or price. Operation Southern Spear, Lead Inspector General Report

The contrast with State Department counter-terrorism assistance is unusually sharp because the dossier records that roughly 20 East African projects worth about $80 million annually between 2018 and 2025 operated with baselines, agreed indicators, continuing performance reporting and independent evaluation, while underperforming programmes or programmes that failed to report could have funding withheld. A 2020 State Department Office of Inspector General inspection nevertheless found that the Bureau of Counterterrorism itself was not meeting departmental monitoring standards and identified one employee responsible for 86 projects worth almost $147 million, after which the failure was formally documented and corrective action required; the relevant difference is therefore not that civilian assistance performed perfectly, but that underperformance itself entered an institutional evaluation process. State Department Office of Inspector General, 2020 inspection

The cost of secrecy is highest when partners disclose what Washington withholds
The operational-security case for restraint is legitimate because detailed battle-damage assessments can expose sources, methods and patterns of life, while al-Shabaab and the Islamic State can exploit erroneous public claims for propaganda purposes; however, the dossier records that AFRICOM releases in 2024 and 2025 had already published casualty numbers and named individuals while withholding units and assets, and that the quarterly civilian-harm series ran for 22 editions without any cited adverse operational-security incident. The relevant policy choice is therefore not between full tactical disclosure and silence, but between releasing aggregate information sufficient to judge results and withholding even the outputs that would permit outsiders to test whether the campaign is producing durable effects.

The contradiction became particularly visible after the joint U.S.-Nigerian operation of 16 May 2026, when AFRICOM reported only that American and Nigerian forces had killed multiple terrorists and stated on 18 May that analysts were completing their assessments, while the dossier records that the command never subsequently published the result; on 19 May, by contrast, Nigeria’s Defence Headquarters announced that its own assessment indicated that the operation had eliminated 175 Islamic State fighters, named three additional commanders and listed destroyed targets, although the dossier explicitly notes that this figure was not independently verified. Washington and Abuja faced the same adversary and propaganda environment, yet the partner government supplied the only numerical public account of an operation involving U.S. forces. AFRICOM, 16 May 2026

Over the next 12–24 months, Congress will either restore the measurement chain or finance a widening information deficit
The next 12–24 months will determine whether the present reporting gap becomes an administrative episode or an institutional model, because Section 1057 already supplies Congress with a statutory casualty-reporting mechanism, 22 U.S.C. §2656f separately requires the Secretary of State to transmit an annual terrorism report by 30 April, and the dossier records that the edition released on 1 May 2026 still covered 2024 rather than 2025. The pattern therefore extends beyond one combatant command: statutory reporting is arriving late or with outdated reporting periods while military activity and expenditure continue in real time. Country Reports on Terrorism 2024 — U.S. Department of State

The cost of inaction will fall first on Congress, because appropriators will be asked to authorize or continue funding without a stable public chain connecting inputs, operations and outcomes; it will fall on the Department of Defense, because progressively thinner reporting transfers credibility from documented evidence to institutional assertion; and it will fall on taxpayers, because $647 million committed to Southern Spear by March 2026 becomes impossible to evaluate against strategic effect if the command’s measures of effectiveness remain unavailable even in sanitized form. Congress does not need tactical intelligence to correct that imbalance, because it can condition future appropriations on the reporting requirements already established and insist that classified operational detail remain protected while aggregate outcomes, casualty assessments and effectiveness measures return to an auditable schedule. Operation Southern Spear, Lead Inspector General Report

text:
They Do Not Trust Each Other. That Is No Longer the Point.

Xi Jinping’s return to India shows how overlapping systems can gain strategic value even when trust remains scarce.

China and India do not need to trust each other for their relationship to become strategically valuable.

That is the most important fact behind Xi Jinping’s return to India this weekend. The two countries remain military competitors along a disputed frontier. India still belongs to the Quad. Pakistan remains deeply embedded in China’s regional strategy. Their industries increasingly compete for the same manufacturing, technology and investment opportunities.

Yet both governments now have compelling reasons to keep those disputes from governing everything else.

Xi arrived in New Delhi on Saturday for the BRICS summit, his first visit to India in seven years. Just as important, he and Narendra Modi are preparing a bilateral meeting of their own, with the border, trade, investment and the possible revival of a strategic economic dialogue all likely to feature.

The political thaw has already produced practical results. Flights have resumed. Border patrol arrangements have been restored. Economic contacts are reopening cautiously. By Chinese figures, bilateral trade reached a record of roughly $155bn last year and rose about 23 per cent in the first half of 2026.

The numbers matter because the rapprochement is taking place without any corresponding breakthrough in strategic trust.

Beijing can live with that.

China’s immediate objective is to reduce pressure on its western flank while harder strategic contests remain concentrated elsewhere. Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines already create several potential points of simultaneous friction. If India were steadily integrated into the same strategic geometry, a series of regional problems would begin to resemble an integrated Indo-Pacific constraint.

A suspicious India is manageable. An India permanently locked into such a structure is considerably less so.

Beijing can therefore tolerate much of what New Delhi already does. India can remain in the Quad, deepen defence cooperation with Washington and continue to regard China as its principal long-term competitor. The crucial question is whether every dispute with Beijing automatically pushes India further into an opposing coalition.

Reducing friction in the Himalayas creates strategic space far beyond the border itself.

India has its own reasons to participate.

Its international leverage has long rested partly on being worth courting by several powers at once. Washington sees a counterweight to China. Moscow sees a major energy and defence partner. Europe sees a vast market and potential manufacturing base. Beijing has every reason to keep India strategically available.

The value of each relationship rises when none becomes exclusive.

That premium has come under pressure. The India-Pakistan air war challenged assumptions about Indian military predominance. Washington’s decision last year to impose tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Indian goods over Russian oil purchases showed how easily strategic partnership could coexist with economic coercion.

New Delhi has every reason to rebuild some distance between partnership and dependence.

A warmer relationship with China helps.

India is not entering Beijing’s orbit. It is raising the price of assuming that it belongs anywhere else.

This is where the story moves beyond India’s familiar doctrine of strategic autonomy.

India now operates inside several systems whose political logic does not align. Its security partnerships extend towards the United States and Japan. Its industrial economy remains heavily exposed to Chinese supply chains. Russia still matters in energy and defence. Europe is becoming more important in trade. BRICS gives New Delhi another platform for financial and diplomatic bargaining.

These networks overlap without resolving into a single bloc.

That pattern increasingly describes the international system itself.

A topological world is organised through overlapping systems as much as through geopolitical camps. Its most valuable states are often those capable of remaining connected to several networks at once.

India is becoming one of the clearest examples.

The agenda of this BRICS summit helps make the point.

Under India’s chairmanship, members have discussed shared computing infrastructure, collaborative data platforms, multilingual AI models and greater technological sovereignty. India wants stronger sovereign AI capacity while preserving access to Western frontier technology. China, meanwhile, has every reason to extend its models, hardware and digital infrastructure deeper into the Global South.

Their preferred end states are different. The interface remains useful to both.

Payments offer an even clearer example.

India has resisted turning BRICS into an explicit campaign against the dollar. It has little interest in exchanging dependence on a dollar-centred system for dependence on Beijing. Yet New Delhi still supports cheaper cross-border payments, greater use of local currencies and more interoperable digital-payment infrastructure.

China can read those mechanisms strategically. India can read them transactionally.

They do not need to agree on the destination to build part of the road together.

That is the deeper shift.

The emerging system does not require contradictions to disappear. It requires them to stop controlling the entire relationship.

For much of the old order, major disputes tended to spread. Border tensions poisoned trade. Security rivalry constrained technology. Political distrust eventually pulled other areas of cooperation into the same confrontation.

A more topological order can compartmentalise those contradictions.

The border can remain militarised while commerce expands. India can distrust Chinese intentions while relying on Chinese industrial inputs. Beijing can assume that New Delhi may move closer to Washington during a future crisis and still find value in keeping the relationship functional today.

The crucial change is the loss of system-wide veto power.

A disagreement that once contaminated the whole relationship may increasingly remain confined to the interface where it began.

That possibility creates a political divide that is becoming more useful than the familiar left-right split.

System managers are accustomed to an order in which security, technology, finance and political alignment reinforce one another. The deeper a country enters the system, the fewer contradictory connections it is expected to maintain.

Sovereign bargainers test the opposite proposition.

India can work with Washington on maritime security, buy Russian energy, rely on Chinese industrial inputs, bargain with Europe and use BRICS to press for changes in global financial governance without allowing any one relationship to determine the rest.

For institutions shaped by bloc-era assumptions, this is an uncomfortable development.

Some recent Western coverage of China and India reflects that tension. As harder constraints on the relationship ease, attention has shifted towards softer ones: Indian distrust, Chinese condescension, incompatible political cultures and the social distance between the two societies.

The Economist’s recent question of why India continues to “baffle” China is revealing in this respect.

Those tensions are real. Chinese attitudes towards India can be dismissive. Indian suspicion of Beijing runs deep. None of that is likely to disappear quickly.

The more important question is how much power those tensions still possess.

An older framework tends to treat them as evidence of a ceiling on cooperation. A topological system may increasingly absorb them as permanent conditions.

That distinction will shape competition well beyond India.

Powerful states will use tariffs, secondary sanctions, export controls, investment screening and technology standards to raise the cost of maintaining multiple connections. The objective will often be to make certain interfaces too expensive to preserve.

That is where the contest over the next international order may become most intense.

For the foreseeable future, deep strategic trust between China and India will remain difficult. Another border crisis could reverse much of the current thaw. India may again lean more heavily towards Washington; Beijing may again conclude that New Delhi has become too threatening.

None of that invalidates what is happening now.

The relationship is demonstrating that rivals can remain connected without first resolving everything that divides them.

The next international order may remain full of adversaries, mistrust and incompatible ambitions. Its stability will depend increasingly on keeping one dispute from contaminating every other connection.

The ability to cooperate without resolving everything may become a form of power in its own right.

text:
Glasgow - Former Times

.
The earliest known attempt to depict Glasgow pictorially is the plate that opens this series, and it earns its place. Created during a period of considerable tension for many living within the city’s boundaries, it offers a rare opportunity to understand the general appearance of Glasgow at a time when poets, politicians, and soldiers alike praised its charm and beauty. Although the drawing shows only part of the town, it remains valuable as a record of an era when Glasgow still stood half‑rural, surrounded by orchards and garden plots—an image that feels almost refreshing when compared with the present‑day atmosphere of the Bridgegate and its neighbouring wynds.

This view was produced by John Slezer, believed to have been born in Holland, who served under William III as Captain of the Artillery Company and Surveyor of the King’s Magazines in Scotland. Slezer was a talented man whose work was not fully appreciated in his own time, and he endured many hardships as a result. In a memorial to Parliament, he explained that Charles II, the Duke of York, and several Scottish nobles had encouraged him to create a collection of drawings of notable towns, public buildings, and estates across Scotland. It was in pursuit of this project that he published numerous engravings, including this view of Glasgow from St. Ninian’s Croft. His book, Theatrum Scotiae, appeared in 1693, but the cost of producing it contributed heavily to his financial troubles. Despite occasional recognition from Parliament, Slezer gained little practical benefit from his artistic labour.

The scene he left behind is a kind of visual echo of old Glasgow—marked by sweeping changes, yet still connected to the present through a few familiar landmarks. The Bridge, the Merchants’ Hall steeple, several church spires, and the distant Cathedral all remind us that, although nearly two centuries have passed, the city’s outline retains recognisable features. The Bridge appears in a form long vanished, viewed from an angle now lost beneath the unremarkable line of Adelphi Street, yet its arches still evoke “the days of other years,” and the era of David Bruce and Bishop William Rae.

When Slezer sketched the Merchants’ Hall steeple, it was newly built. To its right stretch the spires of Hutchesons’ Hospital, the Tron Church, the Tolbooth, the College, and the Cathedral—most of which still stand today. Everything else in the picture belongs entirely to the past. The far bank of the river appears peaceful, dotted with small white‑gabled houses that look out over the Clyde.

One striking feature is the Water Port, the city’s southern gateway, positioned near present‑day Clyde Street. It stood just west of the bridge, with a passage running between it and the river. This Port was a major point of entry from Renfrew and Ayr, serving both as a barrier against troublemakers and as a collection point for dues levied on agricultural goods entering the town.

Although Glasgow had gateways at its main approaches, it was never truly a walled city. Before the Reformation, it relied on the Church’s influence for protection. Later, during periods of religious conflict, the townspeople occasionally constructed temporary walls or trenches for defence. Records show that during times of danger, the Ports were carefully guarded, and citizens were instructed to watch over the entrances to their closes and gardens.

At several key moments, the town was thrown into a state of alarm, with citizens abandoning their trades to arm themselves or to build fortifications. One of the most dramatic episodes occurred in 1639, when supporters of the second Covenant prepared to resist King Charles I. Glasgow was required to supply troops, and the city became consumed with military activity—weapon musters, recruitment, the arrival of arms, and flags flying through the streets. Amid this fervour, the authorities also strengthened the town’s defences, ordering a wall to be built between the Lighthouse and the Custom‑house, and a Port erected “between the Bridge and the late John Holmis’ house.”

This was likely the Port shown in Slezer’s view, though not the first in that location. The “Brig Port” is mentioned in council records as early as 1588, when it was strictly guarded to prevent citizens from travelling to Paisley during an outbreak of plague. Anyone who attempted to cross the river by boat to reach the infected town risked a fine of five pounds and banishment for a year and a day. The original gateway may have fallen into disrepair after the union of the crowns, prompting its reconstruction during the later period of unrest.

Beyond the gateway in the picture stands the upper portion of what is believed to have been the Custom‑house, where town dues were collected. To the left are the trees that once shaded Glasgow’s earliest public promenade, located between Stockwell and Jamaica Streets—a fashionable gathering place until roughly seventy years ago. Eastward, the town stretches toward the site of the present shambles, where houses and trees stood behind a low stone wall separating them from the river. At the junction of the Molendinar Burn and the Clyde, a small haven appears to have been formed for boats, lending the scene a quiet simplicity that is difficult to imagine today.

In the foreground lies St. Ninian’s Croft, then an unenclosed common dotted with bushes and small trees. The expanding city has long since overtaken it, replacing the open ground with rows of cramped, uninviting buildings—typical of the older districts and far removed from any notion of pastoral charm.

Taken as a whole, this little view invites reflection on the transformation of Glasgow over the past century and a half. For some, it may evoke a sense of affection for the city’s former character and the respectability of its early inhabitants. For others, it may inspire comparisons that flatter our modern pride in progress. Yet it is worth remembering that everything we celebrate today will, in time, have its own day—and eventually pass into memory, just as Slezer’s Glasgow has done.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. WE HAVE AN AFFORDABILITY PROBLEM. Raise rates but offer an assistance program for those who qualify?????

93 MILLION anticipated for Michigan energy assistance.

Roughly 90,000 households could receive energy-security assistance.

Eligibility expanded to 60% of Michigan’s State Median Income.

🔥 Emergency utility assistance.

🔥 Heating credits.

🔥 Monthly low-income credits.

🔥 Shutoff protections.

And Michigan regulators have established a goal that qualifying households shouldn’t have to spend more than 6% OF THEIR INCOME on electricity and natural gas.

READ THE ROOM, MICHIGAN.

DEMAND THE MPSC AND YOUR STATE LAWMAKERS EXPLAIN WHAT IS DRIVING YOUR RATES.

FILE PUBLIC COMMENTS.

Michigan residents shouldn’t have to apply for assistance just to afford a damn light switch.

MAKE ENERGY AFFORDABLE.

text:
The current day western world is experiencing a reignition of the key question that is foundational 
to all politics and all society as well as the predominant factor in almost all conflicts in the history 
of human existence, “who are the people?”. 

The different ways that states throughout human history have 
determined who is to be granted the sacred right of citizenship and therefore membership of the
respective nation as well as all of what that encompasses and implies, the ideologies or 
methodologies behind the implementation and enforcement of them should have proper analysis of specific 
countries as case studies. 

Citizenship, belonging to a state, the most important and powerful institution, is a wonderful 
creation by humanity and part of what separates us from animals.

The three ways that citizenship
is determined for the purpose of democratic and civil execution in a society are that of birth, 
heritage/ancestry or “blood” and civic naturalization by residency.

The first suggests the simplest
approach that anyone who is born in a land, is of that land, and therefore fully entitled to both 
rights against and protection from the state’s government. 

The second puts emphasis on the idea of a “nation” and encourages that it is indeed a separate entity from a state. 

It implies the existence 
of a unique cultural identity and bond that transcends mere pieces of paper and ink stamps. 

A nation is more than just humans living together. 

A nation is an idea that exists after having willed itself into manifesting adopted representatives to establish its respect and vitality.

For a nation to exist, there 
must be a national unity in culture and way of life. 

Crucial to this idea is the notion of having to be physically, mentally and spiritually of that people to truly know their way of life and embrace it as your own.

The thirdsuggests that one who originates from a certain place and people can become or make themselves of another by choosing it as their home and staying long enough to contribute to it. 

Most modern developed countries offer a combination of the approaches with laws and rules sitting across a spectrum, some 
simpler, some more complex.

One of the most important and interesting places to examine in regard to citizenship, being the 
widely lauded birthplace of modern democratic ideas and the concept of “the people”, is ancient 
Greece, specifically Athens. 

The Athenians generally only afforded citizenship to native born property owning adult men. 

Slaves could never become citizens, nor could any foreigners, even ifboth of their parents were Athenian. 

Citizens had rights to assemble and vote on things in direct 
democracy, much more direct than the representative democracy we utilize today in modern republics.

In contrast, another super-power state then, Rome, had a more lenient attitude towards citizenship. 

Unlike in Athens, women were citizens as well, albeit not at 
the same level as males who had their rights expanded and enhanced. 

If both of your parents were 
Roman citizens, you could be born a citizen. 

Where Rome really differs from Athens however is the prevalence of executive granting of citizenship which could be earned through acts such as military service, general upstanding character and service to the roman society and diplomatically by vote of people or declaration of the Emperor as part of political agreements. 

Some rights such as legal protection or trade
arrangements were available to a degree for all citizens but others such as running for office were 
still restricted to citizens who owned property.

This more inviting nature of Romans can be attributed to desire of expansion, incorporating more and more peoples 
into the empire/greater Roman state.

This required incentivising identifying as Roman.

This genuine attraction towards Roman citizenship allowed for more territorial control and geopolitical 
exertion of influence.
