C.S. McDonald taught dance and choreographed shows for twenty-six years before turning to writing. She lives with her husband Bill and their dogs on a Thoroughbred farm near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Trump’s people in Ireland this weekend are attending a courtesy call and a golf tournament at a course the family has owned for years. Don Jr. and the grandchildren showed up for an arrival ceremony. text:
🚨 A single British political party, already amplified by a billionaire-funded propaganda channel in GB News, receiving £72 MILLION in 48 hours is not only unprecedented, it’s also profoundly antidemocratic.

Sale of the Century: Two Men, £72 Million, 48 Hours

On Friday 11 September, Ben Delo, co-founder of the crypto trading platform BitMEX, gave Reform UK £36 million, writing in the Telegraph that he wanted “a fair fight and a level playing field.”

On Saturday, Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman already Reform’s largest donor, matched it pound for pound, telling the Daily Telegraph his “competitive spirit” had inspired him to do so.

Nigel Farage said he was honoured and humbled by the confidence shown in his party.

Let’s set this against what the law currently allows a party to spend fighting a general election. A party contesting all 632 seats in Great Britain at the 2024 election faced a national party spending limit of just over £34 million, rising to about £46 million once candidates’ own short-campaign spending is added.

Two men have handed one party, in two days, more than double that £34 million national limit.

None of this money is campaign spending yet, and it only hits any cap if and when Reform deploys it during a future regulated period. But it can be spent for years beforehand on permanent staff, data operations, social media messaging and infrastructure that a spending cap never touches at all.

A donation cap that doesn’t exist

The reason this is legal is that UK election law regulates spending, not giving. Currently, there is no ceiling on what an individual can donate to a party, only a ceiling on what a party can spend once an official campaign period begins. The £72 million doesn’t breach that rule. It exposes how narrow the rule is.

Who is actually giving it

Neither donor arrives with a clean slate. Harborne, who holds dual British and Thai citizenship under the name Chakrit Sakunkrit, has appeared in the Panama Papers on multiple occasions, named as an intermediary or shareholder in offshore entities registered in the British Virgin Islands. No wrongdoing was established from that leak, but it has fuelled years of questions about the transparency of his financial dealings, dealings that now underwrite a British political party.

Delo’s history is more direct. He co-founded BitMEX, pleaded guilty in 2022 to a US Bank Secrecy Act offence for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls, paid a $10 million fine and served probation. In March 2025, Donald Trump granted him a full and unconditional pardon.

There’s no evidence the pardon was granted with this donation in mind, and the plea he entered was for failing to run adequate controls, not for personally laundering money. But the timeline, a US presidential pardon for a Bank Secrecy Act offence followed, eighteen months later, by a gift which was the largest single donation to a UK political party on record (until Harborne matched it the next day), is worth stating plainly rather than glossing over.

Concentration, not participation

This is not the aggregated preference of a mass membership. Research from Democracy for Sale found that, as of late 2025, three-quarters of all Reform’s donations since 2019 had come from just three men, Harborne, Jeremy Hosking and Richard Tice.

That snapshot predates Delo’s 2026 surge, but the underlying pattern it describes, a handful of very wealthy individuals accounting for most of the party’s money, has only deepened since. Two donors writing cheques worth more than a full general election campaign is patronage, not the expression of thousands of individual votes made with wallets.

In a democratic system meant to translate the preferences of an electorate into political power, this inverts the process: a handful of individuals substitute for millions.

Investigations Reform would rather you forgot

The donations land while the party’s finances are under scrutiny on more than one front, though not from either of these donations themselves. The Metropolitan Police is investigating separate matters, including donations linked to Fiona Cottrell, payments routed via a company connected to Richard Tice, and, following a Channel 4 sting, alleged workarounds for taking foreign money. Farage is separately under investigation by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards over an earlier £5 million personal gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP.

Farage and Harborne both deny wrongdoing. Harborne's £5 million personal gift to Farage is the subject of the standards inquiry; Delo is not part of either investigation. But a party already facing live scrutiny into how it handles money receiving a record-shattering sum from two of its biggest backers, publicised for maximum effect, invites the obvious question of what future scrutiny it may attract.

The crypto problem is bigger than Reform

Reform was the first major UK party to start accepting cryptocurrency donations, though this £72 million itself arrived as two conventional sterling gifts, not cryptocurrency. Harborne and Delo made their fortunes in crypto, but neither gift used it.

Separately from this donation, governments and campaigners have flagged the wider industry as a live risk to political finance. Transparency International UK has warned that crypto’s anonymity “could provide a backdoor for foreign interference” in British democracy, and Spotlight on Corruption has flagged the difficulty of tracing crypto funds back to their true source.

The Commons Library’s own briefing notes that a government-commissioned review found “deep reservations” about political donations made in cryptoassets, and the same review, the Rycroft Review into foreign financial interference, led to a temporary ban on crypto donations to UK parties as well as the donor rules discussed below. None of that applies to these two named, sterling, on-the-record gifts. It is the reason regulators are already looking hard at the industry both men made their money in, not a claim about how this particular £72 million moved.

The megaphone already exists

GB News calls itself a news channel. Its weekday mornings still run newsroom-style programmes, but the schedule beyond that is built around opinion and current-affairs shows, several of them hosted by politicians.

Despite not hosting a show since March 2026, Farage has held a primetime slot for years, is due back on air shortly, has earned over £700,000 from the channel since becoming an MP, and holds a declared stake of close to half a million shares in its parent company.

Lee Anderson, Reform’s party chair, presents Lee Anderson’s Real World. Matt Goodwin, who has stood as a Reform candidate, hosts a Friday-night show. Martin Daubney, a former Brexit Party MEP, has a weekday programme. Richard Tice, Reform’s deputy leader, was himself a GB News presenter and remains a frequent guest. Zia Yusuf and other Reform figures, as well as representatives from Tufton Street think tanks not unsympathetic to Reform UK’s policy platform, are also frequent guests.

None of this makes a profit.

GB News is owned by Sir Paul Marshall and the Dubai-based investment firm Legatum, not by Reform, and has been subsidised by them to the tune of well over £100 million just to stay on air.

Regulator @Ofcom has struggled to keep up. It found several politician-presented shows, including one fronted by the then-Conservative MP Jacob Rees-Mogg, in breach of impartiality rules. GB News took that ruling to the High Court and won; Ofcom then dropped its remaining cases against politician-presenters, including one involving Farage’s own show, and is now rewriting the rule rather than enforcing it.

Andrew Neil, the channel’s former chairman, put it plainly in March 2026: its investors “see themselves as in the vanguard of the Reform movement.” That’s not a legal claim about ownership, but a paid presenter’s seat, a declared shareholding, that massive subsidy and the former chairman’s own account of the channel's purpose are more than enough to earn the word propaganda.

The comparison to Fox News, which Neil has drawn, holds for the format (loud, provocative, partisan opinion television), but not for scale (GB News’s audience averages around 90,000 to 100,000 viewers, a fraction of Rupert Murdoch’s Fox News’s) or for one British peculiarity Fox has never copied: sitting MPs in regular, paid, primetime presenters’ chairs.

The donation and the broadcaster are not the same story, but they’re not separate ones either.

Wealthy backers fund the channel that shapes how Reform is covered. Other wealthy backers fund the party the channel is friendliest towards. Neither transaction is capped, declared as campaigning, or weighed against the safeguards that exist precisely to stop concentrated wealth converting directly into political power.

What Big Money buys

American elections offer a useful check on how far to push this argument. In US House and Senate races, the higher-spending candidate wins the vast majority of the time. But that correlation weakens sharply at presidential level: Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Kamala Harris in 2024 both outspent Donald Trump and lost. Money does not reliably buy the result once both sides can raise enough to be heard by voters.

What it buys is what happens before that point: who can afford to run at all; who looks like a serious contender; who can build a permanent campaigning apparatus in the years before any spending cap ever applies.

£72 million doesn’t mean Reform or their donors or supporters have simply bought the next general election. It means a party that didn’t exist in its current form seven years ago has just acquired, in 48 hours, the kind of clout and infrastructure older parties needed decades of subscriptions and affiliation fees to build.

Why this matters

Democratic legitimacy rests on the idea that political influence should track the number of people persuaded, not the size of a donor’s bank balance. Nobody needs to prove that Reform has effectively bought the next election to see the problem.

A system that lets just two men, one who pleaded guilty to a Bank Secrecy Act offence for failed anti-money-laundering controls before being pardoned, the other repeatedly named in an offshore leak, hand a party more than double its own national spending cap in 48 hours, feeding into a party already amplified by a broadcaster it doesn’t own but pays its leader, gives him shares in, and whose own investors treat as their movement’s vanguard, has let the price of competing and the reach of the megaphone stop being set by the electorate.

The £72 million is not evidence of grassroots enthusiasm for Reform, and on private donations since 2021 it doesn’t yet make the party richer overall than Labour or the Conservatives, both of which still lead on cumulative totals. Labour, unlike Reform, also draws on union and Co-operative Party affiliation income on top of its private donations.

In July 2026, the government added a “minimum residency” rule to the existing £100,000 overseas-donor cap, in response to the Rycroft Review into foreign financial interference: anyone returning to live in the UK stays capped at £100,000 a year in donations until they have been back a full calendar year, and reporting on the rule named Harborne and Delo among those it was expected to affect.

Delo has since returned to the UK from Hong Kong, and Reform has accepted his gift as that of a permissible donor. Writing in the Telegraph this week, Delo said he wanted to give Reform £1 million/month until the next possible election in 2029 and had “front-loaded these donations” into the single £36 million payment.

The Electoral Commission has separately modelled what a £100,000 cap, applied to all donors, would have done to money raised between 2020 and 2025: Reform would have lost 72% of it, Labour 71%, the Conservatives 55%, the Liberal Democrats 15% and the Greens 7%. Capped at £100,000 each, the two gifts become £200,000 rather than £72 million.

On the Commission’s 2020–25 figures plus those two new gifts, Reform’s actual running total is about £96 million; under a cap it would be about £7 million.

Those are the stakes in the rule Delo’s own words say he moved to beat. His stated objection was to a residency rule aimed at returning overseas donors specifically, not to donation caps in general, but the practical effect is the same either way: two men judged it worth moving £72 million in 48 hours to get it declared before that rule took effect.

The £72 million is evidence of how little separates wealth from political power in Britain, how easily that wealth converts into power in plain sight, and how urgently the loophole they raced to exploit needs to be closed.

text:
One candle.
One signal.
One of the most powerful reversals in trading.

Let me break down the Dragonfly Doji — and why smart money respects it more than most indicators ever will.

WHAT IS A DRAGONFLY DOJI?

→ Open, High, and Close are at the SAME level
→ Long lower wick, no upper wick
→ Body sits at the very top of the candle
→ Looks exactly like a dragonfly — hence the name

This isn't just a pretty pattern.

It's a battlefield report printed on your chart.

WHAT IT'S TELLING YOU:

During that candle, this happened:
→ Bears drove price aggressively lower
→ They pushed hard, looked in control
→ Then buyers stepped in with force
→ Price was driven ALL the way back up
→ Candle closed at the open price

Translation:

Bears tried. Bulls rejected everything.

The longer the lower wick, the more brutal the rejection.

WHERE IT MATTERS:

A Dragonfly Doji means nothing in the middle of a range.

It becomes powerful when it appears at:

① Key Support levels
→ Price tapped a level institutions care about
→ The rejection happened exactly where it should
→ High probability the level holds

② Demand Zones / Order Blocks
→ Smart money loaded positions here
→ Dragonfly confirms they defended the zone
→ Bears got absorbed completely

③ After an extended downtrend
→ Sellers exhausted
→ Buyers stepping in fresh
→ Momentum about to rotate

④ At HTF liquidity pools
→ Stop losses below got swept
→ Liquidity collected
→ Engine now has fuel to reverse

HOW TO TRADE IT:
Entry:

→ Next candle opens bullish after the Dragonfly
→ Enter on confirmation, not anticipation
→ Or enter at the close of the Dragonfly in strong zones

Stop Loss:
→ Below the low of the lower wick
→ Below the Dragonfly tail
→ If price breaks the wick low, the signal failed

Take Profit:
→ Previous structure high
→ Next liquidity pool above
→ FVG or OB overhead that hasn't been filled

Risk:Reward:
→ Dragonfly Doji setups consistently offer 3:1 minimum
→ At key HTF levels, 5:1 to 8:1 is common
→ The wick gives you a precise invalidation point

THE PSYCHOLOGY BEHIND IT:
Most traders see a long red wick and think weakness.

Smart traders see a long red wick with a close at the top and think:

"Someone defended this level with serious capital."

That's not retail money pushing price back up.

Retail was selling that wick.

That's institutional buying absorbing every single sell order until there was nothing left to sell.

The candle is the receipt.

WHAT MAKES IT FAIL:
→ Appearing in a choppy, ranging market with no clear structure
→ No volume confirmation behind it
→ Occurring at a random level with no confluence
→ Ignoring the higher timeframe trend direction

A Dragonfly Doji at a random price level is just noise.

A Dragonfly Doji at a 4H Order Block after a liquidity sweep during a BOS?

That's a setup.

THE SIMPLE CHECKLIST:

✅ Appears at a key structural level
✅ Lower wick is long and decisive
✅ Close is at or near the open/high
✅ HTF trend supports a bullish reversal
✅ Confluence with OB, FVG, or Demand zone
✅ Next candle confirms bullish momentum

All 6? Size up.
3 or less? Pass.

One candle can change your entire trade.

Because it reveals exactly what institutions did at that level — and gives you the blueprint to follow them.

The market leaves clues on every single candle.

Most traders just don't know how to read them.

Now you do.

Which reversal candle do you trust most in your trading?

text:
Revelation 8 deepens the picture. After the seventh seal is opened, “there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour.” The worshipping host falls silent. Seven angels receive seven trumpets, and another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer. Incense is offered with “the prayers of all saints,” and the smoke ascends before God. The angel then fills the censer with fire from the altar and casts it into the earth, producing voices, thunderings, lightnings, and an earthquake. The prayers that rose from suffering saints return to earth in the form of judgment. The world calls prayer useless because the world judges everything by immediate appearances. Heaven keeps accounts longer than the world keeps attention. A prayer may seem to disappear into the ceiling, but Revelation shows it reaching an altar. A martyr may die while his persecutor celebrates, but Revelation shows the prayer preserved until the fire falls. God may delay His answer, but He never misplaces the request.

The same heavenly command structure continues through the trumpets and vials. Angels sound, announce, restrain, release, reap, and pour. Revelation 10 presents a mighty angel with a little book. Revelation 11 announces the kingdoms of this world becoming the kingdoms of Christ. Revelation 14 sends angels through Heaven with proclamations concerning the everlasting gospel, Babylon, the Beast’s worshippers, and the harvest of the earth. Revelation 15 shows seven angels receiving the seven last plagues, while Revelation 16 begins with “a great voice out of the temple” commanding them to pour out the vials of God’s wrath. The judgments are neither accidental natural disasters nor random outbursts of cosmic violence. They are measured operations issued from the heavenly sanctuary. The Beast can sign decrees, and the False Prophet can enforce an image, but they are working on borrowed time. The Tribulation is not managed from Babylon, Rome, New York, Brussels, or Jerusalem. It is governed from the throne of Almighty God.

5. “What Are These Which Are Arrayed in White Robes?” — Saints Arrive in Heaven

The raptured Church is not the only redeemed company seen in Heaven during the Tribulation. Revelation 6:9–11 shows souls under the altar who have been slain “for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held.” Revelation 7 then shows “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They wear white robes, carry palms, and cry, “Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb.” One of the elders asks John who they are and where they came from. The answer is explicit: “These are they which came out of great tribulation.” They are not the Church renamed. The Church has already been caught up under the pre-Tribulation chronology. These are people saved in connection with the Tribulation who suffered on earth and now appear before the throne. The distinction matters because if every saved group in Revelation is carelessly called “the Church,” the entire prophetic map turns into a bowl of theological oatmeal.

Welcome to the post-Western weapons market
Moscow showcased more than 500 products in Egypt as foreign buyers searched for weapons built for real war
Published 12 Sep, 2026 
By Dmitry Kornev, military expert, founder and author of the MilitaryRussia project
https://t.co/h5yRI6Gdsz
The second El Alamein International Airshow took place on September 8-10 at El Alamein International Airport in Egypt. The airshow reaffirmed its status as one of the premier military exhibitions in North Africa and the Middle East. Its international prestige was confirmed by the list of participating nations; the organizers succeeded in bringing together fierce rivals – the leading players in the global defense industry from Russia, the US, China, and Europe.
The airshow’s target audience included defense officials, military commanders, government delegations, and the business elite. Overall, it attracted over 250 exhibitors from 50 countries. More than 12,000 industry professionals visited the stands and displays. The roar of jet engines shook the skies over the Mediterranean Sea as aerobatic teams from Egypt, the UAE, and Türkiye, as well as renowned Russian aerobatic pilots, performed complex maneuvers and showcased their skills. Meanwhile, on the ground, multibillion-dollar contracts were signed.
Why sanctions failed to sideline Russia
Russia’s participation was a distinctive feature and highlight of this year’s airshow. Perhaps the largest and most compelling display was mounted by Russian arms exporter Rosoboronexport (part of the Rostec state corporation). In total, Russia showcased over 500 military-grade products at El Alamein.
The key geopolitical and marketing takeaway from the event was clear: Despite unprecedented sanctions pressure from the West, the Russian defense industry not only maintains its position but also generates huge interest among global players.
Foreign delegations lined up at the Russian exhibit. The reason for this intense interest was pragmatic: Russian weaponry has proven its effectiveness in actual high-tech combat scenarios. The performance characteristics of Western systems are often exaggerated in marketing brochures, while their costs are exorbitantly high; however, Russian equipment has undergone real-world testing against modern reconnaissance, electronic warfare, and air defense systems (including in the zone of Russia’s military operation).
Buyers from around the globe – from the Middle East to Latin America – also appreciate the fact that Moscow offers fair contract terms, free from political blackmail or ideological demands. Historical continuity also plays a major role; many so-called ‘Third World’ countries have traditionally relied on Soviet and Russian weaponry and are familiar with it. Consequently, many of these countries are unwilling to trade reliable Russian equipment for pretty ‘toys’ from other manufacturers.
Combat experience reshapes Russia’s export arsenal
What did Russia showcase at the El Alamein airshow? The star of both the static display and the flying display was the Russian Su-57E fifth-generation multi-role fighter jet. The aerobatic performance by Sukhoi Company chief pilot, Hero of Russia Sergey Bogdan, demonstrated the unsurpassed aerodynamics of modern aviation technology. The aircraft embodies a rich legacy of excellence: Unique aerobatic maneuvers combined with powerful missile and electronic warfare capabilities define the modern Su-57. It carries a new generation of weapon systems – specifically, missiles housed in internal bays. text:
$DHT $FRO $INSW $LPG $BWET VLCC CONCENTRATION RANKING ACROSS THE TANKER PEER GROUP

Based on the data retrieved from company filings (as of Q2 2026), here is the VLCC concentration ranking across the listed tanker peer group.

THE RANKING IS UNAMBIGUOUS

1. DHT Holdings (100%) — The only pure-play VLCC company in the listed universe. All 23 vessels are VLCCs. This is what makes DHT the cleanest single-instrument expression of VLCC spot rate moves, even if INSW has higher per-share EPS sensitivity due to its smaller share count.

2. Frontline (52%) — 40 of 77 vessels are VLCCs, with the remainder split between Suezmax (19) and LR2 product tankers (18). The largest absolute VLCC fleet among listed peers.

3. CMB Tech (~21%) — Only 4 VLCCs in a fleet increasingly oriented toward Suezmax and alternative-fuel vessels (ammonia, hydrogen carriers). VLCC exposure is marginal to the overall earnings story.

4. NAT, TNK, TK (0%) — No VLCC exposure. NAT is a pure Suezmax play; Teekay Tankers operates Suezmax and Aframax; Teekay Corp is a holding company.

INSW's VLCC count (~13 vessels) is not yet confirmed from filing data, but based on company disclosures it would place INSW at approximately ~35–40% VLCC by fleet count — between FRO and CMBT. Its per-share earnings leverage remains the highest in the group due to the small share count, regardless of fleet concentration percentage.

BOTTOM LINE

DHT is the highest VLCC-concentration name by a wide margin (100%), followed by FRO (52%). For a PM wanting maximum fleet-level purity to VLCC spot rates, DHT is the clearest expression — though FRO offers greater absolute earnings scale.

DHT HOLDINGS: DOES 100% VLCC CONCENTRATION HELP EARNINGS GOING FORWARD?

The short answer is yes, materially — but with important nuances around the direction of rates, booking strategy, and the 2027 normalization risk. Here is the full picture.

CURRENT EARNINGS MOMENTUM: 100% VLCC = MAXIMUM RATE CAPTURE

In Q2 2026, DHT's spot VLCCs earned an average of $162,600/day, with the combined fleet (spot + TC) averaging $126,700/day. Adjusted EBITDA rose to $231M from $69M a year prior — H1 2026 earnings already surpassed DHT's previous full-year record.

DHT's P&L breakeven is $29,700/day and cash breakeven is $23,400/day. With VLCC spot rates currently at ~$579K/day (as of September 11), the company is generating extraordinary discretionary cash flow above breakeven.

Because every vessel in the fleet is a VLCC, there is no drag from lower-earning Suezmax, Aframax, or product tanker segments — unlike FRO (which blends in LR2s) or CMBT (which blends in Suezmax and alternative-fuel vessels). Every dollar of VLCC rate upside flows directly to the consolidated P&L.

Q3 2026 FORWARD BOOKINGS: LOCKING IN ELEVATED RATES

For Q3 2026, DHT has booked approximately 48% of available spot days at $139,700/day, with overall fleet coverage (spot + TC) at 74% of available revenue days at $94,300/day.

DHT is deliberately increasing spot exposure — targeting approximately three-quarters of capacity in the spot market — to capitalize on the elevated rate environment while developing new time-charter contracts at improved rates.

In July 2026, DHT locked in a three-year time charter for the DHT Jaguar at $75,000/day, commencing September 2026 — a strategically timed TC that secures above-historical-average income on one vessel while keeping the rest spot-exposed.

CONSENSUS EARNINGS TRAJECTORY

Note the sharp step-down in consensus: full-year 2026E EPS of ~$4.04 compresses to ~$2.12 in 2027 — a ~47% decline — reflecting the market's expectation of partial rate normalization. Q3 2027E is the trough, implying analysts are pricing in a significant softening in VLCC spot rates by mid-2027. Given that Q3 2026E was set before the September 11 Saudi pipeline attack and the current $579K/day VLCC spot level, Q3 2026 consensus likely has meaningful upside if current rates are sustained through quarter-end.

STRUCTURAL TAILWINDS SPECIFIC TO VLCCs

VLCC spot rates, which were around $161,000/day in mid-July 2026, were projected to stay above $80,000/day through late 2026, supported by structural factors and geopolitical risks — even before the September escalation.

The VLCC market is undergoing structural transformation driven by strong demand, geopolitical volatility, an aging global fleet, and significant consolidation. DHT is positioned to benefit from fleet renewal and newbuildings delivering into a strong market.

A potential longer-term catalyst: sanction releases and trade normalization could shift volumes from the shadow fleet to compliant operators like DHT, adding incremental demand for Western-flagged VLCCs.

Solid fundamentals are expected to continue bolstering crude tanker earnings heading into 2027, even in a partial normalization scenario.

DHT's record Q2 results and strong forward bookings indicate that VLCC earnings can remain elevated even with potential increases in traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — the company's earnings power is not solely dependent on the chokepoint remaining fully closed.

KEY RISKS TO THE CONCENTRATION THESIS

Symmetrical downside: 100% VLCC concentration cuts both ways. If Hormuz reopens and rates normalize sharply, DHT has no lower-earning but more stable segments to cushion the decline — unlike FRO's LR2 exposure or CMBT's diversified fleet.

Fleet avoidance of Persian Gulf: During the current conflict, DHT's fleet has avoided trading in the Persian Gulf, rerouting through the Suez Canal and adding significant transportation distances. This limits direct Hormuz exposure but also constrains the volume of Middle East crude DHT can lift.

Insider selling: DHT's Chartering & Operations officer sold $525,000 of shares on September 4, 2026 — a modest but notable signal at current elevated price levels.

Fleet growth constrained: DHT acknowledges that current secondhand VLCC values make acquisitions challenging, emphasizing patience. The company has ordered only one additional VLCC for delivery in August 2028.

SELL-SIDE POSITIONING

Consensus stands at 7 Buy / 3 Hold / 0 Sell across 10 analysts, with a consensus price target of $21.62.

Options market: DHT call volume on September 11 was 1.8x normal, with a put/call ratio of just 0.11 — directionally bullish positioning. December 2026 $24 calls and September 2026 $22 calls were the most active strikes.

Next earnings expected: October 28, 2026.

text:
$FRO  $INSW  $LPG  $BWET  RED SEA & STRAIT OF HORMUZ: IMPACT ON GLOBAL TANKER DAY RATES

The simultaneous disruption of both the Strait of Hormuz (Iranian-controlled) and the Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb (Houthi-controlled) has created an unprecedented dual-chokepoint crisis, eliminating the two primary energy export arteries from the Middle East and driving crude tanker spot rates to historic highs. As of this morning, the situation has intensified further: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline — the last meaningful bypass route for Hormuz — was shut on September 11 following drone attacks launched from Iraq, while Houthi forces are reportedly advancing on Mokha near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

GEOPOLITICAL BACKDROP

Strait of Hormuz: Daily transits plunged 97% in August 2026, with a network of stealthy crude tankers managing to restore flows to only roughly half prewar levels via shuttle runs to ports outside the chokepoint by end of August. Iran and Oman have reportedly reached an agreement in principle on a proposed shipping lane through the strait, with a joint statement in final drafting — but Iran is seeking transit fees, which European nations reportedly now accept as inevitable.

Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb: Houthis have enforced a blockade, turning back vessels bound for Saudi ports. Nippon Yusen has stated its earnings outlook assumes Cape of Good Hope rerouting continues throughout FY2026 (ending March 2027).

Saudi East-West Pipeline: Shut as of September 11, eliminating the primary overland bypass that allowed Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea without transiting Hormuz.

IEA Assessment: A recovery in Middle East oil flows is now expected to stretch into 2027, with global oil demand cut to 102.4 mb/d in 2026 (down 2.5 mb/d from prior forecast).

CRUDE TANKER DAY RATES

The Hormuz disruption obstructed approximately 20–25% of global seaborne crude oil trade in H1 2026, causing historical highs in crude tanker earnings across all vessel classes.

VLCC spot rates on the TD3C benchmark route (Middle East Gulf to China) reached $218,154/day on February 27, 2026, then surged above $423,000/day in early March as the Hormuz closure took hold, before reaching a new high of $579,443/day as of September 11 — coinciding with the Saudi pipeline attack.

Commercial shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz decreased by over 85% at peak disruption.

The displacement effect from VLCCs concentrating on long-haul routes to Asia has indirectly tightened the Suezmax and Aframax markets, lifting demand and freight rates for smaller tanker classes.

Time-charter rates in H1 2026 increased 74% year-over-year for Aframax crude tankers, significantly above the ~10–20% YoY growth that had been forecast.

PRODUCT TANKERS (MR, LR1, LR2)

The product tanker market has been supported by refinery dislocations caused by the Hormuz disruption, with LR2 vessels switching into dirty trades (crude carrying), tightening clean tanker supply.

MR tanker time-charter rates increased 38% YoY in H1 2026, well above prior forecasts.

Handy chemical tanker TC rates rose 32% YoY in H1 2026.

Security risks around Hormuz and Red Sea avoidance have lengthened shipping routes and tightened vessel availability, pushing freight rates higher across clean tanker segments.

Escalating hostilities caused shipping costs for refined products to increase by nearly 20% to East Asia and 40% to East Africa within a short window, with several tanker owners pausing new vessel offers due to regional uncertainty.

Hull and machinery insurance for ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz increased from 0.125% to 0.2% of ship value.

It is worth noting that prior to the Hormuz escalation, the product tanker market faced structural headwinds: supply growth was projected to outpace demand by 630 basis points in 2026, and MR tanker rates from the Middle Eastern Gulf to Singapore had already declined 48% on average in 2025. The geopolitical shock has overridden these fundamentals, at least in the near term.

LNG CARRIERS

Approximately 20% of global LNG supply originates from Qatar and the UAE, relying on unobstructed passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Any restriction or halt in tanker traffic could force major LNG buyers such as China to rely on the spot market.

The LNG carrier market in 2026 remains mixed — carriers are under pressure from a period of vessel oversupply, but the Hormuz disruption has added significant volatility, impacting LNG and LPG flows from Qatar and the wider Gulf.

The LNG carrier market was expected to see a 19% structural surge in tonne-miles in 2026 driven by new supply coming online, but the Hormuz closure has disrupted the realization of that demand.

Disruptions through Hormuz — through which 20% of global LNG trade passes — could cause supply chain disruptions similar in magnitude to the Red Sea situation in December 2023.

REROUTING: TONNE-MILE IMPACT

The Cape of Good Hope detour adds 15–20 days per voyage versus Suez Canal routing. Hormuz transit was down 97% in August 2026, while Suez Canal crossings were up 37% in August as rerouted flows bypass Hormuz via Red Sea alternatives. Rerouting from the Red Sea/Suez crisis has increased voyage distances by 30–50% overall. These longer voyages absorb vessel capacity, structurally tightening supply across all tanker classes.

The tanker freight market is expected to remain firm through the remainder of 2026, supported by ongoing geopolitical disruptions and structural shifts in global oil trade flows that have significantly increased tonne-mile demand.

FORWARD RATE OUTLOOK

Bull case (escalation): Oil tanker spot rates are projected to surge approximately 37% to $300,000/day by October if Hormuz tensions escalate, driven by a prolonged recovery and a shift to long-haul Cape of Good Hope routes.

Base case (slow normalization): VLCC spot rates are expected to end 2026 in the $90,000–$110,000/day range, supported by a significant backlog of vessels awaiting Hormuz passage and a global effort to rebuild depleted energy inventories.

Reopening scenario: A full Hormuz reopening with fast production recovery could trigger a race to book shipping capacity, driving a sharp increase in Gulf shipping rates as the market shifts from "low volume + high rates" to "high volume + high rates."

Bear case (2027 normalization): If shipping activity normalizes, tanker rates could decline approximately 30% from current levels.

Important caveat: A complete and sustained Hormuz closure would likely be net-negative for tanker rates, as the volume loss would not be offset by longer-distance routes — with VLCCs being the most impacted segment.

The key variable for the remainder of 2026 is whether the Iran-Oman Hormuz deal is finalized and what transit fee regime emerges. The Saudi East-West pipeline attack this morning eliminates the primary bypass option and raises the stakes materially for any near-term resolution.

text:
A very interesting short story: A very interesting short story: AITA for not wanting to go a childfree wedding

My husband's cousin is getting married this year and is having a child free wedding.  We have two kids under 4.  I don't want to go for a variety of reasons.  

1.  We are covering the travel costs of his parents and the 4 of us already.  Including flights (3k one way), car $300, hotel $500, food, sitter care for a 2 day wedding is north of $600.    This is for a 4 day trip

2.  I don't feel comfortable leaving my kids with an unknown nanny even vetted by an agency.   The reviews are hit and miss and I dont have or know anyone in that city.   If anything happened to them because of a party, I would regret this forever.  When we've previously had similar situations, sitters were vetted by friends in those towns. 

3.   The venue is in the middle of nowhere.  The nearest hotel is over 30 min drive away. Theres no where closer to put the kids 

4.  Culturally its unheard of to not have kids at a wedding.  Enough that it didn't even occur to him that it was childfree until I had him ask his family.   

5.  Its a pain in the ass to drag 2 kids on a 3h+ flight and another 1h drive each way so they can marinate in a room.  

I offered to stay home alone with the kids, daycare, and my army of sitters.  I offered to stay at the hotel for the duration of the wedding and the 3 of them could go.   Its led to multiple huge fights where he accuses of me being unreasonable.   

I think they are entitled to whatever wedding they want.  What they arent entitled to is requiring me to attend.  I feel like I've given every reasonable option and he is refusing to budge.  

I ran this through a few friends and he thinks they're biased so I posted here for an unbiased opinion.  

Background.  Some of it is because he and his parents feel indebt to that side of the family for all their help early in his career.  His parents aren't happy about it but haven't pushed the issue. He is otherwise a great father and usually very reasonable.  

EtA. His parents live with us and help watch the kids.  They're lovely and we are glad to cover their trip.  

#fyp

text:
She volunteered to grow Britain’s food. Britain rejected her for being Black — DISGRACE!

Amelia King was a box maker from Stepney who wanted to swap factory work for Britain’s wartime fields.

In 1943, she applied to the Women’s Land Army. The Essex committee turned her away.

The Land Army placed women with farmers and found them somewhere to live. Officials said both would be “extremely difficult” in Amelia’s case because of the colour of her skin. They advised her to choose other war work instead.

That answer carried a bitter insult. Amelia’s father was serving in the Merchant Navy. Her brother was in the Royal Navy. They were accepted for dangerous work, while she was judged unacceptable for a harvest.

Her rejection did not stay private.

Campaigners organised meetings. Newspapers carried the story. A Holborn Trades Council leaflet put Amelia’s face beneath the words: “They tried putting a colour ban on harvests.” Her MP, Walter Edwards, demanded an answer in the House of Commons.

The Minister of Agriculture defended the decision. The problem, he said, was not Amelia’s willingness. It was the supposed difficulty of persuading a farm and a household to take her.

Then people proved that excuse wrong.

In Hampshire, farmer A. E. Roberts offered Amelia work at Frith Farm. The women already working there said they were wholeheartedly ready to welcome her. A village household offered the lodging that officials had claimed would be so difficult to find.

Public pressure had turned one rejected application into a test of what Britain’s wartime appeals to service really meant.

Weeks after the refusal was challenged in Parliament, ministers returned with a different answer. Amelia’s enrolment was expected that very week. Once placed, they confirmed, she would receive the same Land Army uniform as the other women.

She joined and worked at Frith Farm, then later transferred to the London and Middlesex branch. Her service ended on medical grounds.

The surviving Land Army card records the work she finally did. Yet the Essex files do not record the discrimination that tried to stop her.

The refusal is missing from the official account. Amelia’s service is not.

text:
If you ask any car enthusiast which prewar American manufacturers offered supercharged cars and the answer is almost always the the same: Duesenberg. Auburn. Cord. The most prestigious names of the 1930s. The cars that cost more than houses. The cars that movie stars and bootleggers drove. What nobody says is Graham. And Graham built more supercharged cars than Duesenberg, Auburn, and Cord combined. Between 1934 and 1941, Graham-Paige Motors Corporation of Evansville, Indiana, produced more supercharged automobiles than all other American manufacturers put together. The company that nobody remembers owned the technology that everybody credits to someone else.

Floyd F. Kishline was Graham's assistant chief engineer. He was friends with Louis Switzer, the supercharger pioneer whose Switzer-Cummins company had built the centrifugal blower systems for Duesenberg and Auburn. Kishline adopted the same general centrifugal layout but reengineered it for bare minimum cost. The Duesenberg supercharger sat on a car that cost $15,000 in the middle of the Depression. Kishline's supercharger sat on a car priced in Oldsmobile territory: $750 to $1,330. The engineering challenge was not building a supercharger. Switzer had proven that worked. The challenge was building a supercharger cheap enough that a middle-class buyer could afford it. Kishline solved it.

The 1934 Supercharged Custom Eight was first. A conventional L-head flathead straight-eight displacing 265.4 cubic inches. Normally aspirated: 95 HP at 3,400 RPM. With Kishline's centrifugal supercharger at a conservative 3.5 PSI of boost, the impeller is spinning at 23,000 RPM (5.75 times crankshaft speed): 135 HP at 4,000 RPM. Forty additional horsepower from 3.5 pounds of boost. The blower both lifted and extended the power range, giving the Graham acceleration that the naturally aspirated version couldn't match and a top speed approaching 90 mph. The supercharger option added approximately $170 to the list price. The complete Supercharged Custom Eight started at $1,295. America's first moderate-cost supercharged car.

When Graham dropped the straight-eight after 1935, Kishline transplanted the supercharger to the company's L-head inline-six engines. The unit moved from the right side of the engine to the left with a belt drive added, but the operating principle was identical. The supercharged 217.8 cubic inch six made 116 HP. The supercharged 199.1 cubic inch six made 106 HP. By 1941, the final Graham supercharged six made 124 HP at 4,000 RPM. A supercharged flathead six making 124 HP in 1941, the same year the Slant Six's ancestor was still two decades away and the overhead-valve revolution hadn't reached most manufacturers. Graham was using forced induction on flathead sixes while the rest of the industry was still debating whether overhead valves were worth the manufacturing cost.

The Graham supercharger used the same centrifugal principle that every turbocharger mentioned so far uses: a spinning impeller accelerates air through a housing and delivers it at higher pressure than atmospheric. The difference is the drive method. A turbocharger spins from exhaust gas energy. Kishline's centrifugal blower was driven mechanically from the crankshaft through the water pump drive, spinning the 7.5 inch impeller at 5.75 times engine speed. No exhaust plumbing required. No lag. Boost proportional to RPM. The same operating principle that the Paxton and Vortech centrifugal superchargers use on modern V8s traces directly to the Switzer-Cummins and Kishline designs of the 1930s. The aftermarket centrifugal supercharger industry started here. Not with a V8. With a flathead six in a car priced like an Oldsmobile.

Graham's "sharknose" styling of 1938 gave the company its most distinctive visual identity: a dramatically protruding grille that the public either loved or hated. The supercharged sharknose could reach 50 mph in 10.9 seconds and returned up to 25 mpg on the highway. Performance and fuel economy from a supercharged flathead six in 1938. The combination sounds modern because it is modern. Graham was doing in the 1930s what Buick would do with the turbocharged 3800 Grand National fifty years later: adding forced induction to a six-cylinder for performance that embarrassed larger naturally aspirated engines. The Grand National gets the credit. Graham got there first. By five decades.

Graham-Paige ceased automobile production in 1940. Kaiser-Frazer acquired the automotive assets in 1947. The company that built more supercharged cars than everyone else combined disappeared into corporate consolidation. Auburn is remembered. Cord is remembered. Duesenberg is the name that defines prewar American luxury. Graham is forgotten. Despite building more blown cars than all of them put together. Despite pioneering affordable forced induction. Despite proving that a supercharger didn't require a $15,000 price tag. Graham put a centrifugal blower on a car that a factory worker could finance and made forced induction democratic twenty years before the hot rod community discovered surplus GMC 6-71 blowers.
